Option D Correct Feedback: Argument II is strong because it highlights a valid, practical negative impact on needy students.

title: Statement: "Ensure good Slight's sleeps for your family with safe
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
text:
Statement:
"Ensure a good Slight's sleeps for your family with safe and effective X mosquito coil." - An advertisement.

Assumptions:

I. X mosquito coil is better than any other mosquito coil.

II. A good night's sleep is desirable.
solution: The statement mentions the good qualities of X coil but this does not mean it is the best. So, I is not implicit. Besides, an advertisement highlights the feature which is desirable by customers and can lure them. So, II is implicit.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The advertisement says the X mosquito coil is safe and effective, but it does not claim that X is better than every other mosquito coil. That is an unwarranted stronger conclusion. The statement does, however, assume that a good night's sleep is desirable, which the ad appeals to.

Correct. The ad implies that a good night's sleep is desirable because it promises to help the family sleep well. It does not assert that X is superior to all other mosquito coils, so the claim that X is better than any other is not implied.

Incorrect. This choice suggests an either/or, but the advertisement actually implies the desirability of a good night's sleep while it does not imply that X is better than every other coil. Therefore the correct inference is that only the desirability of good sleep is implicit.

Incorrect. The advertisement does imply that a good night's sleep is desirable—this is the benefit it promises—so it is not true that neither assumption is implicit. However, the ad does not imply that X is better than all other coils.

title: Statement: "Z-T.V, the only T.V. which gives the viewers chance
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
text:
Statement: "Z-T.V, the only T.V. which gives the viewers a chance to watch two programmes simultaneously." - An advertisement.

Assumptions:

I. Sale of Z-T.V will increase because of the advertisement.

II. Some people may be influenced by the advertisement and buy Z-T.V.

III. The sale of Z-T.V. may be on the downward trend.
solution:
An assumption in a Statement-and-Assumption question is something that is not stated but is silently taken for granted for the statement to make sense — a background premise, not a fresh prediction. The standard check is the negation test: negate the candidate assumption; if doing so does not touch the validity of the statement, the assumption was never implicit in the first place. A claim that predicts a specific, separate future outcome, rather than describing why the statement is being made at all, is a conclusion to be verified, not a silent premise, and therefore fails this test.

Assumption I claims Z-T.V.'s sales will increase because of the ad. This describes a hoped-for result of the campaign, not a premise the advertisement quietly depends on — an advertiser can run this exact ad, believing in it fully, and still see no rise in sales; the statement does not fall apart if this prediction fails, so I is not implicit. Assumption II claims some viewers may be swayed to buy after the ad. This is the ordinary working premise behind placing any advertisement — a company would have no reason to publicise a claim like this unless it believed the message could reach and influence at least some buyers; this is exactly the kind of background premise the negation test flags as implicit, so II holds. Assumption III claims Z-T.V.'s sales may currently be on a downward trend. Highlighting a distinctive, differentiating feature ("the only T.V. which...") is a common, unstated reason companies advertise at all — when a product's sales are healthy, there is less pressure to publicise a unique selling point this way; so a soft, unasserted concern about sagging sales is a reasonable premise quietly behind the statement, and III holds too.

  • Ruling out every assumption (denying that any premise underlies the statement) overlooks that placing this advertisement at all already presupposes some ordinary premise about its purpose.

  • Treating every assumption as implicit, or keeping the sales-increase claim alongside the persuasion premise, both smuggle in a guaranteed future result as if it were a silent premise — but a predicted outcome must be argued for, not assumed.

Only the two modest, unasserted premises about persuasive intent and a plausible motive for advertising survive the negation test, so "Only II and III are implicit" is the answer that matches the statement's own quiet assumptions.

optionFeedback.html: This choice rules out every listed assumption at once. But the statement is an advertisement making a specific claim about a product feature, and running any such advertisement rests on some ordinary background premise about why publicising the claim is worthwhile for the company — dismissing every assumption ignores that an advertisement is never placed in a vacuum.

This choice treats every listed assumption as already taken for granted, including the claim that the advertisement will in fact push sales upward. That is a specific predicted outcome, not a quiet premise — an advertisement can be run, and can rest on ordinary persuasive intent, without that campaign being guaranteed to actually raise sales. Folding a guaranteed result into what is "assumed" overreaches.

This pairing keeps the claim that the advertisement will definitely push sales up. Guaranteeing a sales rise is a specific future outcome that the mere act of advertising does not require to be true, so it cannot be treated as a quiet premise the statement relies on — a statement can presuppose ordinary persuasive intent without presupposing that the campaign will succeed.

This pairing keeps only the modest, unasserted premises: that some viewers may be swayed to buy after seeing the claim, and that the company's sales may currently be under pressure — a plausible unstated reason for spotlighting a unique feature right now. Neither premise commits to a guaranteed result, which is exactly what a statement can be assumed to quietly rely on without over-claiming success.

title: Which of the following best completes the passage below? In
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
text:
Which of the following best completes the passage below?
In a survey of job applicants, two-fifths admitted to being at least a little dishonest. However, the survey may underestimate the proportion of job applicants who are dishonest, because __________.

options.html: some dishonest people taking the survey might have claimed on the survey to be honest
some generally honest people taking the survey might have claimed on the survey to be dishonest
some people who claimed on the survey to be at least a little dishonest may be very dishonest
some people who claimed on the survey to be dishonest may have been answering honestly

solution: The survey relies on self-reporting, which is prone to bias. Dishonest applicants are likely to lie about their honesty during the hiring process to appear trustworthy. Consequently, the number of applicants admitting dishonesty will be lower than the actual number of dishonest individuals, causing the survey to underestimate the true proportion.

optionFeedback.html: When dishonest applicants claim to be honest, they are excluded from the survey's count of dishonest people. This results in a lower reported proportion than reality.
If honest applicants claim to be dishonest, the survey count of dishonest people would increase. This suggests overestimation rather than underestimation.
This option discusses the intensity of dishonesty among those who admitted it. It does not explain why the total number of dishonest applicants might be higher than reported.
This option addresses the truthfulness of those who admitted dishonesty. It does not explain why the reported proportion might be lower than the actual proportion.

title: Many business offices are located in buildings having floors. If
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
text: Many business offices are located in buildings having 2-8 floors. If a building has more than 3 floors, it has a lift. If the above statements are true, which of the following must be true?

options.html: Only floors above the 3rd floors have lifts
All floors may be reached by lifts

solution: The problem states that any building with more than 3 floors must have a lift. To determine which statement must be true, we analyze the options based on this rule.\nOption B is correct because a building with a 7th floor necessarily has at least 7 floors. Since 7 is greater than 3, the condition 'more than 3 floors' is satisfied. Therefore, such a building must have a lift, making the presence of lifts on 7th floors logically necessary.\nOption A is incorrect because buildings with exactly 2 or 3 floors are not required to have lifts, but the statement implies they definitely do not, which is an assumption. Option C is wrong because it claims only floors above the 3rd have lifts, ignoring that buildings with more than 3 floors might also have lifts on lower floors. Option D is too broad, as buildings with only 2 or 3 floors might not have lifts at all. Thus, Option B is the only statement that must be true based on the given premises.

optionFeedback.html: The rule applies only to buildings with more than 3 floors. It does not imply that buildings with fewer floors lack lifts.
Since a 7th floor means the building has more than 3 floors, the rule requiring lifts applies.
The rule guarantees lifts for buildings over 3 floors, but it does not prevent them on lower floors. Thus, claiming only upper floors have lifts is not necessarily true.
The condition only applies to buildings with more than 3 floors. Buildings with 3 or fewer floors might not have lifts, so all floors is not guaranteed.

title: Statement followed by two assumptions are given below. Select the
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
text:
A statement followed by two assumptions are given below. Select the assumption(s) from the options which is implicit in the statement. Select : (A) If only assumption (i) is implicit (B) If only assumption (ii) is implicit (C) If both (i) and (ii) are implicit (D) If neither (i) nor (ii) is implicit

Statement: We should work hard to be successful in our life

Assumptions:
i) Being successful in our life is desirable
ii) We will be happy if we work hard
solution:
To determine which assumptions are implicit in the statement "We should work hard to be successful in our life," we need to evaluate whether the assumptions are logically necessary for the statement to be valid.

Step-by-Step Analysis
Analyze the Statement: The statement encourages working hard for the purpose of being successful. This implies that success is a goal that people want to achieve.

Evaluate Assumption (i): "Being successful in our life is desirable."

If success were not desirable, there would be no logical reason to "work hard" to achieve it. Therefore, this is an implicit assumption that underpins the entire motivation of the statement.

Evaluate Assumption (ii): "We will be happy if we work hard."

The statement links hard work to success, not directly to happiness. While many people might believe hard work leads to happiness, the statement itself does not claim this. It is possible to be successful without being happy, or to work hard and not be happy. Thus, this is not an implicit assumption of the statement.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. Assumption (i) is essential because the recommendation to work hard for success only makes sense if success is something worth striving for. Assumption (ii) is not implicit because the statement focuses on success, not happiness.
Incorrect. This incorrectly assumes that the statement is about happiness, whereas the statement specifically defines the goal as success.
Incorrect. Assumption (i) is definitely implicit because it provides the value proposition for working hard.
Incorrect. Since the statement does not explicitly or implicitly claim that hard work guarantees happiness, assumption (ii) cannot be considered implicit.

title: Statement followed by two assumptions are given below. Select the
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
text:
A statement followed by two assumptions are given below. Select the assumption(s) from the options which is implicit in the statement. Select (A) If only assumption (i) is implicit (B) If only assumption (ii) is implicit (C) If both (i) and (ii) are implicit (D) If neither (i) nor (ii) is implicit

Statement: Detergents should be used to clean clothes

Assumptions: i) Detergents form more lather ii) Detergents help to dislodge grease and dirt
solution:
To determine which assumption is implicit in the statement "Detergents should be used to clean clothes," we must analyze the purpose behind the recommendation. An assumption is considered implicit if it logically supports the necessity or reason for the statement.

Step-by-Step Analysis
Analyze the Statement: "Detergents should be used to clean clothes." This is a recommendation for a cleaning method.

Evaluate Assumption (i): "Detergents form more lather."

Lather (bubbles/foam) is often a byproduct of cleaning agents, but it is not the primary mechanism that cleans clothes. Whether a substance forms a lot of lather or not is secondary to its cleaning effectiveness. Therefore, this assumption does not provide a compelling reason for why detergents should be used.

Evaluate Assumption (ii): "Detergents help to dislodge grease and dirt."

The primary goal of "cleaning clothes" is the removal of stains, grease, and dirt. If detergents are recommended for this purpose, it is implicitly assumed that they are effective at performing the actual task of cleaning. This assumption directly explains the purpose behind the statement.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Lather formation is not the functional reason for using detergents.
Correct. Assumption (ii) provides the functional reason (removing dirt) that makes the use of detergents a logical recommendation for cleaning clothes.
Incorrect. Since lather formation is not essential for the cleaning process, it is not a required assumption for the statement to hold true.
Incorrect. Assumption (ii) is a strong, logical basis for the recommendation.

title: Each question below consists of statement followed by two assumptions
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
text:
Each question below consists of a statement followed by two assumptions numbered I and II. Consider the statement and decide which of the assumptions is implicit in the statement.

Statement: The civic body put up a large notice board on the beach located at an isolated part of the city, stating "Many picnickers drowned while swimming in the sea during the last few months."

Assumptions:

(I) The picnickers may ignore the notice and continue to take risks by entering the sea.

(II) The picnickers may read this and become cautious while entering the sea.

options.html: If either assumption I or II is implicit
If neither assumption I nor II is implicit

solution:
The board is a warning. The purpose of any warning notice is to inform people so that they act with caution. Hence the civic body assumes that people will read the board and become more careful — Assumption II is implicit.

Assumption I says people may ignore the notice and keep taking risks. If the authority believed people would simply ignore it, there would be no point in putting up the board at all. So Assumption I works against the very reason for the action and is NOT implicit.

Since only Assumption II underlies the statement, the correct response is: only Assumption II is implicit.

optionFeedback.html: This choice rests on Assumption I being implicit. Assumption I supposes people will ignore the warning and keep taking risks. An authority does not install a warning board while taking for granted that it will be ignored, so this assumption does not lie behind the statement.

This choice rests on Assumption II being implicit. Assumption II supposes people will read the board and become cautious. Re-examine whether the purpose of putting up a warning depends on this idea, and weigh it against Assumption I before settling on your response.

'Either I or II' fits only when the two assumptions are mutually exclusive alternatives covering the same possibility. Here the two assumptions point in opposite directions (ignore the warning versus heed it), so they are not interchangeable alternatives of the either/or type.

'Neither I nor II' would fit only if no assumption at all lay behind the statement. Re-check each assumption individually against the reason an authority would put up such a warning board before concluding that none of them is implicit.

title: Each question below consists of statement followed by two assumptions
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
text:
Each question below consists of a statement followed by two assumptions numbered I and II. Consider the statement and decide which of the assumptions is implicit in the statement.

Statement: Recently, the government has asked all public sector banks to reduce the interest rate on housing loans up to ₹25 lakh.

Assumptions:

(I) Public sector banks may reduce the interest rate on all housing loans up to ₹25 lakh.

(II) People may take undue advantage of the government's decision.

options.html: If either assumption I or II is implicit
If neither assumption I nor II is implicit

solution:
In assumption questions, an assumption is something the speaker takes for granted while making the statement. To be implicit, it must be a necessary, unstated supposition behind the statement.

Assumption I: When the government directs the public sector banks to reduce the interest rate on housing loans up to ₹25 lakh, it is taken for granted that the banks can and will act on this directive. The government would not issue such an instruction unless it assumed the banks may carry it out. Hence, assumption I is implicit.

Assumption II: That people may take undue advantage of the decision is only a possible future consequence or apprehension. It is not a supposition on which the government's decision rests; in fact, an expectation of misuse would be a reason against the decision, not a basis for it. Hence, assumption II is not implicit.

Therefore, only assumption I is implicit in the statement.

optionFeedback.html: Choose this only if exactly one of the two assumptions is a necessary unstated premise behind the statement. Test each assumption: does the directive depend on it being taken for granted, or is it merely a possible outcome or apprehension? Confirm that precisely one passes that test before selecting this.

Choose this only if exactly one of the two assumptions is a necessary unstated premise, and it is the second one. Check carefully whether a possible future misuse is something the decision is built upon, and whether the other assumption is instead the one taken for granted by issuing the directive.

This fits only when the two assumptions are mutually exclusive alternatives covering the same ground, so that one or the other must hold but not both can be evaluated independently. Check whether these two assumptions are actually such alternatives, or whether they are independent claims to be judged separately.

Choose this only if BOTH assumptions fail the implicit-premise test, i.e. neither is something the statement takes for granted. Verify each one independently; if even a single assumption is a necessary unstated supposition behind the directive, this choice does not apply.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q15
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
text:
Statement: “Put a notice on the board informing all employees that they should arrive at the office on time,” an officer tells his assistant.

Assumptions:

  1. All the employees come late.

  2. Employees read such a notice on the board.

  3. Employees will follow the instructions.

Which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement?
solution:
Concept

An implicit assumption is an unstated condition that must be accepted for a statement, instruction, or proposed action to have its intended purpose. The test is necessity: deny the assumption and ask whether the instruction still makes practical sense.

Application

  1. Assumption 1 is not necessary. The officer may want timely attendance even if only some employees are late or merely as a preventive reminder; the instruction does not require every employee to be late.

  2. Assumption 2 is necessary. A notice can communicate the instruction only if employees are expected to read notices displayed on the board.

  3. Assumption 3 is necessary. Issuing the notice for punctuality presupposes that employees are expected to act on the instruction.

Contrast

  • Assumption 1 is a universal status claim. Denying it still permits the officer to address partial lateness or issue a preventive reminder, so the instruction remains meaningful.

  • Assumption 2 is the communication link. Denying expected notice-reading removes the board’s ability to convey the instruction to employees.

  • Assumption 3 is the intended-response link. Denying any expectation of compliance removes the practical purpose of issuing the punctuality instruction.

Result

Therefore, assumptions 2 and 3 are implicit.

optionFeedback.html: For assumptions 1 and 2, the denial test gives two different outcomes: the notice remains meaningful even if not every employee is late, while it cannot communicate through the board if employees are not expected to read it.

For assumptions 2 and 3, the denial test examines message uptake and intended response: without expected notice-reading the board cannot convey the instruction, and without any expected compliance the punctuality directive loses its practical purpose.

For assumptions 1 and 3, the denial test gives two different outcomes: the notice can still serve as a reminder even if not every employee is late, while its practical purpose depends on some expectation that employees will act on it.

For assumptions 1, 2, and 3, the denial test gives three outcomes: the notice can still function when not every employee is late; it cannot use the board as a communication channel when employees are not expected to read; and it loses practical purpose when no compliance is expected.

title: Consider the given statement and decide which of the given
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
text:
Consider the given statement and decide which of the given assumptions is/are implicit in the statement.

Statement: Instructions were given to the counsellors in a coaching institute, to help the students who appeared for the first time in the NEET examination to fill up the form.

Assumption: I. Entries in the form are very complicated.
II. Candidates can appear more than once for this examination.

options.html: Both assumptions I and II are implicit
Neither assumption I nor II is implicit

solution:
Step 1: Analyze Assumption I
The statement says help is given to "first-time" students. This just means they are new to the process, not necessarily that the form entries are "very complicated." If it were very complicated, all students would need help. Thus, Assumption I is not implicit.

Step 2: Analyze Assumption II
The specific mention of students appearing "for the first time" logically creates a distinction from students who are appearing for a second or third time. This confirms that candidates can take the exam more than once. Thus, Assumption II is implicit.

Final Answer: Option 2

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect - The form may not be complicated; beginners might just need routine guidance.
Correct - Specifying "first time" clearly implies that students have the option to appear multiple times.
Incorrect - Since Assumption I is not logically guaranteed, both cannot be implicit.
Incorrect - This is wrong because Assumption II is strongly implied by the statement's phrasing.

title: Statement: The Chairman stressed the need for making education system
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
text:
Statement: The Chairman stressed the need for making the education system more flexible and regretted that the curriculum has not been revised in keeping with the pace of the changes taking place.

Courses of Action:

  • I. Curriculum should be reviewed and revised periodically.

  • II. System of education should be made more flexible.
solution:
Concept

A course of action is a practical administrative step proposed to remedy a problem or improve a situation described in a statement. A course FOLLOWS when it satisfies two tests: (i) relevance — it addresses a need, grievance or problem that the statement itself actually raises; and (ii) practicability — it is a reasonable, proportionate step, not an extreme, vague or impossible one. Courses are judged independently of one another: two courses can both follow, because a statement that voices more than one concern can warrant more than one remedy. ‘Either-or’ applies only when the two courses are rival substitutes for a single problem, and ‘neither’ applies only when both fail the tests.

Applying it to this statement

  1. Isolate what the statement raises. It carries two distinct concerns: (a) the Chairman STRESSED the need to make the education system more flexible; and (b) he REGRETTED that the curriculum has not been revised to keep pace with change.

  2. Test course I — ‘Curriculum should be reviewed and revised periodically.’ It speaks directly to concern (b), and periodic review is an ordinary, workable administrative measure. It passes both tests.

  3. Test course II — ‘System of education should be made more flexible.’ It speaks directly to concern (a), and it is the very measure the Chairman asked for. It passes both tests.

  4. Combine. Each course clears the tests on its own, and they remedy two different concerns rather than competing for one, so they are complementary, not alternatives.

Cross-check against the other verdicts

  • ‘Only I follows’ and ‘Only II follows’ each drop a course that survives the tests, on the mistaken assumption that a single statement can support just one remedy.

  • ‘Either I or II follows’ would require the two courses to be substitutes for the same problem, so that one makes the other unnecessary — but here they answer two different concerns.

  • ‘Neither I nor II follows’ would require both to fail relevance or practicability, whereas each addresses a concern the statement itself raises.

Hence the correct verdict is: Both I and II follow.

optionFeedback.html: Picking this means you judged that one proposal clears the tests of relevance and practicability while the other does not. It is a verdict most often reached by locking on to the statement's concrete complaint and skim-reading the rest, so the second proposal is never actually put to the test. Whatever you conclude in the end, each proposal must be examined against the statement in its own right — one is never ruled out simply because the other was ruled in.

Picking this means you judged that the proposal about flexibility clears the tests while the proposal about periodic curriculum review does not. That verdict usually comes from anchoring on the need the Chairman emphasised and letting his other remark slide past unexamined, so the curriculum proposal is dismissed without ever being weighed. A proposal is dismissed on its own failings, not because attention settled elsewhere.

An either-or verdict is a claim of substitutability: it holds only when two courses are rival remedies for one and the same problem, so that carrying out one would make the other pointless — two different ways of filling a single vacancy, say. Choosing it here means reading the two proposals as competitors for one slot. Before you can do that, you have to identify the single problem they are supposed to be competing over.

A ‘neither’ verdict is a strong claim: that BOTH proposals fail outright — unrelated to the statement, unworkable, or wildly out of proportion to it. It is usually chosen by treating the Chairman's words as commentary rather than as a grievance calling for a response, so no proposal is tested at all. To land here legitimately you must be able to say, for each proposal separately, which test it fails.

The statement raises two separate matters — the stressed need for a more flexible system, and the regret that the curriculum has not kept pace with change — and one proposed step answers each: periodic review and revision addresses the stale curriculum, while making the system more flexible addresses the flexibility need. Each is relevant, practicable and proportionate, so the two stand together.

title: Statement: Exporters in the capital are alleging that commercial banks
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
text:
Statement: Exporters in the capital are alleging that commercial banks are violating a Reserve Bank of India directive to operate a post-shipment export credit denominated in foreign currency at international rates from January this year.
Courses of Action:

  1. The officers concerned in the commercial banks are to be suspended.

  2. The RBI should be asked to stop giving such directives to commercial banks.
solution: The statement indicates that exporters are alleging violations of RBI directives by commercial banks. Course I suggests suspending officers immediately, but this is too drastic without an official inquiry or concrete proof of guilt. Course II suggests stopping RBI directives, which undermines the regulatory framework meant to support exporters and manage economic issues. Since both courses are either too extreme or counterproductive, neither logically follows.

optionFeedback.html: Immediate suspension without an official inquiry is too extreme and violates due process.
Stopping regulatory directives contradicts the framework designed to support exporters.
Both courses are extreme measures not supported by the statement. Suspension requires investigation, and halting directives contradicts regulatory authority.
Suspension needs proof of guilt, and RBI directives serve a regulatory purpose. Neither action is logically necessary based on the statement.

title: Statement is given followed by two courses of actions and
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
text:
A statement is given followed by two courses of action I and II. You have to assume everything in the statement to be true, then decide which of the given courses of action logically follows.

Statement: It is estimated that in this year's International Trade Fair 25 lakh people will visit Pragati Maidan, Delhi.

Courses of action:

I. The Delhi Police should be on high alert and discourage people from visiting the fair.
II. The fair management should have enough ticket booths and shuttle services to avoid long queues.
solution:
Concept

In a Statement–Courses of Action item, a proposed course of action follows only if it is a practical, feasible administrative step that a responsible authority would reasonably take in response to the stated situation, and if it does not work against the underlying purpose implied by the statement. A course of action that is impractical, merely restates the problem, or conflicts with that purpose does not follow, even if it appears superficially related to the situation.

Application to This Item

Statement:
It is estimated that 25 lakh people will visit the International Trade Fair at Pragati Maidan, Delhi.

We need to determine which course of action logically follows.

Analysis of Course of Action I:

“The Delhi Police should be on high alert and discourage people from visiting the fair.”

  • Being on high alert may be reasonable for crowd management.

  • However, discouraging people from visiting the fair is not logical because trade fairs are organized to attract visitors, not prevent them.

Therefore, Course of Action I does not logically follow.

Analysis of Course of Action II:

“The management of the fair should have enough ticket booths and shuttle services to avoid long queues.”

  • A very large crowd is expected.

  • Additional ticket booths and shuttle services would help manage the crowd efficiently.

Therefore, Course of Action II logically follows.

Why the Other Options Don't Hold

  • Both I and II follow — this fails because course of action I's instruction to discourage attendance conflicts with the very purpose of holding a trade fair; grouping it with the genuinely sound course of action II is not justified.

  • Neither I nor II follows — this fails because the ticket-booth and shuttle-service measure genuinely responds to the anticipated 25-lakh crowd and does not conflict with the fair's purpose, so ruling out every course of action is too sweeping a conclusion.

  • Only I follows — this fails because approving the whole of course of action I overlooks that its discourage-attendance clause conflicts with the fair's purpose, even though the high-alert part alone would be reasonable.

Correct Option:
Only II follows

optionFeedback.html: Arranging enough ticket booths and shuttle services directly targets the likely overcrowding from an estimated 25 lakh visitors — it is a practical, feasible administrative step that supports the smooth conduct of the fair rather than working against its purpose, so it holds up as a sound course of action in its own right.

This groups course of action I in its entirety with course of action II — but a compound course like I needs each of its two clauses tested individually (staying alert, and separately, discouraging attendance) against whether it conflicts with the fair's purpose, rather than being accepted as one bundle just because part of it sounds reasonable.

This rejects both proposed courses of action outright, based only on the scale of the anticipated crowd, without separately testing either course of action against whether it is a practical step that avoids conflicting with the fair's purpose — skipping that check for both, rather than applying it to each in turn.

This accepts course of action I in full on the strength of its first clause — staying alert for the expected crowd — without separately testing the second clause, discouraging attendance, against whether it conflicts with the fair's own purpose; treating a compound course of action as pass/fail in one piece skips that check.

title: You find that friend whom you trusted for long time
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
text: You find that a friend whom you trusted for a long time is a self-centered person and has no respect for others. The best decision you can make is:

options.html: Asking him to change his behavior in order to continue the relationship.
Sending him for a special training on traditional relations.
Continuing your relationship and trying to understand your friend's feelings.

solution: 1. Analyze the situation: You have discovered a negative trait (self-centeredness, lack of respect) in a friend you have trusted for a *long time*. 2. Evaluate the options based on emotional intelligence and interpersonal relationship management. 3. Options A and B are highly reactive and confrontational. They risk destroying a long-term bond without addressing why the behavior is happening. Option C is completely impractical. 4. Option D focuses on open communication and empathy. Understanding *why* the friend is acting this way is the most constructive and mature first step to address issues in a long-standing relationship. Final Answer: Option D

optionFeedback.html:
Option A – Incorrect
Feedback: Abruptly separating from a long-trusted friend without attempting to resolve or understand the issue is an extreme and premature reaction.

Option B – Incorrect

title: In this question, statement is followed by two courses of
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
text:
In this question, a statement is followed by two courses of action, numbered I and II. You must assume everything in the statement to be true and, on the basis of the information given in the statement, decide which of the courses of action logically follow(s).

Statement: Company A conclusively found that there is a severe dysfunction in one of the components used in their smartphones, which can cause the phone to suddenly swell up or catch fire.

Courses of Action: (I) Company A should keep the findings about such dysfunctional components confidential, as it affects the company's stock price. (II) Company A should immediately recall the defective batch and adequately compensate its customers.
solution:
Concept: In a statement and course of action item, a suggested step follows only when it is practical, ethical and aimed directly at the problem the statement describes. A step whose purpose is to protect the decision maker's own interest — image, revenue or share price — while the stated harm continues does not follow. A step that removes the stated harm and repairs the damage it has caused does follow.

Application: the statement fixes three facts — the dysfunction is conclusively established, it is severe, and it can make a smartphone built with that component suddenly swell or catch fire. So every unit carrying the faulty component is a live safety risk to whoever ends up using it, and each suggested step must be judged against that risk.

  1. Course of Action I asks the company to keep the finding confidential because disclosure would move the share price. This protects the company's market valuation, not the user: the defective handsets stay in the market, so the hazard the statement describes is left entirely untouched, and concealing a known safety defect exposes the company to far larger legal and reputational damage later. It is therefore not a step that follows from the statement.

  2. Course of Action II asks the company to recall the defective batch immediately and compensate its customers. The recall withdraws the hazardous units from circulation before the risk the statement establishes can materialise, and the compensation answers for the defective, unsafe handsets the company has supplied. It is practical, immediate and entirely within the company's power, so it is a step that follows.

Cross-check: apply the standard test — does the step end the problem stated? Concealment leaves the hazard live and adds liability, while recall with compensation ends it. Hence only Course of Action II follows, and the answer is “Only II follows”.

optionFeedback.html: This combination holds only if neither of the two suggested steps — withholding the defect finding because of its effect on the share price, and recalling the defective batch with compensation — qualifies as a practical, ethical action warranted by a conclusively confirmed safety defect.

This combination holds only if withholding the defect finding because of its effect on the share price qualifies as a practical, ethical action warranted by a conclusively confirmed safety defect, while recalling the defective batch with compensation does not.

This combination holds only if both withholding the defect finding because of its effect on the share price and recalling the defective batch with compensation qualify as practical, ethical actions warranted by a conclusively confirmed safety defect.

This combination holds only if recalling the defective batch with compensation qualifies as a practical, ethical action warranted by a conclusively confirmed safety defect, while withholding the defect finding because of its effect on the share price does not.

title: Statement is given followed by two courses of actions and

text:
A statement is given followed by two courses of actions I and II. You have to assume everything in the statement to be true, then decide which of the suggested given courses of action logically follows for pursuing.

Statement: The consumption of junk food in school going children is leading to obesity and early onset of diabetes.

Courses of action:
I. The sale of junk food in the school canteens should be banned
II. The sale of junk food should be disallowed in the 100 meter area around schools.
solution:
CONCEPT: A course of action follows only when it is a practical, administratively feasible step that would work to remove, reduce, or address the problem stated — not one that is impractical, extreme, unrelated to the stated cause, or a mere suggestion to inquire further. Each course must be judged independently against this test.

APPLICATION: The statement says junk food consumption among school-going children is causing obesity and early-onset diabetes, so the sensible remedy is to cut off the sources through which children access junk food:

  • Course I bans the sale inside the school canteen, the most direct on-campus source, mirroring food-safety steps schools already follow — practical and directly on point.

  • Course II extends the same restriction to vendors within 100 metres of the school gate, closing the obvious workaround of buying just outside the campus — equally practical and equally on point, consistent with real restrictions education authorities place on vendors near school premises.

CROSS-CHECK: Both restrictions are feasible and both target the same stated cause, and the statement gives no reason to shut one supply route while leaving the other open. Admitting only one of the two courses would leave part of the stated cause unaddressed. Both courses therefore hold together, so 'Both I and II follow' is the answer fully consistent with the statement.

optionFeedback.html: This choice bans junk-food sale inside the school canteen and disallows it within the 100-metre zone outside the gate, closing both the on-campus route and the near-campus route through which children reach junk food, the exact source of the obesity and early diabetes risk named in the statement.

This choice bans junk-food sale inside the school canteen but leaves the 100-metre zone outside the gate unrestricted, closing the on-campus route while the near-campus route through which children reach junk food — the same source of the obesity and early diabetes risk named in the statement — stays fully open.

This choice leaves junk-food sale unrestricted both inside the school canteen and within the 100-metre zone outside the gate, so neither the on-campus route nor the near-campus route through which children reach junk food — the source of the obesity and early diabetes risk named in the statement — is closed.

This choice disallows junk-food sale within the 100-metre zone outside the gate but leaves the school canteen unrestricted, closing the near-campus route while the on-campus route through which children reach junk food — the same source of the obesity and early diabetes risk named in the statement — stays fully open.

title: Directions: Read the following information carefully and answer the questions
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
text:
Directions: Read the following information carefully and answer the questions given beside.

Five weekly trains – Rajdhani Express, Samta Express, Duranto Express, Shatabdi Express and Bhopal Shatabdi Express run on different days of a week starting from Monday and ending on Saturday such that one day of a week was holiday i.e. No train run on that particular day.No train runs between Rajdhani Express and Samta Express. Shatabdi Express runs after but not immediately after Duranto Express, which is not the first train to run. Bhopal Shatabdi runs before Rajdhani Express, which runs on third day of the week. Rajdhani Express runs before Samta Express. First day of the week is not a holiday. Neither Friday nor Saturday is a holiday.

Four of the following five are alike in a certain way and thus form a group. Which of the following does not belong to the group?
solution:
CONCEPT: In day-and-holiday scheduling puzzles, first anchor the entity whose day is stated outright, then use the ordering, running before or after, and adjacency clues to place every other entity relative to that anchor; whichever day is left unassigned is the holiday. When such a puzzle is turned into a four-alike-one-odd-one-out question, the shared property linking four of the five choices is usually ‘a train runs on this day’; the odd one out is the day that fails that property, i.e. the holiday.

  1. Rajdhani Express runs on the third day of the week, i.e. Wednesday (Monday is the 1st day, ... Saturday is the 6th day).

  2. Bhopal Shatabdi Express runs before Rajdhani Express, so it runs on Monday or Tuesday.

  3. Monday (the first day) is not a holiday, and Wednesday is not a holiday either since Rajdhani Express runs there, so the holiday must be Tuesday or Thursday. Friday and Saturday are ruled out by the given clue.

  4. Rajdhani Express runs before Samta Express with no train running between them, so Samta Express must run on the very next train day after Wednesday, skipping over the holiday if it falls in between.

  5. If Tuesday were the holiday, the next train day after Wednesday would be Thursday, so Samta Express would run on Thursday, leaving only Friday and Saturday, two consecutive days, for Duranto Express and Shatabdi Express. Shatabdi Express must run after Duranto Express without running on the immediately following day, which is impossible on two consecutive days. So Tuesday is not the holiday.

  6. This leaves Thursday as the holiday. The next train day after Wednesday is then Friday, so Samta Express runs on Friday.

  7. Duranto Express is not the first train to run, so it cannot run on Monday; it must run on Tuesday or Saturday. If Duranto Express ran on Saturday, no day would remain after it for Shatabdi Express, which must run after it, so Duranto Express runs on Tuesday.

  8. Shatabdi Express must run after Tuesday but not on the very next calendar day; the only day left is Saturday, which satisfies both conditions, so Shatabdi Express runs on Saturday.

  9. The one remaining day, Monday, is assigned to Bhopal Shatabdi Express, consistent with it running before Rajdhani Express (Wednesday).

Day

Train

Monday

Bhopal Shatabdi Express

Tuesday

Duranto Express

Wednesday

Rajdhani Express

Thursday

Holiday (no train)

Friday

Samta Express

Saturday

Shatabdi Express

This arrangement satisfies every clue: no train runs between Rajdhani Express (Wednesday) and Samta Express (Friday) since Thursday is the holiday; Shatabdi Express (Saturday) runs after Duranto Express (Tuesday) but not on the immediately following day; Bhopal Shatabdi Express (Monday) runs before Rajdhani Express; Rajdhani Express runs before Samta Express; and neither Monday, Friday, nor Saturday is a holiday.

A train runs on Monday, Tuesday, Friday, and Saturday, so these four days share the property of having a scheduled train and form the group. Thursday is the day on which no train runs at all, so Thursday does not belong to the group.

optionFeedback.html: A train runs on Friday (Samta Express), so this day matches the other running days and does not stand apart from the group.
A train runs on Saturday (Shatabdi Express), so this day matches the other running days and does not stand apart from the group.
A train runs on Tuesday (Duranto Express), so this day matches the other running days and does not stand apart from the group.
No train runs on Thursday; it is the designated holiday in the schedule, while every other day in the group has a train assigned to it, so this is the day that does not belong.
A train runs on Monday (Bhopal Shatabdi Express), so this day matches the other running days and does not stand apart from the group.

title: Fact Pictures can tell story. Fact All storybooks have pictures.
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
text:
Fact 1: Pictures can tell a story.

Fact 2: All storybooks have pictures.

Fact 3: Some storybooks have words.

If the first three statements are facts, which of the following statements must also be a fact?

  1. Pictures can tell a story better than words can.

  2. The stories in storybooks are very simple.

  3. Some storybooks have both words and pictures.

options.html: None of the statements is a known fact

solution:
Concept: A statement can be treated as a known fact only when it is forced to be true by the given facts through strict logical entailment — not because it sounds plausible, adds an unstated comparison, or introduces an unmentioned quality. If any situation could satisfy all the given facts while making a statement false, that statement is not a guaranteed fact.

Application: Check each statement against exactly what the three facts state:

  • Fact 1 only says pictures are capable of telling a story; it makes no comparison between pictures and words, so the claim that pictures tell a story better than words adds a comparison the facts never make — it is not forced to be true.

  • The facts describe what storybooks contain, not how simple or complex their stories are, so a claim about the stories being very simple introduces a quality the facts never establish.

  • Fact 2 says every storybook has pictures, and Fact 3 says some storybooks have words. The storybooks referred to in Fact 3 are still storybooks, so by Fact 2 they must also have pictures — so those particular storybooks have both words and pictures. This is a direct, forced consequence of Facts 2 and 3 taken together.

Cross-check: Try to build a scenario where Facts 1-3 all hold but the words-and-pictures statement is false — that would need some storybook with words to lack pictures, which Fact 2 rules out directly, so no such scenario exists. The other two statements, by contrast, can easily be false while every fact still holds (pictures and words could be equally effective at storytelling, and stories could be long or complex), which confirms that only the words-and-pictures statement must be a fact.

optionFeedback.html: Fact 1 states only that pictures are capable of telling a story; it makes no comparison between pictures and words, so a claim that one medium tells a story better than the other goes beyond what the facts establish.

The facts describe what storybooks contain — pictures, and in some cases words — but say nothing about how simple or complex the stories themselves are, so a claim about story complexity is not something the given facts support.

Fact 2 places every storybook in the picture-having group, and Fact 3 places some storybooks in the word-having group. Whichever storybooks that second group contains are still storybooks, so they must also belong to the first group — meaning those particular storybooks carry both pictures and words, a relationship the two facts guarantee together.

This choice assumes that only statements explicitly written among the given facts can count as a known fact. But a valid logical inference can produce a new true statement that is not explicitly among the given facts, and such a derived statement is just as much a known fact as the ones stated outright. Re-examine whether any of the three statements can be derived this way before concluding that none of them can.

54.0 is incorrect. The correct calculation is: eldest son = 20 + 9 = 29; Gopal = 26 + 29 = 55; Radha = 55 - 2 = 53. 54 likely comes from a small arithmetic or off-by-one error; remind to follow each relation step-by-step.

title: RSSB Patwar 2025 Shift 2 Q96
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
text:
Below is given a passage followed by several possible inferences which can be drawn from the facts stated in the passage. You have to examine each inference separately in the context of the passage, decide upon its degree of truth or falsity and choose your answer accordingly from amongst the alternatives provided thereafter. (Q. No. 94 to 96)

Wind is an inexhaustible source of energy and an aerogenerator can convert it into electricity. Though not much has so far been done in this field, the survey shows that there is a vast potential for developing wind as an alternative source of energy. On this basis, U.P.’s hilly areas have been found to be an ideal place for setting up aerogenerators. In U.P. hills alone, as many as 56 sites have been identified.

Inference to examine: The survey was conducted by the Government of U.P. (Choose the most appropriate option from below)
solution:
In a Statement-and-Inference reasoning question, each inference is judged strictly against the facts stated in the passage, never against outside information. An inference is Definitely True only when it is directly stated or is an unavoidable logical consequence of the passage; Probably True when the stated facts make it more likely than not without confirming it outright; Probably False when the stated facts make it less likely than not without ruling it out; and Definitely False when it contradicts a fact stated in the passage.

The passage reports that a wind survey found vast potential for wind energy and that, on this basis, U.P.'s hilly areas — with 56 specific sites — were identified as ideal for aerogenerators. The passage never names the body that carried out the survey. The finding is presented as regional energy planning: sites are counted specifically for U.P., which is the kind of exercise a state typically initiates or sponsors for its own territory. No other agency — a private company, a central body, or otherwise — is mentioned as the source of the survey.

  • Definitely true would require the passage to name the surveying agency outright; it does not, so certainty is not available.

  • Probably false or Definitely false would require the passage to point to a different agency, or to otherwise work against government involvement; nothing in the passage does either.

So the U.P.-specific framing of the finding supports, without confirming, involvement of the Government of U.P. — making the inference Probably true.

optionFeedback.html: This category covers an inference the stated facts make more likely than not, without the passage confirming it outright — the given information leans toward the claim without settling it.
This category covers an inference the stated facts make less likely than not, without the passage ruling it out outright — the given information leans away from the claim without eliminating it.
This category covers an inference that is either stated outright in the passage or is an unavoidable logical consequence of what is stated, leaving no room for doubt.
This category covers an inference that directly contradicts a fact stated in the passage, making it impossible given what is stated.

solution:

Explanation:

Therefore, it is reasonable to assume that Tim's commute has become less comfortable since the schedule change, because it is very crowded and he can no longer find a seat. There is no information given that supports choices a, c, and d.

The passage states Tim could read comfortably when there were seats, but now the train is crowded with no seats available. This change directly supports the statement that his commute is less comfortable.
The passage focuses only on Tim's experience. There is no information provided about how other commuters feel or react to the schedule change.

title: If Ram studies, he will pass his exam. Ram fails
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
text: If Ram studies, he will pass his exam. Ram fails the exam. Which of the following statements is true?

options.html: Ram did not study for the exam
Ram may or may not have studied for the exam

solution:
Solution: Use the contrapositive of the conditional statement.

Let S be "Ram studies for the exam" and P be "Ram passes the exam".

We are given S → P (if Ram studies then he will pass) and that Ram failed, i.e. not P.

The contrapositive of S → P is not P → not S, which is logically equivalent to the original conditional. From not P we can therefore conclude not S.

Hence, Ram did not study for the exam.

  • The statement "Ram studied for the exam" is false because it contradicts the conclusion that he did not study.

title: Statements: The private medical colleges have increased the tuition fees
subject: Reasoning
topic: Deductive and Inductive Reasoning (Logical Deduction and Induction) (Prepositional Reasoning)
text:
Statements:

1. The private medical colleges have increased the tuition fees in the current year by 200 per cent over the last year's fees to meet the expenses.

2. The Government medical colleges have not increased their fees in spite of price escalation.

options.html: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes

solution:
In 'Statement - Cause and Effect' reasoning, two given statements are classified by the causal relationship between them: one statement may be the cause of the other and the other its effect; both may be independent causes with no traceable driving factor of their own; both may be effects of two separate (independent) underlying causes; or both may be effects of one shared/common cause. A statement counts as an effect, not a raw cause, whenever it already carries -- explicitly or by implication -- a reason behind the outcome it reports.

Statement I reports a fee hike and states its own reason inside the sentence, 'to meet the expenses', so the hike is the outcome of rising costs at private colleges, not an unexplained originating action. Statement II reports that government colleges held fees steady 'in spite of' price escalation; holding the line against an expected upward pressure signals a separate, unstated policy consideration, such as keeping medical education affordable, driving that outcome. Neither statement is triggered by the other, since private-college fee policy and government-college fee policy are unrelated administrative decisions, so no cause-effect link runs between Statement I and Statement II.

  • Statement I is the cause and Statement II is its effect, or Statement II is the cause and Statement I is its effect: both require one statement to trigger the other; private and government college fee policies are set independently, so no such link exists.

  • Both statements are independent causes: this fits only when neither statement shows any traceable reason behind it; here, Statement I openly states 'to meet the expenses' as its reason, so it is a resulting action, not an unexplained originating one.

  • Both statements are effects of independent causes: each statement's outcome (the fee hike, the fee freeze) is driven by its own separate factor (rising costs versus an affordability-focused policy); the two colleges' outcomes are unrelated to each other but each is explainable by its own reason.

Since each statement reports an outcome traceable to its own distinct, unstated underlying cause, and neither outcome causes the other, the two statements are best classified as effects of independent causes.

optionFeedback.html: Reading Statement I as the cause of Statement II would mean the private colleges' fee decision drives the government colleges' fee decision. Private and government medical colleges are governed by separate administrative bodies that set fee policy independently, so a decision at one carries no bearing on a decision at the other -- no such trigger relationship exists between the two statements.

Reading Statement II as the cause of Statement I would mean the government colleges' decision to hold fees steady drives the private colleges' fee hike. These are unrelated administrative decisions taken by different types of institutions, so the government-college outcome cannot be what triggers the private-college outcome.

Reading both outcomes as unexplained, self-originating causes would require that neither statement supply any reason for what it reports. Statement I, however, states its own reason -- 'to meet the expenses' -- so the fee increase follows from that cost pressure rather than standing as an action with nothing behind it.

Reading both outcomes as effects of independent causes matches the wording of both statements: the fee hike follows from rising costs at private colleges, and holding fees steady despite price escalation points to a separate, affordability-driven policy at government colleges. Neither outcome triggers the other, and each traces to a cause particular to its own institution type.

title: Read the given statements and conclusions carefully. Assuming that the
subject: Reasoning
text:
Read the given statements and conclusions carefully. Assuming that the information given in the statements is true, even if it appears to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which of the given conclusions logically follow(s) from the statements.

Statements:

All Turquoise are Beige.
All Beige are Pink.
Some Pink are Maroon.

Conclusions:

(I) All Beige are Maroon.
(II) Some Pink are Turquoise.
solution:
Concept: A conclusion follows from a set of categorical statements only when it is true in every arrangement of the classes that satisfies all the statements; one consistent arrangement in which it fails is enough to reject it. Two rules settle such items. First, a universal chain: if the whole of class A lies inside class B and the whole of B lies inside C, then the whole of A lies inside C, and because a named class is taken to be non-empty, this also guarantees that some C are A. Second, a particular statement of the form “Some X are Y” guarantees only that an overlap exists somewhere, so on its own it can never force a universal claim about a third class.

Application to the given statements:

  1. “All Turquoise are Beige” places the whole Turquoise class inside Beige.

  2. “All Beige are Pink” places the whole Beige class inside Pink, so chaining the two universals puts the whole Turquoise class inside Pink.

  3. Turquoise is a non-empty class, so at least one Pink item is Turquoise. “Some Pink are Turquoise” therefore holds in every arrangement that satisfies the statements, so it follows.

  4. “Some Pink are Maroon” fixes only that Pink and Maroon overlap somewhere; it says nothing about where that overlap sits, so it cannot force the universal claim “All Beige are Maroon”.

Cross-check with a counter-arrangement:

  • Let Turquoise = {t}, Beige = {t, b}, Pink = {t, b, m} and Maroon = {m}. Every Turquoise item is Beige, every Beige item is Pink, and m is both Pink and Maroon, so all three statements hold.

  • In this arrangement b is Beige but not Maroon, so “All Beige are Maroon” is false; t is both Pink and Turquoise, so “Some Pink are Turquoise” is true. One such arrangement is enough to reject the first conclusion, and no arrangement can defeat the second because the chain already proves it.

Conclusion

Status

All Beige are Maroon

Does not follow — a consistent arrangement makes it false

Some Pink are Turquoise

Follows — guaranteed by the Turquoise → Beige → Pink chain

Hence only conclusion (II), “Some Pink are Turquoise”, logically follows from the statements.

title: Decide which of the given conclusions logically follow from the
subject: Reasoning
text:
Decide which of the given conclusions logically follow from the given statement(s)

Statement:

Some metals are alloys.

No metal is a stone.

Conclusions:

I. No alloy is stone. II. At least some alloys are metals

options.html: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both Conclusion I and II are true

solution:
Concept: Two standard syllogism rules decide conclusions like these. First, a particular affirmative statement ("Some X are Y") converts simply and validly to "Some Y are X" — no second premise or extra condition is needed; a particular negative ("Some X are not Y"), by contrast, never converts this way. Second, a universal claim ("All" or "No") about an entire class can only be drawn from premises that fix that class's whole extent — a premise that establishes merely a partial ("some") overlap with a class can never license a universal statement about that class.

Applying this to the two statements:

  1. "Some metals are alloys" is a particular affirmative (I-type). By the first rule, it converts directly to "Some alloys are metals" — this alone establishes Conclusion II, with no need for the second statement.

  2. "No metal is a stone" excludes stones from the metal class specifically. Since "Some metals are alloys" fixes only a partial overlap between metals and alloys — not that every alloy is a metal — this exclusion covers just that overlap; alloys outside it are never brought under it.

  3. Conclusion I ("No alloy is stone") would need the metal–stone exclusion to hold across the WHOLE alloy class. By the second rule, a partial ("some") premise cannot support that universal a conclusion, so Conclusion I does not follow.

Cross-check with a Venn diagram: draw the alloy circle overlapping the metal circle (as "some" requires), and place the stone circle entirely outside the metal circle. Nothing stops the alloy circle from ALSO overlapping the stone circle in the region lying outside the metal circle — so "no alloy is stone" is never guaranteed, while "some alloys are metals" is fixed the moment the metal-alloy overlap is drawn.

Hence only Conclusion II follows: the correct choice is "Only Conclusion II is true."
