title: Three statements are given followed by four conclusions II, III
subject: Reasoning
text:
Three statements are given followed by four conclusions I, II, III and IV. You have to consider these statements to be true, even if they seem at variance from commonly known facts. Decide which of the given conclusions logically follow/s from the given statement.

Statements:

A. All beetroots are carrots.

B. All carrots are radishes.

C. All radishes are white.

Conclusions:

I. All beetroots are white.

II. All white are carrots.

III. All radishes are beetroots.

IV. All carrots are white.
solution:
Treat each statement as true and arrange them as a single chain of subsets:

All beetroots are carrots → Beetroots ⊆ Carrots.

All carrots are radishes → Carrots ⊆ Radishes.

All radishes are white → Radishes ⊆ White.

Combining: Beetroots ⊆ Carrots ⊆ Radishes ⊆ White.

Now test each conclusion:

I. All beetroots are white — beetroots lie inside white through the chain → FOLLOWS.

II. All white are carrots — this is the converse of 'all carrots are white'; the chain does not guarantee a converse, so 'white' need not lie inside carrots → does NOT follow.

III. All radishes are beetroots — this is the converse of 'all beetroots are radishes'; the statements establish only that beetroots are radishes, not the reverse, so it is not guaranteed → does NOT follow.

IV. All carrots are white — carrots lie inside white through the chain → FOLLOWS.

Therefore only conclusions I and IV follow, which matches the option 'Only conclusions I and IV follow.'

optionFeedback.html:
Both these conclusions are invalid. Conclusion II ('All white are carrots') reverses the chain — the statements tell us all carrots are white, but the converse does not follow, so 'white' (the outermost set) need not lie inside 'carrots'.

Conclusion III ('All radishes are beetroots') also reverses the direction — the statements only establish that beetroots are radishes, so the reverse, 'all radishes are beetroots', is not guaranteed and does not follow.

Not all four conclusions follow. Conclusions II and III each state the converse of a given relation (the chain runs Beetroots ⊆ Carrots ⊆ Radishes ⊆ White), and a converse is not guaranteed by an 'All A are B' statement, so neither II nor III follows.

Since two of the four conclusions do not follow, the claim that all of them follow is incorrect.

Correct. The statements form the chain Beetroots ⊆ Carrots ⊆ Radishes ⊆ White. By transitivity every beetroot is white, so Conclusion I follows; and every carrot is white, so Conclusion IV follows.

Conclusions II and III each state the converse of a given relation, and a converse is not guaranteed by an 'All A are B' statement — so neither need follow from the chain. Hence only I and IV follow.

Conclusion I ('All beetroots are white') does follow by transitivity, but Conclusion II ('All white are carrots') does not. The chain guarantees that carrots are white; the converse — that white things are carrots — is not guaranteed by the statements, so pairing I with II is wrong.

title: Four sets of three statements each are given below. Take
subject: Reasoning
text: Four sets of three statements each are given below. Take these statements to be true even if they look factually absurd. Select one alternative in which third statement is implied by the first two statements.

options.html: All bats are balls. All stumps are bats. Therefore, all balls are stumps.
All fruits are flowers. All vegetables are fruits. Therefore all vegetables are flowers.
All trains are buses. All buses are roads. Therefore, all roads are buses.
All R's are T's. All T's are Q's. Therefore, all Q's are R's.

solution:
Concept

A categorical syllogism of the form "All A are B" and "All B are C" lets you validly conclude "All A are C" — the subset relation is transitive: A is inside B, and B is inside C, so A must be inside C. The direction matters: you may chain forward through the middle term, but you may NOT reverse a universal statement. From "All X are Y" it does not follow that "All Y are X" (that is illicit conversion).

Application

Examine the pair "All vegetables are fruits" and "All fruits are flowers." Here the middle term is "fruits": vegetables sit inside fruits, and fruits sit inside flowers. Chaining forward, vegetables must sit inside flowers, so "All vegetables are flowers" is a valid conclusion that follows directly from the two premises. The conclusion keeps the same subject-to-predicate direction as the premises, so nothing is reversed.

Cross-check / Contrast

Each of the other three sets draws a conclusion that reverses one of its premises, which is the classic illicit-conversion error:

  • From "All bats are balls" and "All stumps are bats," the only valid conclusion is "All stumps are balls." Concluding "All balls are stumps" reverses the chain and is invalid.

  • From "All trains are buses" and "All buses are roads," the valid conclusion is "All trains are roads." Concluding "All roads are buses" reverses "All buses are roads" and is invalid.

  • From "All R are T" and "All T are Q," the valid conclusion is "All R are Q." Concluding "All Q are R" reverses the chain and is invalid.

Only the vegetables-fruits-flowers set chains the middle term forward without reversal, so it is the alternative whose third statement is genuinely implied by the first two.

optionFeedback.html: "All bats are balls" and "All stumps are bats" place stumps inside bats inside balls, so what follows is that stumps are balls. Reading it as "all balls are stumps" flips a universal statement around — an illicit conversion — so the third line does not follow from the first two.

"All vegetables are fruits" and "All fruits are flowers" nest vegetables inside fruits inside flowers, so vegetables must lie inside flowers. The conclusion "all vegetables are flowers" simply chains the middle term forward without reversing any premise, which is exactly the valid pattern the question asks for.

"All trains are buses" and "All buses are roads" chain forward to trains being roads. Turning the second premise into "all roads are buses" reverses "all buses are roads," and a universal statement cannot simply be turned around, so the conclusion is not implied.

"All R are T" and "All T are Q" chain forward to R being Q. Stating "all Q are R" reverses the direction of the premises, which is an invalid conversion, so this third statement does not follow from the two given ones.

title: Four sets of three statements are given below. Suppose these
subject: Reasoning
text: Four sets of three statements are given below. Suppose these statements are true even if they differ from known facts. Select the option in which the third statement follows the first two statements.

options.html: All foxes are wild. All jackals are wild. Therefore, all jackals are foxes.
All fruits are leaves. All flowers are fruits. Therefore, all flowers are leaves.
All pens are pencils. All rubber are pens. Therefore, all pencils are erasers.
All buses are roads. All cars are buses. Therefore, all roads are cars.

solution:
Concept:

A categorical syllogism is valid only when its conclusion is forced by its two premises through term chaining. "All A are B" places set A entirely inside set B. When two "All ... are ..." premises share a common middle term, the chain A ⊆ B ⊆ C lets you conclude A ⊆ C — but only in that direction and only for terms that actually appear in the premises.

Two rules decide every such item:

  • Chain rule — the conclusion must run along the inclusion direction (subset → superset), never reversed.

  • No new term rule — the conclusion may use only the terms present in the premises; a fresh term that never appeared cannot be concluded.

Application to each set:

  • foxes ⊆ wild and jackals ⊆ wild: both are inside "wild," but two subsets of the same set need not overlap, so "all jackals are foxes" does not follow.

  • flowers ⊆ fruits and fruits ⊆ leaves: chaining gives flowers ⊆ leaves, so "all flowers are leaves" follows in the correct direction — this is the valid set.

  • rubber ⊆ pens ⊆ pencils: the premises never mention "erasers," so concluding anything about erasers breaks the no-new-term rule.

  • cars ⊆ buses ⊆ roads: this forces "all cars are roads," but the stated conclusion "all roads are cars" reverses the direction (illicit conversion).

Cross-check: Only the flowers–fruits–leaves set keeps both the same terms and the subset → superset direction, confirming it is the one whose third statement is forced by the first two.

optionFeedback.html: Both "foxes" and "jackals" are placed inside "wild," but two groups that each sit inside the same larger group need not be linked to each other at all; nothing forces one to lie inside the other, so this conclusion is not compelled by its premises.

The premises put flowers inside fruits and fruits inside leaves, so the inclusion chain runs flowers → fruits → leaves; the third statement simply reads off the ends of that chain in the same direction, so it is genuinely forced by the first two.

The premises only relate rubber, pens and pencils; "erasers" appears for the first time in the conclusion. A term that was never introduced in the premises can never be validly concluded, so this set fails regardless of the chain.

The premises chain cars inside buses inside roads, which would force "all cars are roads." The third statement instead claims "all roads are cars," flipping the direction of inclusion — a reversal the premises do not license.

title: Two statements are given followed by two conclusions II, III
subject: Reasoning
text:
Two statements are given followed by four conclusions I, II, III and IV. You have to consider these statements to be true, even if they seem at variance from commonly known facts. Decide which of the given conclusions logically follow/s from the given statement.

Statements:

  1. All judges are lawyers.

  2. Some lawyers are seniors.

Conclusions: I. Some seniors are judges. II. Some seniors are lawyers. III. Some lawyers are judges. IV. Some judges are seniors.
solution:
Concept: Two rules of immediate inference decide which conclusions validly follow from two categorical statements.

  • A particular statement ("some A are B") converts simply to "some B are A" -- no information is lost.

  • A universal statement ("all A are B") converts by limitation to "some B are A", valid once the subject class A is taken to be non-empty (the standard assumption in these questions).

  • No conclusion may validly link two classes unless the class shared between the statements (the middle term) is distributed -- used as the subject of a universal statement -- in at least one of them; appearing only as a predicate, or as the subject of a "some" statement in both places, is not enough (the undistributed-middle fallacy).

Application: Statement 1, "All judges are lawyers", is universal with judges as the distributed subject; statement 2, "Some lawyers are seniors", is particular with lawyers as its (undistributed) subject.

  1. Convert statement 1 by limitation (judges non-empty): "All judges are lawyers" gives "Some lawyers are judges" -- this is exactly conclusion III.

  2. Convert statement 2 simply: "Some lawyers are seniors" gives "Some seniors are lawyers" -- this is exactly conclusion II.

  3. Lawyers is the predicate of the universal statement and the subject of the particular statement -- undistributed in both -- so no statement distributes lawyers, and no valid judges-seniors relationship can be drawn in either direction. Conclusions I and IV therefore do not follow.

Cross-check: Draw the judges circle wholly inside the lawyers circle (per statement 1), then draw the seniors circle overlapping lawyers only in a region placed entirely outside the judges circle (statement 2 only requires some lawyer-senior overlap, not that it touch the judges subset). This diagram satisfies both statements while making I and IV false, and no diagram consistent with the statements can make II or III false, confirming the split.

Result: Only conclusions II and III follow, matching "Only conclusions II and III follow."

Why the other combinations fall short:

  • "Only conclusions I and IV follow" chains the two statements straight through to a judges-seniors claim, ignoring that lawyers is undistributed in both statements.

  • "Only conclusions III and IV follow" keeps the valid judges-lawyers restatement but adds the unsupported judges-seniors claim.

  • "Only conclusions I and II follow" keeps the valid lawyers-seniors restatement but adds the unsupported judges-seniors claim.

optionFeedback.html: This combination reads statement one ('all judges are lawyers') and statement two ('some lawyers are seniors') as one continuous chain, and carries that chain all the way from judges to seniors, in both directions, in a single step. A conclusion spanning both statements needs the class connecting them to be pinned down precisely by at least one of the statements, not merely mentioned in each -- treating this pair as automatically valid skips that check for both of the conclusions listed here.

Conclusion IV states a direct relationship between judges and seniors. Statement one only says every judge is a lawyer, and statement two only says some (unspecified) lawyers are seniors -- nothing pins those senior lawyers to the judges subset specifically, so this judges-seniors claim is not available from the two statements. Pairing it with a second, independently-argued conclusion in the same option does not change that -- each conclusion bundled into an option has to individually clear this bar for the option as a whole to be acceptable.

Conclusion I states a direct relationship between seniors and judges. Statement one only says every judge is a lawyer, and statement two only says some (unspecified) lawyers are seniors -- nothing pins those senior lawyers to the judges subset specifically, so this seniors-judges claim is not available from the two statements. Pairing it with a second, independently-argued conclusion in the same option does not change that -- each conclusion bundled into an option has to individually clear this bar for the option as a whole to be acceptable.

Statement two, 'some lawyers are seniors', is a particular statement, and every particular statement converts simply -- read the other way round it directly gives 'some seniors are lawyers', with nothing extra assumed. Statement one, 'all judges are lawyers', is universal; a universal statement converts by limitation into a particular one the other way round, giving 'some lawyers are judges', valid as long as the judges class is non-empty (the standard assumption here). Both of these are direct restatements of a single given statement each, not claims that need the two statements chained together through lawyers -- which is exactly why they hold while any judges-seniors relationship, needing that chaining, does not.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q6
subject: Reasoning
text:
If the statement “Some residents are voters” is true, consider the following conclusions:

  1. No voter is a resident.

  2. All residents are voters.

  3. Some voters are residents.

  4. No resident is a voter.

Which of the above conclusion(s) follow?
solution:
Concept

An existential affirmative statement says that the two named sets share at least one member. Such a statement permits simple conversion: “Some A are B” implies “Some B are A.”

It does not establish universal inclusion, and it is incompatible with a universal statement that the two sets are disjoint.

Application

  1. Let R be the set of residents and V the set of voters. “Some residents are voters” means that at least one person lies in R ∩ V.

  2. The same shared person is both a voter and a resident, so conclusion 3, “Some voters are residents,” follows by simple conversion.

  3. Conclusion 2 says R is entirely contained in V. One shared member does not prove that every resident belongs to V.

  4. Conclusions 1 and 4 both say R and V are disjoint. That contradicts the given non-empty intersection.

Cross-check and contrast

  • “Only 1 and 2” combines two universal claims that are not established by the existential statement.

  • “Only 2” strengthens “some” to “all,” which is not licensed.

  • “Only 3” preserves the same shared witness while reversing the order of the two classes.

  • “Only 3 and 4” combines the shared-witness claim with a disjointness claim, so the pair is internally inconsistent.

Therefore, conclusion 3 alone follows, so the answer is “Only 3.”

optionFeedback.html: Logical form: conclusions 1 and 2 assert R ∩ V = ∅ and R ⊆ V. Premise form: R ∩ V ≠ ∅. The selection combines two universal relations with an existential-overlap premise.
Logical form: conclusion 2 asserts R ⊆ V. Premise form: R ∩ V ≠ ∅. Universal inclusion concerns every R-member, while existential intersection concerns at least one shared member.
Logical form: conclusion 3 asserts V ∩ R ≠ ∅. Premise form: R ∩ V ≠ ∅. Intersection is commutative, so reversing the class order leaves the shared-member relation unchanged.
Logical form: conclusions 3 and 4 assert V ∩ R ≠ ∅ and R ∩ V = ∅. Premise form: R ∩ V ≠ ∅. The selection assigns nonempty and empty status to the same intersection.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q7
subject: Reasoning
text:
Consider the following arguments.

A. No athletes are vegetarians.

B. All football players are athletes.

C. Therefore no football players are vegetarians.

If the statements A and B are true, then the statement C is
solution:
Concept

A categorical syllogism treats each named group as a set. A universal affirmative statement places one set inside another, while a universal negative statement says that two sets have no common member.

If one set is contained in a second set and the second set is disjoint from a third, then the first set is also disjoint from the third. This is a necessary implication, not a probabilistic estimate.

Application

  1. Let F be the set of football players, A the set of athletes, and V the set of vegetarians.

  2. Statement B gives F ⊆ A: every football player belongs to the set of athletes.

  3. Statement A gives A ∩ V = ∅: no athlete belongs to the set of vegetarians.

  4. Because F ⊆ A, any member of F would also be in A. Since A has no member in V, F ∩ V must also be empty.

  5. Therefore statement C follows necessarily: no football player is a vegetarian.

Contrast

  • “Probably true” describes a conclusion supported by likelihood but not forced by the premises.

  • “True” describes a conclusion that holds in every interpretation in which the premises hold.

  • “Uncertain” describes a conclusion for which the premises permit both a confirming model and a countermodel.

  • “Probably false” describes a conclusion disfavoured by evidence but not logically contradicted by the premises.

Cross-check

In a Venn diagram, the football-player circle lies entirely inside the athlete circle, and the vegetarian circle cannot overlap the athlete circle. It therefore cannot overlap the football-player circle either.

Result

Statement C is true because it is logically entailed by statements A and B.

optionFeedback.html: A likelihood-in-favour judgment requires a probability or weighting over premise-satisfying interpretations that favours C over ¬C, while still admitting at least one ¬C interpretation.
A deductive-entailment judgment requires every premise-satisfying interpretation to make C hold, leaving no premise-satisfying interpretation for ¬C.
An underdetermination judgment requires premise-satisfying interpretations for both C and ¬C, with no supplied probability or weighting favouring either.
A likelihood-against judgment requires a probability or weighting over premise-satisfying interpretations that favours ¬C over C, while still admitting at least one C interpretation.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q38
subject: Reasoning
text: Which Venn diagram represents the statement “Some men are not great scientists”?
solution:
Concept

In a categorical Venn diagram, shading means that a region is empty, while a cross means that at least one member exists in that region.

The statement “Some A are not B” is existential: it requires at least one member inside A but outside B.

Application

  1. Let one circle represent men and the other circle represent great scientists.

  2. The phrase “some men” requires an existing member of the set of men.

  3. The phrase “are not great scientists” places that member outside the overlap with great scientists.

  4. Therefore, put a cross in the part of the men circle that excludes great scientists.

Cross-check and contrast

  • Shading the overlap would assert that no men are great scientists.

  • Shading the great-scientists-only region would assert that every great scientist is a man.

  • Shading the men-only region would assert that every man is a great scientist.

  • A cross in the men-only region directly represents the required existential member.

Hence, the required representation is the diagram with a cross in the men-only region.

optionFeedback.html: For the overlap-marked figure, the set statement is M ∩ G = ∅, describing shared membership.
For the great-scientists-only shaded figure, the set statement is G ∖ M = ∅, describing great-scientist-only membership.
For the men-only shaded figure, the set statement is M ∖ G = ∅, describing men-only membership.
For the men-only crossed figure, the set statement is |M ∖ G| ≥ 1, describing men-only membership.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q67
subject: Reasoning
text: Which symbol is used to express a universal negative proposition?
solution:
Concept

In traditional categorical logic, a standard-form proposition is classified by quantity (universal or particular) and quality (affirmative or negative). The four forms are conventionally labelled A, E, I, and O.

A proposition with the form “No S are P” ranges over the whole subject class and denies membership in the predicate class.

Application

The phrase “universal negative” corresponds to the form “No S are P.” In the traditional A–E–I–O notation, that form is represented by E.

Contrast

  • A represents “All S are P,” the universal affirmative form.

  • I represents “Some S are P,” the particular affirmative form.

  • O represents “Some S are not P,” the particular negative form.

Result

Therefore, the symbol for a universal negative proposition is E.

optionFeedback.html: A is conventionally illustrated by the standard form “All S are P.”
I is conventionally illustrated by the standard form “Some S are P.”
E is conventionally illustrated by the standard form “No S are P.”
O is conventionally illustrated by the standard form “Some S are not P.”

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q73
subject: Reasoning
text: Under the conventional existential-import rule used in aptitude-test syllogisms, if “All successful administrators are intelligent” is true, which of the following statements follows?

options.html: Some intelligent people are not successful administrators

solution:
CONCEPT

A universal affirmative proposition has the form “All S are P”, represented as S ⊆ P. In the conventional syllogism rules used in aptitude tests, the subject class S is treated as non-empty, so the universal affirmative has existential import.

Under subalternation, an A-form proposition therefore supports the corresponding I-form proposition “Some S are P”. It does not support the contrary E-form, the contradictory O-form, or an existence claim about the part of P outside S.

APPLICATION

  1. Let S be the set of successful administrators and I be the set of intelligent people.

  2. The premise “All successful administrators are intelligent” gives S ⊆ I.

  3. By the conventional existential-import assumption, S is non-empty; choose an element x in S.

  4. Since S ⊆ I, the same element x is also in I. Hence at least one successful administrator is intelligent.

CONTRAST

  • “No successful administrator is intelligent” makes S and I disjoint, contrary to S ⊆ I with non-empty S.

  • “Some successful administrators are not intelligent” requires an element of S outside I, contradicting S ⊆ I.

  • “Some intelligent people are not successful administrators” needs an element in I outside S; the premise does not guarantee that region is occupied.

CROSS-CHECK

Draw the S circle entirely inside the I circle and place one witness in S. That witness necessarily lies in both circles, while no witness is forced into the I-only region.

Therefore, the statement that follows is “Some successful administrators are intelligent”.

optionFeedback.html: This proposition has the E-form universal-negative structure. Its diagram encodes complete exclusion by shading the shared subject-and-predicate region.
This proposition has the I-form particular-affirmative structure. Its diagram encodes existential intersection by placing a witness in the shared subject-and-predicate region.
This proposition has the O-form particular-negative structure. Its diagram encodes existential exclusion by placing a witness in the subject region outside the predicate.

This proposition has the O-form particular-negative structure, with intelligent people as the subject term. Its diagram places a witness in the intelligent region outside the successful-administrator region.

title: In each of the questions below are given few statements
subject: Reasoning
text:
In each question below, a few statements are followed by three conclusions. Treat the statements as true, even if they differ from commonly known facts. Use the convention of this exam that every class named in a universal ‘All A are B’ statement is non-empty. Read all the conclusions and decide which logically follow from the statements.

Statements

  • All chairs are tables.

  • All tables are bottles.

  • Some bottles are jars.

  • No jar is a bucket.

Conclusions

I. It is possible that some tables are jars.

II. Some bottles are chairs.

III. Some bottles are not buckets.

options.html: Both conclusions I and II are true

solution:
Concept

In categorical syllogisms, treat each universal statement as a set inclusion and each particular statement as proof that at least one member exists. A possibility conclusion is admissible when it can be added without contradicting any stated inclusion or exclusion.

This item explicitly stipulates existential import for universal statements: if all A are B, then A is non-empty and some B are A. Also, if some B are C and no C are D, those existing B–C members are not D.

Application

  1. Let C, T, B, J, and K denote chairs, tables, bottles, jars, and buckets. From C ⊆ T and T ⊆ B, transitivity gives C ⊆ B. Because the stem stipulates that C is non-empty, choose c in C; then c is also in B. Hence some bottles are chairs, so conclusion II follows.

  2. Some bottles are jars, so choose an existing member x in B ∩ J. No jar is a bucket, hence x is not in K. Thus x lies in B but not in K, so conclusion III follows.

  3. No statement forbids T ∩ J. A table may be placed inside the jar region while every jar remains outside the bucket region and C ⊆ T ⊆ B is preserved. Therefore conclusion I is possible.

Cross-check

A consistent model can contain one chair–table–bottle member and one table–bottle–jar member, with every jar outside the bucket set. The explicit non-empty-class convention rules out an empty chair set; the model satisfies all four statements and supports conclusions I, II, and III.

Therefore, all conclusions follow.

optionFeedback.html: The set {I} adopts only the table–jar possibility claim; neither existential claim about bottles is part of this selection.
The set {I, II} adopts the table–jar possibility and bottle–chair existence claims; the bottle–non-bucket claim is outside this selection.
The set {I, II, III} adopts the possibility claim and both existential claims together.
The set {II} adopts only the bottle–chair existence claim; the table–jar possibility and bottle–non-bucket claims are outside this selection.

title: In each of the questions below are given few statements
subject: Reasoning
text:
Directions: Read the statements as true and decide which conclusions logically follow, ignoring commonly known facts.

Statements:

  • All apartments are huts.

title: In each of the following questions two statements are given
subject: Reasoning
text:
In each of the following questions two statements are given and these statements are followed by two conclusions numbered (1) and (2). solution:
Concept: Two syllogism rules govern this pair of statements. (1) Conversion - a universal affirmative statement "All A are B" always converts validly to the particular statement "Some B is A." Application: applying both rules to the given statements:

Cross-check: conclusion (1) depends on chaining both statements together, while conclusion (2) depends only on converting Statement 1 - two independent derivations using two different rules, so the outcome is not an either/or relationship between them.

Result: since both derivations are valid, both conclusions follow.

solution:
Concept: A direct syllogism (the Barbara pattern) draws a conclusion from a universal premise "All A are B" together with a particular case "x is A" to validly infer "x is B". Converting a universal affirmative statement -- turning "All A are B" into "All B are A" -- is not a valid inference, and a particular statement that directly contradicts a stated universal premise can never be validly drawn from it. Application:

title: All flowers are toys. Some toys are trees. Some butterflies
subject: Reasoning
text:
All flowers are toys. Some toys are trees. Some butterflies are trees, then

A. No butterfly is flower

B. Some butterflies are toys

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
solution:
Concept: A universal statement “All A are B” converts only by limitation to “Some B are A” (never to “All B are A”). A particular statement “Some A are B” converts simply to “Some B are A”, and this holds with full certainty. When a term that links two statements is particular (“some”) in both of them, that term is undistributed in each, so no valid conclusion can be drawn connecting the other two end terms.

  1. Does not follow.

  3. Conclusion C (Some toys are flowers): “All flowers are toys” converts by limitation directly to “Some toys are flowers”. Follows.

  4. Conclusion D (Some trees are flowers): no premise relates trees and flowers directly, and the toys–trees and flowers–toys relations cannot be chained to fix any trees–flowers overlap. Does not follow.

  5. Conclusion E (Some trees are butterflies): a particular statement converts simply, so “Some butterflies are trees” gives “Some trees are butterflies” directly. Follows.

So only conclusions C and E necessarily follow — the correct choice is “C and E only”.

title: Read the given statements and conclusions carefully. Assuming that the
subject: Reasoning
text:
Read the given statements and conclusions carefully. Assuming that the information given in the statements is true, even if it appears to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which of the given conclusions logically follow from the statements.

Statements: All chairs are mirrors. Some eagles are mirrors. No mirror is a horse.

Conclusions: (I) No horse is a chair. (II) Some eagles are horses.
solution:
Two syllogism rules govern this pair of conclusions. First, a universal premise ("All A are B") combined with a universal negative premise sharing the middle term ("No B is C") places the entire A category outside the C category, and a universal negative relationship converts simply: "No A is C" and "No C is A" are logically equivalent. Second, a particular premise ("Some A are B") combined with the same universal negative premise only excludes the overlapping part of A from C; it can never be strengthened into a claim that A and C share members.

  1. "All chairs are mirrors" (universal) combined with "No mirror is a horse" (universal negative) places the entire chair category outside the horse category, so no chair is a horse.

  2. A universal negative relationship converts simply, so "no chair is a horse" is logically equivalent to "no horse is a chair" -- exactly what conclusion (I) states, so conclusion (I) follows.

  3. "Some eagles are mirrors" (particular) combined with "No mirror is a horse" (universal negative) can only exclude the overlapping eagles from the horse category; the statements say nothing about the eagles that fall outside the mirror category.

  4. Because a particular-plus-negative pairing can only produce an exclusion result, it cannot be strengthened into a claim that eagles and horses share members -- so conclusion (II), which asserts exactly that, does not follow.

A quick model confirms this: let Mirrors = {1, 2, 3, 4}, Horses = {5, 6} (disjoint from Mirrors, as the third statement requires), Chairs = {1, 2} (a subset of Mirrors, as the first statement requires), and Eagles = {3, 7} (element 3 overlaps Mirrors, satisfying the second statement; element 7 lies outside Mirrors, which the statement allows). In this valid model, no horse is a chair -- confirming conclusion (I) is guaranteed -- while no eagle is a horse at all, showing conclusion (II) is not guaranteed by the statements.

Only conclusion (I) follows from the given statements.

optionFeedback.html: This choice is right that the chair-mirror-horse combination is a universal-plus-negative pairing, which is enough on its own to fix chairs entirely outside horses. But the eagle-mirror-horse combination is a particular-plus-negative pairing, and that weaker combination can only exclude the specific eagles that overlap with mirrors from the horse category -- it cannot be pushed further into a claim that eagles and horses share members. Applying the strength of the first combination to the second is the overreach here.

This choice keeps the eagle-related claim and drops the chair-related one -- the reverse of what each premise pairing supports. The chair-mirror-horse combination is universal-plus-negative, the strongest pairing available, and it settles a mutual-exclusion relationship between chairs and horses that holds equally in either direction; dropping it ignores that strength. The eagle-mirror-horse combination, by contrast, is only particular-plus-negative, a weaker pairing that can exclude the overlapping eagles from horses but never establish that eagles and horses share members; keeping it treats a weak pairing as if it were as strong as the first.

This choice discounts the chair-related claim entirely, but the chair-mirror-horse combination is a universal-plus-negative pairing -- the one combination among the three that is strong enough to fix a determinate, direction-reversible, mutual-exclusion relationship between its two end categories rather than an uncertain one. Treating this pairing as inconclusive misses that a universal statement placing one category wholly inside a second, combined with that second category being wholly excluded from a third, is one of the few premise combinations in syllogistic reasoning that always yields a settled result.

"All chairs are mirrors" places the entire chair category inside the mirror category, and "no mirror is a horse" excludes that whole mirror category from the horse category, so every chair is excluded from horses too -- and because a mutual-exclusion relationship holds equally in both directions between two categories, this is exactly what "no horse is a chair" states. "Some eagles are mirrors" only places part of the eagle category inside the mirror category; since that overlapping part is already excluded from horses, the statements support only that some eagles are excluded from horses, not that eagles and horses share any members -- so the claim that some eagles are horses goes beyond what the statements establish.

title: Statements No women teacher can play. Some women teachers are
subject: Reasoning
text:
Statements : No women teacher can play.

Some women teachers are athletes.

Conclusions : I. Male athletes can play.

II. Some athletes can play (Tough).
solution:
Concept

In categorical syllogisms, a conclusion 'follows' only when it is a NECESSARY logical consequence of the statements — not merely something that could also happen to be true. Two rules decide necessity: (1) if either premise is negative, any valid conclusion must also be negative — a premise that only denies an ability can never necessitate a positive claim of that ability; and (2) a valid conclusion can never introduce a term absent from both premises. A conclusion that is merely POSSIBLE (not contradicted by the premises) but not FORCED by them does not follow.

Application

  1. Statement 1 ('No women teacher can play') is a universal negative linking women teachers with the ability to play; Statement 2 ('Some women teachers are athletes') is a particular affirmative linking women teachers with athletes.

  2. Conclusion I talks about 'male athletes' — a term present in neither statement — so it fails the no-new-term rule outright and cannot be deduced.

  3. Converting Statement 2 gives 'Some athletes are women teachers'. Combining this with the negative Statement 1 forces only a NEGATIVE conclusion about athletes — 'some athletes are not able to play' — this is the one thing the statements actually guarantee.

  4. Conclusion II claims the POSITIVE 'some athletes can play'. The statements never establish this — they say nothing about any athlete outside the women-teacher group — so it is at best a possibility, never a necessary consequence, and hence does not follow.

Cross-check

Picture three circles: 'women teachers' and 'able to play' never overlap (Statement 1), while 'women teachers' and 'athletes' partly overlap (Statement 2). Every athlete inside that overlap is, by Statement 1, forced outside the 'able to play' circle — so the only guaranteed fact is that some athletes cannot play. Whether any athlete OUTSIDE the women-teacher circle can play is left completely open by this picture — a possible case, not a certainty — so Conclusion II is not forced true. Conclusion I's 'male athletes' has no circle at all here, so it cannot even be checked.

  • 'Only conclusion I follows' fails because 'male athletes' never appears in the statements.

  • 'Only conclusion II follows' fails because the statements never force the positive claim 'some athletes can play' — they force only its negative counterpart.

  • 'Either I or II follows' applies when two conclusions share the same subject and predicate as an affirmative/negative pair; conclusion I ('male athletes') and conclusion II ('athletes') do not share a common subject, so the either/or format itself does not fit this pair.

  • 'Neither I nor II follows' matches the derivation: conclusion I fails the no-new-term rule, and conclusion II is only a possible, not a necessary, consequence of the statements.

Result

Since Conclusion I introduces an undefined term and Conclusion II is only a possible — not a necessary — consequence of the statements, neither conclusion validly follows: the correct choice is 'Neither I nor II follows'.

optionFeedback.html: Conclusion I is invalid because it talks about 'male athletes' — a term that appears nowhere in the two statements, so it cannot be deduced from them.

Conclusion II is invalid because the statements never force the positive claim 'some athletes can play' — everything they establish about athletes is negative ('some athletes are not able to play'); a merely possible outcome is not the same as a conclusion that necessarily follows.

The either/or reading applies only when two conclusions share the same subject and predicate as an affirmative/negative pair. Conclusion I is about 'male athletes' and Conclusion II is about 'athletes' in general — different subjects — so this pair simply does not fit the either/or pattern.

Conclusion I fails because 'male athletes' is not a term found in either statement, and Conclusion II fails because it claims a positive ability the statements never force — only the negative counterpart ('some athletes cannot play') is guaranteed. So neither conclusion is a necessary, valid consequence of the statements.

title: Which of the following statements are so related that if
subject: Reasoning
text:
Which pair of the following statements is contradictory, i.e. exactly one must be true and the other must be false?

A. All pitcher-plants are carnivores.

B. No pitcher-plants are carnivores.

C. Some pitcher-plants are carnivores.

D. Some pitcher-plants are not carnivores.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
solution:
Correct answer: A and D only

Two categorical statements are contradictory when exactly one of them must be true and the other must be false. They cannot both be true and cannot both be false.

  • A: All pitcher-plants are carnivores. This becomes false if even one pitcher-plant is not a carnivore.

  • D: Some pitcher-plants are not carnivores. This becomes true exactly in that case.

  • A and D are contradictories: if A is true, D is false; if D is true, A is false.

  • A and B are only contraries: they cannot both be true, but they can both be false if some, but not all, pitcher-plants are carnivores.

Hence, only A and D satisfy the required relationship.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. A and D cannot both be true and cannot both be false.
Not correct. C and D can both be true when some pitcher-plants are carnivores and some are not.
Not correct. A and B are contraries, not contradictories, because both can be false.
Not correct. B and D do not force exactly opposite truth values.

title: Four sets of three statements each are given below. Take
subject: Reasoning
text: Four sets of three statements each are given below. Take these statements to be true even if they look factually absurd. Select one alternative in which third statement is implied by the first two statements.

options.html: All tables are chairs. All cupboards are tables. So, all chairs are cupboards.
All J’s are K’s. All K’s are M’s. So, all M’s are J’s.
All apples are red. All bananas are apples. So, all bananas are red.
All locks are keys. Some balls are keys. So, all locks are balls.

solution:
A categorical syllogism with two universal-affirmative premises sharing one middle term (“all A are B”, “all B are C”) validly yields “all A are C” — the chain must run in the same subject-to-predicate direction as the premises, through the shared middle term. Two things break this: reversing the derived relationship (a converse fallacy — “all C are A” does NOT follow from “all A are C”), and a particular premise (“some X are Y”), which leaves its middle term undistributed and permits no universal conclusion at all.

  1. Tables/chairs/cupboards statement: the premises chain cupboards → tables → chairs, giving “all cupboards are chairs.” The stated third line, “all chairs are cupboards,” reverses this — a converse fallacy, so it is NOT implied.

  2. J/K/M statement: the premises chain J’s → K’s → M’s, giving “all J’s are M’s.” The stated third line, “all M’s are J’s,” reverses this — again a converse fallacy, so it is NOT implied.

  3. Apples/bananas/red statement: the premises chain bananas → apples → red through the shared middle term “apples,” giving “all bananas are red” — exactly the stated third line, in the same direction as the premises, so it IS implied.

  4. Locks/keys/balls statement: the second premise, “some balls are keys,” is particular, so the middle term “keys” is undistributed. No universal relationship between locks and balls can be derived, so “all locks are balls” is NOT implied.

Cross-check by tracing the subset direction independently for each pair: only the bananas → apples → red chain preserves the same subset order from both premises through to the stated conclusion, with no reversal and no undistributed middle term — confirming the apples/bananas/red statement as the only one where the third statement follows from the first two.

So the alternative built on the apples/bananas/red statement is the one in which the third statement is implied by the first two.

title: Choose the Venn diagram from the given options which represents

Choose the Venn diagram from the given options which represents the correct relationship amongst the following classes:

solution:
Concept

These are class-relationship (syllogism) diagrams. The link between any two named groups is one of three kinds: one group is wholly a sub-type of the other (one circle drawn entirely inside the other), the groups partly share members (two circles that overlap), or the groups have nothing in common (two circles drawn fully apart). The correct diagram is the one whose circle arrangement matches the real-world relationship of every pair.

Application

Test each pair among Pen, Chair and Stationery:

  • Pen and Stationery: a pen is a kind of stationery, so the whole Pen group sits within the Stationery group — the Pen circle must lie completely inside the Stationery circle.

  • Chair and Stationery: a chair is furniture, not stationery, so they share no members — the Chair circle must stay completely apart from the Stationery circle.

  • Pen and Chair: a pen is not a chair and a chair is not a pen, so these two also share no members — their circles must stay apart.

The arrangement that satisfies all three at once is: one smaller circle fully enclosed by a larger circle, plus a third circle standing entirely on its own, separate from both.

Cross-check

Reject any diagram with overlap (overlap would wrongly claim a chair is partly a pen or partly stationery) and reject any diagram that places two circles inside one outer circle (that would wrongly make a chair a type of stationery). Only the enclosed-circle-plus-one-detached-circle layout keeps Pen inside Stationery while leaving Chair unrelated to both.

optionFeedback.html: This figure has a small circle inside one circle, but that outer circle overlaps a third circle. The overlap claims two of the groups share members, which cannot be true for chair against pen or stationery, so this arrangement does not fit the three classes.

This figure is a chain of circles where neighbouring circles overlap. Any overlap implies the two groups it touches share members, yet a chair shares nothing with a pen or with stationery, so any layout that makes the chair overlap another group misrepresents these classes.

This figure places two separate circles inside one larger circle. That would mean both inner groups are sub-types of the outer one, i.e. both pen and chair are kinds of stationery, but a chair is furniture and is not stationery, so this layout is wrong.

This figure has one smaller circle fully enclosed by a larger circle and a third circle standing completely apart. The enclosed circle captures pen sitting wholly within stationery, and the detached circle captures chair sharing nothing with either, so this arrangement matches all three relationships.

title: Which diagram best represents the relationship among Doctor, Women, and

In a class-relationship (Venn) diagram, the way two circles are drawn encodes the logical connective between the categories: a universal statement ("every A is B") forces circle A entirely inside circle B; a partial-overlap statement ("some A are B", with also "some A are not B" and "some B are not A") forces the two circles to intersect without either containing the other; and when a third category relates to both groups by such "some" statements on each side, its circle must cross into both regions at once.

So the only diagram consistent with all three facts is the one with the small circle (Mother) wholly inside the larger circle (Women), crossed by a third circle (Doctor).

title: Identify the diagram that best represents the relationship among classes

text: Identify the diagram that best represents the relationship among classes given below. Boy, Girl, Student
solution:
Concept

A Venn (logic) diagram shows how categories relate by how their circles overlap. Two categories that can never share a member are drawn as separate, non-touching circles (disjoint); a category whose members can also belong to a second category is drawn so the two circles overlap; and a category fully inside another means every one of its members belongs to the larger one.

Application

Test each pair among Boy, Girl and Student:

  • Boy and Girl: no person is both a boy and a girl, so these two categories share no member — their circles must be separate (disjoint).

  • Student and Boy: some students are boys (and some boys are not students), so these two circles must partly overlap.

  • Student and Girl: some students are girls (and some girls are not students), so these two circles must partly overlap as well.

So the matching diagram has two non-touching circles (Boy and Girl) that each overlap a third, central circle (Student), while Boy and Girl never touch each other — the row of three circles in which the middle circle overlaps each of the outer two, and the two outer circles stay apart.

Cross-check

Three fully separate circles would wrongly say no student is a boy or a girl. Three concentric circles (one inside another inside another) would wrongly say every boy is a girl and every girl is a student. A small circle inside a large one with a third circle apart would wrongly make one category a complete subset and leave a category sharing nothing — none of these fits all three real relationships, so they are rejected.

optionFeedback.html: These three fully separate circles claim that no two of the three categories have any member in common. But that picture cannot model a case where a single person can belong to two of the named categories at the same time, so a diagram with zero overlaps is too restrictive here.

In this row of three circles the two outer circles never touch while the middle circle overlaps each of them. That captures the only consistent picture: the two categories that can never share a member stay apart, and the third category, which can share members with each of them, sits in the middle overlapping both.

Three circles drawn one inside another claim a full chain of containment — every member of the inner one is also in the next, and every member of that is also in the outer one. The named categories do not line up as one-entirely-inside-another in a single chain, so this nested picture overstates the relationship.

This picture claims one category is wholly contained in another while a third shares nothing with either. Treating any one of the named categories as a complete subset of another, or as having no member in common with the rest, does not match how these three actually relate, so this layout is incorrect.

title: Choose the Venn diagram from the given options which represents

Choose the Venn diagram from the given options which represents the correct relationship amongst the following classes:

Starfish, Shark, Fish
solution:
In a classification Venn diagram, the circles for two classes must match how those classes actually relate: one circle sits fully inside the other only when EVERY member of the smaller class is also a member of the larger class (full inclusion); the circles intersect only when the classes share SOME but not all members (a partial overlap); and the circles stay completely separate when the classes share NO members at all (a disjoint relationship).

  1. A shark is a type of cartilaginous fish, so every shark is classified as a fish: the class “Shark” is entirely contained within the class “Fish” — a full-inclusion relationship, not a partial overlap.

  2. A starfish, despite its name, is not a fish at all — it belongs to a completely different animal group (Echinodermata) and shares no members with either “Fish” or “Shark” — a fully disjoint relationship.

  3. Combining both facts: the correct diagram needs one small circle placed wholly inside a larger circle (Shark inside Fish), plus one separate circle that does not touch either of the other two (Starfish, standing apart).

  • A diagram built as a chain of partial overlaps (each circle touching only its immediate neighbour, so the two end circles never meet) wrongly treats every pairing here as a partial overlap — but the Shark–Fish relationship is full inclusion, not a partial share, and Starfish shares nothing with either, so no pair here is a genuine partial overlap.

  • A diagram with two equal, separate circles both sitting inside one larger circle wrongly treats the two smaller classes as equally-ranked subsets of the larger class — but only one of the two smaller classes here actually belongs inside the larger one; the other does not belong inside it at all.

  • A diagram with two overlapping circles plus a smaller circle nested specifically inside their shared overlap region wrongly assumes two of the three classes partially overlap each other, with the third confined to just that shared zone — but none of the three pairs here is a partial overlap in the first place.

  • The diagram with a small circle fully inside a larger circle, plus a separate third circle touching neither, is the only pattern that captures both facts at once: full inclusion for the Shark–Fish pair, and complete separation for Starfish from both.

optionFeedback.html: This pattern draws every pair of neighbouring classes as a partial overlap, with the two end classes sharing nothing directly with each other. That is the wrong kind of relationship for this trio: check whether any pair among Starfish, Shark, and Fish is actually a case of one class sitting entirely inside another, or of two classes sharing no members at all, rather than a partial overlap.

This pattern treats both smaller classes as separate subsets equally contained within the larger class. That assumes both smaller classes qualify as members of the larger one — recheck each smaller class against the larger class on its own terms instead of grouping them together.

This pattern assumes two of the three classes share only part of their members with each other, with the third class confined to that shared region. None of the three classes here actually share just a partial set of members with another — reconsider whether any of the relationships involved are partial overlaps at all.

The small circle sits wholly inside the larger circle because every shark is classified as a fish (a full-inclusion relationship), while the separate third circle reflects that a starfish, despite its name, is not a fish — it belongs to an entirely different animal group and shares no members with either Fish or Shark.

title: Among faculty members in an institute, are connected with each
subject: Reasoning
text:
Among 150 faculty members in an institute, 55 have Facebook® accounts and 85 have WhatsApp® accounts.

30 faculty members do not have either Facebook® or WhatsApp® accounts.

The number of faculty members who have only Facebook® accounts is ______________.
solution:
n(F ∪ W) = (total faculty − faculty not connected to anything) = (150 − 30) = 120

By the principle of inclusion–exclusion,

n(F ∪ W) = n(F) + n(W) − n(F ∩ W)

Therefore, n(F) − n(F ∩ W) = n(F ∪ W) − n(W) = 120 − 85 = 35

n(F) − n(F ∩ W) is the number of faculty who have only Facebook® accounts. Hence, the answer is 35.

For two groups A and B within a universe of N people, the smallest possible intersection is max(0, |A| + |B| - N).

Therefore, the required ratio is 3 : 7.

title: Candidates appeared for examination in three subjects, namely, English Mathematics
subject: Reasoning
text:
120 candidates appeared for examination in three subjects, namely, English (E), Mathematics (M) and Science (S). The number of candidates who failed in E, M and S are shown in the diagram given below:

The percentage of candidates who failed in at most two subjects is:
solution:
Key idea: "At most two subjects" means failing in zero, one, or two subjects (everyone except those who failed in all three).

Read the diagram's region counts and sum them:

  • Only English: 13

  • Only Mathematics: 9

  • Only Science: 8

  • English and Mathematics only: 7

  • English and Science only: 8

  • Mathematics and Science only: 10

  • All three subjects: 5

Sum of all regions = 13 + 9 + 8 + 7 + 8 + 10 + 5 = 60. These are the candidates who failed in at least one subject.

Number who failed in at most two subjects = total candidates − those who failed in all three = 120 − 5 = 115.

Percentage = (115/120) × 100 = 95.83%.

Common misunderstandings:

  • Counting only those who failed exactly two gives 25 candidates, which as a percentage is 20.83% (25/120 × 100). That is not what "at most two" asks for.

  • Counting only those who failed one or two subjects gives 55 candidates, which is 45.83% (55/120 × 100). This still excludes those who failed none and so is not the required answer.

Final answer: 95.83%.

optionFeedback.html: 20.83% is the percentage of candidates who failed in exactly two subjects. There are 25 candidates who failed in exactly two subjects (7 + 8 + 10 = 25), and 25/120 × 100 = 20.83%. The question asks for the percentage who failed in at most two subjects (including those who failed in zero), so this value is not the correct answer.

25 is the count of candidates who failed in exactly two subjects (7 + 8 + 10 = 25). The question asks for a percentage of candidates who failed in at most two subjects; if you convert this count to a percentage you get 25/120 × 100 = 20.83%, which is not the requested final answer.

45.83% equals (55/120) × 100, where 55 is the number of candidates who failed in exactly one or exactly two subjects (30 who failed exactly one + 25 who failed exactly two = 55). This excludes the 60 candidates who failed in no subject, but the phrase "at most two subjects" includes those who failed in zero, so this percentage is not correct for the question asked.

95.83% is correct. Only the candidates who failed in all three subjects (5 candidates) are excluded when counting those who failed in at most two subjects. So the number is 120 − 5 = 115, and 115/120 × 100 = 95.83%. This matches the interpretation of "at most two" (zero, one, or two failures).

title: Six people are sitting in two parallel rows containing three
subject: Reasoning
text: Six people are sitting in two parallel rows containing three people each. In row 1, A, B, and C are seated in order, and in row 2, P, Q, and R are seated in order. B is facing Q, and A is to the immediate left of B. Who is facing A?
solution:
Key facts: two rows facing each other; Row 1 has A, B, C in order; Row 2 has P, Q, R in order.

  • Because B is facing Q, B and Q are opposite each other.

  • A is immediately to the left of B, so the left-to-right order in row 1 is A, B, C.

  • To make B opposite Q while keeping the given orders, row 2 must be left-to-right P, Q, R.

  • Therefore A (left position in row 1) is opposite P (left position in row 2).

Answer: P

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Given that B is facing Q and A is immediately to the left of B, the columns line up as A opposite P, B opposite Q, and C opposite R. Therefore R faces C, not A.
Correct. Since B faces Q and A is immediately to the left of B, the seating in the two rows must align so that A is opposite P, B is opposite Q, and C is opposite R. Thus A is facing P.
Incorrect. Q is facing B as given. Because A is immediately left of B, A cannot be facing Q; instead A faces the person to the left of Q, which is P.

Incorrect. The information is sufficient to determine who faces A. With B facing Q and A immediately left of B, the full alignment of both rows can be determined, so the correct person facing A can be identified.

title: Directions Study the following information carefully to answer the given
subject: Reasoning
text:
Directions : Study the following information carefully to answer the given questions:

Ten family members are sitting in two parallel rows containing five people each, in such a way that there is an equal distance between adjacent persons. In row–1 A, B, C, D and E are seated and all of them are facing north. In row-2 P, Q, R, S and T are seated and all of them are facing south. Therefore, in the given seating arrangement each member seated in a row faces another member of the other row.
P faces the one who sits 2nd to the left of his nephew. One person sits between P’s nephew and P’s mother. A is the sister-in-law of D who is not married. S is the granddaughter of B who sits left of P’s mother but not just left. R is the only brother of D who is the only immediate neighbour of B’s wife. Q is the husband of S and sits 2nd to the right of R’s father. A is the daughter of E and faces to the one who sits 2nd to the right of Q’s wife. P is the brother-in-law of R who is the father of C. T’s son sits just right of C’s brother-in-law. A’s father-in-law sits at one of the extreme ends. Both D and A are of same gender but opposite to C’s gender. B is not father of R.

How many persons sit between A’s father and T’s daughter?
solution:
Concept

In a two-parallel-row arrangement, the two rows face each other, so a member of one row faces exactly one member of the other row. “Left” and “right” depend on the direction a person faces: for the north-facing row, left is towards one end and right towards the other, and for the south-facing row these are mirrored. The reliable method is: first fix the family tree (each person’s gender and generation) from the blood- and marriage-relation clues, then seat people using the directional, facing and neighbour clues, and accept only the single layout that satisfies every clue at once.

Building the family tree

  1. R is the only brother of D and is the father of C. D is not married, so the person described as D’s sister-in-law (A) can only be the wife of D’s brother R. Hence A is married to R; A and D are female and C is male.

  2. A is the daughter of E, so E is one of A’s parents. By clue 5, B’s wife sits at an extreme end with D as her only neighbour, which can only be E; hence B and E are husband and wife, making B the other parent — A’s father. The clues “one person sits between P’s nephew and P’s mother” and “P faces the one 2nd to the left of his nephew” also make P a brother of A, consistent with E being the mother of both A and P.

  3. R’s father sits 2nd to the left of Q and at an extreme end. P is only R’s brother-in-law, so R’s father must be T. Thus T is A’s father-in-law, T’s son is R and T’s daughter is D.

Seating the rows

Applying the facing and neighbour clues, the only arrangement that fits is:

Cross-check

  • P faces B, who is 2nd to the left of P’s nephew C — consistent.

  • A faces R, who is 2nd to the right of Q’s wife S — consistent.

  • B’s wife E sits at the extreme end with D as her only adjacent member — consistent.

  • R (T’s son) sits just to the right of Q (C’s brother-in-law) — consistent.

Answer

A’s father is B and T’s daughter is D. Between them sit A and C, so exactly two persons sit between A’s father and T’s daughter.

optionFeedback.html: A count of three appears if A’s father is shifted one seat away from where the “sits to the left of P’s mother but not immediately left” and facing clues actually place him, which inflates the number of intervening seats.
A count of one usually comes from confusing A’s father with A’s father-in-law, or from stopping the count after a single intervening member because the family tree was assigned incorrectly.
In the single valid layout, the members A and C are the two people seated between A’s father and T’s daughter, so the count of two follows directly from the completed arrangement.

Zero results from treating the parent named directly in the clue as A’s father and reading the question as the gap between that parent and T’s daughter, who turn out to be adjacent — but that parent is A’s mother, not her father.

Every directional, facing, blood- and marriage-relation clue resolves together into one unique seating, so the count is fully fixed; “cannot be determined” overlooks that the constraints leave no alternative arrangement.

title: Six participants, and are sitting in two rows, three in
subject: Reasoning
text: Six participants — U, V, W, X, Y and Z — are sitting in two rows of three, with each person facing someone in the other row. X is second to the right of Z. W, who is a neighbour of Y, is sitting diagonally opposite X. V is a neighbour of Z. Y is not at the end of any row. If V and U interchange their positions, who would be the neighbours of U in the new position?
solution:
Step 1 — Build one row. "X is second to the right of Z" places Z and X at the two ends of the same row, with one seat between them. Since "V is a neighbour of Z", V takes that middle seat. So this row reads: Z – V – X.

Step 2 — Build the other row. "Y is not at the end of any row", so Y sits in the middle of the opposite row. "W is the neighbour of Y" and W is diagonally opposite X, so W takes the end of that row that lies diagonally across from X. The only person left, U, takes the remaining end. So this row reads: U – Y – W (or W – Y – U), with U opposite Z.

Step 3 — Apply the interchange. V and U swap seats. U moves into V's old middle seat, which sits between Z and X.

Therefore, after the swap, U's neighbours are Z and X, which is option 4.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. W stays in the opposite row throughout, so W is never a neighbour of U. After V and U swap, U occupies the middle seat between Z and X, not a seat beside W.
Incorrect. Y sits in the middle of the other row, so Y is opposite U, not beside U. The two seats next to U's new position belong to the people at the ends of the Z–V–X row.
Incorrect. After the swap, U does sit next to Z, but Y is in the other row and cannot be a neighbour of U. U's second neighbour is the person at the far end of the same row, not Y.
Correct. V originally sits in the middle seat between Z and X. When V and U interchange, U takes that exact seat, so U's two neighbours are Z and X.

title: Eight people are sitting in two parallel rows, containing four
subject: Reasoning
text:
Eight people are sitting in two parallel rows, containing four people each, in such a way that there is equal distance between adjacent persons.

In row 1 – R, S, T and U are seated and all of them are facing south. In row 2 – L, M, N and O are seated and all of them are facing north.

Thus, each person faces another person from the other row. T sits third to the left of U. The person facing T is an immediate neighbour of O. L sits second to the left of O. The person facing M is an immediate neighbour of U. R sits to the immediate right of S. Which of the following represents both people sitting at extreme ends of the line?
solution:
Concept: In a parallel-row (double-row) arrangement the two rows face each other, so a direction word does not carry the same meaning in both rows: whichever way "left" runs for a person in one row, it runs the opposite way for a person in the row facing it. The dependable method is to fix one drawing frame, restate every left/right clue inside that single frame, and start from the clue that admits the fewest placements. Because the rows face each other, the person in seat n of one row always faces the person in seat n of the other row.

Application:

  1. Set the frame. Draw four seats numbered 1 to 4 from left to right for both rows, so that seat n of Row 1 faces seat n of Row 2. Row 1 (R, S, T, U) faces south, so for a Row 1 person "left" runs toward seat 4 and "right" runs toward seat 1. Row 2 (L, M, N, O) faces north, so for a Row 2 person "left" runs toward seat 1 and "right" toward seat 4.

  2. Apply "T sits third to the left of U" in Row 1. Left for this row means moving toward seat 4, so T's seat is three greater than U's seat. In a four-seat row the only fit is U at seat 1 and T at seat 4.

  3. Apply "R sits to the immediate right of S" in Row 1. Right for this row means one seat toward seat 1, so R sits one seat before S. Only seats 2 and 3 remain, which gives R at seat 2 and S at seat 3.

  4. Apply "L sits second to the left of O" in Row 2. Left for this row means moving toward seat 1, so L's seat is two less than O's seat. That leaves two candidates: O at seat 3 with L at seat 1, or O at seat 4 with L at seat 2.

  5. Apply "the person facing T is an immediate neighbour of O". T is at seat 4, so the Row 2 person in seat 4 must sit next to O, and seat 4 has only one neighbour, seat 3. Hence O is at seat 3, which forces L to seat 1, and M and N are left for seats 2 and 4.

  6. Apply "the person facing M is an immediate neighbour of U". U is at seat 1. If M were at seat 4, the person facing M would be T at seat 4, whose only neighbour is S at seat 3, and that is not U. So M is at seat 2, faced by R at seat 2, and R does sit next to U. N therefore takes seat 4.

  7. Read off the two end seats of each row. Row 1 has U at seat 1 and T at seat 4; Row 2 has L at seat 1 and N at seat 4. The people at the extreme ends are therefore U, T, L and N, so the pair whose two names both belong to that set is L and T.

Cross-check:

  • For a south-facing person, T at seat 4 is three seats to the left of U at seat 1, and R at seat 2 is immediately to the right of S at seat 3.

  • For a north-facing person, L at seat 1 is two seats to the left of O at seat 3; N at seat 4 faces T and sits next to O; R at seat 2 faces M and sits next to U. All five clues hold.

  • Mirroring the whole diagram, that is numbering the seats the other way round, changes every seat number but leaves the same four people on the end seats, so the result does not depend on which way the rows were drawn.

title: Eight people are sitting in two parallel rows, containing four
subject: Reasoning
text:
Eight people are sitting in two parallel rows, containing four people each, in such a way that there is equal distance between adjacent persons.

In row 1 – A, B, C and D are seated and all of them are facing south. In row 2 – L, M, N and O are seated and all of them are facing north.

Thus, each person faces another person from the other row. Only two people sit between N and M. D sits to the immediate left of the person facing N. A sits to the immediate right of C. The person facing O sits to the immediate left of D. Who among the following sits to the opposite of D?
solution:
Concept

In a two-row facing arrangement the two rows have opposite left–right senses: a person facing north has west on the left and east on the right, while a person facing south has east on the left and west on the right. Persons occupying the same seat number in the two rows form a facing pair, and in a four-seat row the statement that exactly two people sit between two persons forces those two persons onto the two end seats.

Applying it here

Row 1 (A, B, C, D) faces south and row 2 (L, M, N, O) faces north, so row 1 lies to the north of row 2. Number the seats of each row 1 to 4 from west to east; seat i of row 1 faces seat i of row 2.

  1. For a south-facing row-1 person the immediate left is one seat to the east, that is seat number + 1; for a north-facing row-2 person the immediate left is one seat to the west, that is seat number − 1.

  2. Only two people sit between N and M, so in a four-seat row N and M take seats 1 and 4 in some order.

  3. The person facing N is the row-1 occupant of N’s seat number, and D sits immediately to that person’s left, so seat(D) = seat(N) + 1.

  4. The person facing O is the row-1 occupant of O’s seat number, and that person sits immediately to D’s left, so seat(O) = seat(D) + 1 = seat(N) + 2.

  5. If seat(N) = 4 then seat(D) = 5, a seat that does not exist. Hence seat(N) = 1, seat(M) = 4, seat(D) = 2 and seat(O) = 3.

  6. Seat 2 of row 2 is the one row-2 seat still free, so it belongs to L.

  7. A sits to the immediate right of C, and for a south-facing person the right is one seat to the west, so seat(A) = seat(C) − 1. Seat 2 is already taken by D, so the fit among the remaining seats 1, 3 and 4 is seat(C) = 4 and seat(A) = 3, leaving seat(B) = 1.

  • L and O are the two people sitting between N at seat 1 and M at seat 4.

  • B faces N, and the seat immediately to B’s left — one step east — is seat 2, held by D.

  • A faces O, and A at seat 3 lies immediately to the left of D at seat 2.

  • C at seat 4 has A at seat 3 immediately to its right.

D occupies seat 2 of row 1, so the person sitting opposite D is the occupant of seat 2 of row 2, namely L.
