L sits in row 2, which faces north, and takes the second seat from the west end, with one seat to its west and two seats to its east.
M sits in row 2, which faces north, and takes the fourth seat from the west end, with three seats to its west and zero seats to its east.
O sits in row 2, which faces north, and takes the third seat from the west end, with two seats to its west and one seat to its east.

title: If the position of Manoj is 25th from one end
subject: Reasoning
text: If the position of Manoj is 25th from one end and 23rd from the other end in his class, what is the total number of students in his class?
solution:
Key formula: Total students = position from one end + position from the other end − 1

Apply the formula with the given positions: position from one end = 25 and position from the other end = 23.

Total = 25 + 23 − 1 = 47.

  • Why subtract 1: when you add the two positions the same person is counted twice, so subtracting 1 corrects the double count.

Therefore, the class has 47 students.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Use the formula: total students = position from one end + position from the other end − 1. Here total = 25 + 23 − 1 = 47, so 45 is not correct.
Incorrect. The correct calculation is 25 + 23 − 1 = 47, so 46 is off by 1. This error commonly comes from miscounting the overlap when adding the two positions.
Correct. Add the two positions and subtract 1 because the same person is counted in both positions: 25 + 23 − 1 = 47. So 47 is the total number of students.
Incorrect. The correct total is 25 + 23 − 1 = 47, so 48 is one too many. The extra 1 comes from not accounting for the overlap properly.

title: Read the data given below and based on it answer
subject: Reasoning
text: Six girls, Pooja, Qimat, Reeti, Shweta, Tejaswini and Vineeta, are sitting around a circular table. All of them are facing towards the centre of the table (but not necessarily in the same order). Tejaswini is the immediate neighbour of Vineeta and Reeti. Pooja is to the immediate left of Vineeta. Qimat is fourth to the right of Pooja. Shweta is to the immediate left of Pooja. Who is sitting to the immediate left of Shweta?
solution:
Concept

In a circular seating arrangement where everyone faces the centre, "immediate left of X" and "immediate right of X" name the two seats adjacent to X in fixed, opposite rotational directions — left is the clockwise neighbour and right is the anticlockwise neighbour, as viewed from above. Every "nth to the left/right of" clue is just an offset around the circle, so a chain of such clues fixes every seat relative to one reference person.

Application

  1. Fix a direction: number the six seats 0-5 going clockwise, so "immediate left of Y" = seat (Y + 1), and "n-th to the right of Y" = seat (Y − n), all taken mod 6.

  2. Place Vineeta at seat 0 as the reference point.

  3. Pooja is the immediate left of Vineeta, so Pooja = 0 + 1 = seat 1.

  4. Shweta is the immediate left of Pooja, so Shweta = 1 + 1 = seat 2.

  5. Qimat is fourth to the right of Pooja, so Qimat = 1 − 4 = seat −3 ≡ seat 3 (mod 6).

  6. Two seats remain, 4 and 5, for Reeti and Tejaswini. Vineeta's (seat 0) two neighbouring seats are 5 and 1; seat 1 is already Pooja, so Tejaswini — who must neighbour Vineeta — has to occupy seat 5, leaving Reeti at seat 4.

  7. This also satisfies the rest of that clue: Reeti (seat 4) and Tejaswini (seat 5) are adjacent, so Tejaswini neighbours Reeti as well.

  8. The full arrangement, going clockwise from Vineeta, is: Vineeta - Pooja - Shweta - Qimat - Reeti - Tejaswini - back to Vineeta.

  9. The immediate left of Shweta (seat 2) is seat 3, which is Qimat.

Cross-check

  • Pooja is Vineeta's immediate left: seat 0 + 1 = seat 1 = Pooja. Holds.

  • Shweta is Pooja's immediate left: seat 1 + 1 = seat 2 = Shweta. Holds.

  • Qimat is fourth to Pooja's right: seat 1 − 4 ≡ seat 3 = Qimat. Holds.

  • Tejaswini neighbours both Vineeta (seat 0) and Reeti (seat 4): Tejaswini at seat 5 is adjacent to both. Holds.

All four original clues hold simultaneously in this one arrangement, so the seat assignment is unique (up to an overall rotation, which never changes anyone's relative order). Therefore, Qimat is sitting to the immediate left of Shweta.

optionFeedback.html: Tejaswini cannot be sitting immediately left of Shweta: the clue that she must neighbour both Vineeta and Reeti forces her into the one seat adjacent to both of them, and that seat is not next to Shweta.

Pooja cannot be sitting immediately left of Shweta. The statements place Shweta one seat to Pooja's left, which is the same as saying Pooja sits one seat to Shweta's right — the opposite side from the seat asked about.

Qimat sits immediately left of Shweta. Taking left as the clockwise direction, Pooja is one seat clockwise of Vineeta and Shweta is one seat clockwise of Pooja; Qimat, being fourth to the right (two seats clockwise) of Pooja, lands exactly one seat clockwise of Shweta — her immediate left.

Reeti cannot be sitting immediately left of Shweta. Once Vineeta, Pooja and Shweta are placed by the earlier clues, working out where Tejaswini must sit (her neighbour clue) leaves only one remaining seat for Reeti, and that seat is not adjacent to Shweta.

title: Seven friends and are sitting in circle facing the center.
subject: Reasoning
text: Seven friends — A, B, C, D, E, F and G — are sitting in a circle, facing the centre. B is sitting immediately to the right of A and immediately to the left of D. Who is sitting immediately to the right of A?
solution:
Concept

In a circular arrangement, directional clues are read from each seated person’s own point of view. Two immediate-adjacency clues that share a person can be combined into a contiguous block before the unused seats are considered.

Application

  1. Use the direct clue about A: B is immediately to the right of A.

  2. Combine the second clue: B is immediately to the left of D. In the stated rightward direction, the three-person block is A – B – D.

Cross-check

In this block, B has A immediately on one side and D immediately on the other, so both adjacency statements hold together. The positions of C, E, F and G cannot alter this local block.

Result

Therefore, B is sitting immediately to the right of A.

optionFeedback.html: D appears in one adjacency clue; D is an endpoint of the contiguous three-seat block formed by the two clues.
C is named only in the roster; no directional clause names C, so C stays outside the block constructed from the clues.
E has no specified immediate neighbour; E can be placed only during the later assignment of the four seats left after the clue-derived block.
B appears in both adjacency clues; B is the shared person that links the two relations into a contiguous three-seat block.

title: Seven friends are sitting in a circle facing the centre.
subject: Reasoning
text: Seven friends—A, B, C, D, E, F and G—are sitting in a circle facing the centre. E is a neighbour of A and D. G is not between F and C. F is to the immediate right of A. C is not a neighbour of D or F. Who is sitting to the immediate right of G?
solution:
Concept

In a circular arrangement, one person may be fixed at any seat because rotation does not change relative positions. When everyone faces the centre, “right” follows the counter-clockwise direction; adjacency and “between” clues then eliminate seats.

Application

  1. Fix A at any seat. Place F immediately to A’s right.

  2. E must be adjacent to both A and D. Since F already occupies one side of A, place E on A’s other side and D next to E.

  3. The three consecutive empty seats between F and D must contain B, C and G.

  4. C cannot be a neighbour of F or D, so C must occupy the middle of those three seats.

  5. G cannot be between F and C, so the seat between F and C belongs to B. G takes the remaining seat between C and D.

  6. The complete rightward order is A → F → B → C → G → D → E → A.

Cross-check

  • E is adjacent to A and D.

  • F is immediately right of A.

  • C is adjacent to neither F nor D.

  • G is not between F and C.

In the rightward order, D comes immediately after G. Therefore, D is sitting to the immediate right of G.

optionFeedback.html: C has B and G as its immediate neighbours in the completed circle.
F has A and B as its immediate neighbours in the completed circle.
D has G and E as its immediate neighbours in the completed circle.
A has E and F as its immediate neighbours in the completed circle.

solution:

title: Six friends are sitting in circle facing the center. Pramod
subject: Reasoning
text: Six friends are sitting in a circle facing the center. Pramod is to the left of Vinod. Tushant is between Pramod and Mayank. Jignesh is in between Vinod and Nitin. Who is to the left of Mayank?
solution:
Concept

When everyone in a circle faces the centre, each person's left hand points along the clockwise direction. So the statement "X is to the left of Y" means X occupies the seat immediately next to Y in the clockwise sense, and "P is between Q and R" means P sits with Q on one side and R on the other.

Application

Fix the seats clockwise using the clues:

  1. "Pramod is to the left of Vinod" places Pramod in the seat clockwise-adjacent to Vinod, so the clockwise pair reads Vinod then Pramod.

  2. "Tushant is between Pramod and Mayank" puts Tushant next to Pramod and Mayank on either side, extending the clockwise run to Pramod, Tushant, Mayank.

  4. The person to Mayank's left is the seat clockwise-adjacent to Mayank, which is Nitin.

Cross-check

title: Seven friends and are sitting in circle facing at the
subject: Reasoning
text: Seven friends – A, B, C, D, E, F and G are sitting in a circle facing at the center. ‘E’ is neighbor of A and D. ‘G’ is between ‘F’ and ‘C’, ‘F’ is to the immediate right of ‘A’. Who is sitting to the right of ‘G’?
solution:
Concept: When every person in a circular arrangement faces the CENTRE, 'immediate right' and 'immediate left' are the mirror image of what an outside observer would call clockwise and anticlockwise. The key point is that this reversal is the SAME for every seat around the circle, so moving 'to a person's right' always means moving one fixed rotational direction all the way around. Chaining every 'X is to the right of Y' or 'X sits between Y and Z' clue in that single consistent direction reconstructs the whole seating order, and any position can then be read off directly.

  1. F is the immediate right of A, so in the fixed right-direction chain: A → F.

  2. G sits between F and C, so G is adjacent to both. A already occupies the seat on F's other side, so G must continue the chain on F's free side, giving A → F → G → C.

  3. E is a neighbour of both A and D. F already holds the seat to A's right, so E must sit on A's other side, and D must be E's remaining neighbour, giving D → E → A → F → G → C.

  4. The one person not yet placed, B, fills the single remaining seat and closes the circle after C, giving the complete right-direction order: D → E → A → F → G → C → B → (back to D).

Cross-check: Reading this order against every original clue confirms it — E's two neighbours are D and A; G's two neighbours are F and C; and F sits immediately to A's right. All three conditions hold at once, so this is the only arrangement consistent with the clues.

Result: In the order D → E → A → F → G → C → B, the seat immediately to the right of G is occupied by C.

A is not seated next to G at all — in the completed arrangement A is F's other neighbour, on the side away from G, so naming A here confuses the clue linking A and F with a direct answer about G's own neighbour.

This carries the letter over from an earlier clue ('F is the immediate right of A') without re-deriving who is actually asked about here — the question is about G's own right-hand neighbour, a different relationship from the one that clue describes, so the full seating order has to be rebuilt from all three clues rather than reusing a letter that already answered a different question.
D is E's other neighbour, on the far side of the circle from G — it satisfies the clue linking E, A and D but has no direct adjacency to G, so it doesn't answer what sits immediately to G's right.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q7
subject: Reasoning
text: Six boys are so standing that they form a circle, each facing the centre. Rabi is to the left of Ramen, Subrata is between Abir and Biman, Bimal is between Rabi and Abir. Who is to the left of Bimal?
solution:
Concept. When people stand in a circle and every one of them faces the centre, "left" is a single fixed rotational sense that is the same for all of them: whichever way round the ring one person's left hand points, every other person's left hand points the same way round. A clue of the form "P is to the left of Q" therefore carries two pieces of information at once — P and Q are neighbours, and P is the very next person after Q when you walk around the ring in that left-sense. Chaining enough such neighbour clues fixes the entire cyclic order, after which "who is to the left of X" is answered simply by reading one step onward from X in the same sense.

Application. Take the "left" sense as the direction of travel and build the ring one clue at a time.

  1. "Rabi is to the left of Ramen" makes the two of them neighbours and puts Rabi immediately after Ramen along the direction of travel: Ramen → Rabi.

  2. "Bimal is between Rabi and Abir" makes Bimal a neighbour of both boys. Rabi already has Ramen on one side, so Bimal can only take Rabi's other side, and Abir sits just beyond Bimal: Ramen → Rabi → Bimal → Abir.

  3. "Subrata is between Abir and Biman" makes Subrata a neighbour of both. Abir already has Bimal on one side, so Subrata takes Abir's other side and Biman follows Subrata: Ramen → Rabi → Bimal → Abir → Subrata → Biman.

  4. All six boys are now placed, so Biman closes the ring back onto Ramen. Reading one step onward from Bimal along the direction of travel gives Abir, so Abir stands to the left of Bimal.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q12
subject: Reasoning
text: Six friends—David, Bhanu, Minto, Krita, John and Nisan—are sitting in a circle with their backs towards the centre. David and Minto are sitting immediately to the left and right of Bhanu, respectively. John is not sitting immediately to the left of David. Nisan is sitting third to the right of Bhanu. Who is sitting second to the left of Bhanu?
solution:
Concept

When people face away from the centre of a circle, their left is in the clockwise direction and their right is in the anticlockwise direction. Fixing one person as a reference removes the effect of rotating the whole circle.

Application

  1. Place Bhanu at a reference seat. Since everyone faces outward, place David immediately clockwise from Bhanu and Minto immediately anticlockwise from Bhanu.

  2. Place Nisan third to Bhanu's right, which is the seat opposite Bhanu.

  3. Two seats remain. The seat immediately to David's left is the clockwise seat next to David. Since John cannot occupy it, Krita occupies that seat and John occupies the other remaining seat.

  4. Moving two seats to Bhanu's left means moving two seats clockwise. That seat is occupied by Krita.

Cross-check

Reading the completed circle in the opposite direction confirms that John is second to Bhanu's right, while Krita is second to Bhanu's left; all four clues remain satisfied.

Result

Krita is sitting second to the left of Bhanu.

In the completed arrangement, Krita is two places to Bhanu's left.
In the completed arrangement, Nisan is three places to Bhanu's right.
In the completed arrangement, Minto is immediately to Bhanu's right.

title: DSSSB TGT Special Education Teacher 24 Jun 2025 Shift 3 Q39
subject: Reasoning
text:
Seven people P, Q, R, S, T, U and V are sitting around a circular table facing the centre.

U sits third to the left of P. R sits third to the right of V. S sits to the immediate right of R. S sits second to the left of U. T sits immediately to the left of P.

Who are the immediate neighbours of Q?
solution:
In a circular seating puzzle where everyone faces the centre, every "X sits nth to the left/right of Y" clue is a fixed directional offset from Y along the circle. Fixing one person as the reference seat and applying each offset in a single consistent rotational direction places every other person; the seats immediately before and after the person asked about then give its immediate neighbours.

Application

  1. Fix P at seat 1 of the 7 circular seats, numbered 1 to 7 in the direction that corresponds to a seated person's left (since everyone faces the centre, moving to a person's right goes the opposite way around the same numbering).

  2. T sits immediately to the left of P, so T takes seat 2 (1 + 1).

  3. U sits third to the left of P, so U takes seat 4 (1 + 3).

  4. S sits second to the left of U, so S takes seat 6 (4 + 2).

  5. S sits immediately to the right of R, so R is one seat further in the left direction than S, taking seat 7 (6 + 1).

  6. R sits third to the right of V, so V is three seats further in the left direction than R: 7 + 3 = 10, which wraps around the 7-seat circle to seat 3.

  7. Seats 1 to 7 are now P, T, V, U, blank, S, R, with only seat 5 left empty, so Q takes seat 5.

Cross-check

  • T immediately left of P: seat 2 minus seat 1 equals 1.

  • U third to the left of P: seat 4 minus seat 1 equals 3.

  • S second to the left of U: seat 6 minus seat 4 equals 2.

  • S immediately to the right of R: from seat 7 (R), one step right lands on seat 6 (S).

  • R third to the right of V: from seat 3 (V), three steps right lands on seat 7 (R), wrapping the same way the arrangement was built.

  • Every one of the five original clues holds in this final order, and it is the only order consistent with all of them together.

With Q fixed at seat 5, the seats on either side of it are seat 4 (U) and seat 6 (S). So the immediate neighbours of Q are U and S.

optionFeedback.html: Combining all five clues into one final order puts R and V three seats apart along the circle, matching the exact distance the second clue states between them directly.
Working every clue into the final order places R and T two seats apart along the circle, a distance produced only by chaining several clues together since none relates R and T to each other directly.
Combining every clue into the final order puts U and S two seats apart along the circle, matching the exact distance the fourth clue states between them directly.

Working all five clues into one final order places T and U two seats apart along the circle, a distance produced only by chaining several clues together since none relates T and U to each other directly.

title: Eight friends and are sitting around square table. Out of
subject: Reasoning
subtopic: Square or Rectangular or Polygonal Arrangement
text:
Eight friends P, Q, R, S, T, V, W and Y are sitting around a square table.

  1. Out of eight, four persons are sitting at the corners of the table and the other four are sitting at the mid-points of each side of the table.

  2. Persons at the corners are facing the centre while the persons at the mid points of side are facing outside.

  3. S is third to the right of P. P is facing the centre.

  4. Y is not sitting beside P or S.

  5. T is third to the right of R.

  6. R is not sitting at the mid-point of any side of the table.

  7. R is also not beside Y.

  8. There is only one person between P and V.

  9. Q is not sitting beside V.


How many people are there between T and Q ?
solution:
Concept: In circular or square seating puzzles, a person's left-right sense depends on which way they face. A person facing the centre has the clockwise direction (as the layout is drawn) as their LEFT, so their RIGHT runs counter-clockwise; a person facing outward has this reversed, with clockwise as their RIGHT. The number of people "between" two seats is counted along the shorter arc joining those two seats.

Application:

  1. Number the eight seats 1 to 8 clockwise, with corners at seats 1, 3, 5, 7 (facing the centre) and mid-points at seats 2, 4, 6, 8 (facing outward). Since P faces the centre, place P at a corner -- seat 1.

  2. P faces the centre, so P's right runs counter-clockwise. S, third to P's right, lands three seats counter-clockwise from seat 1, at seat 6 -- a mid-point.

  3. R never sits at a mid-point, so R must occupy one of the remaining corner seats: 3, 5 or 7.

  4. Only one person separates P and V, so V sits two seats from P along one arc -- seat 3 or seat 7, both corners.

  5. R must be seat 3, 5 or 7, and V must be seat 3 or 7 (clue 6). Testing the four possible pairings against the adjacency clues on Y (clues 2 and 5): V=3 with R=5, V=3 with R=7, and V=7 with R=3 each force Y into a seat that sits beside P, S or R, breaking clue 2 or clue 5. Only V=7 with R=5 leaves a seat for Y that clears every adjacency clue. This pairing also fixes T -- third to R's right, counter-clockwise -- at seat 2.

  6. With P, S, R, T and V fixed, Y cannot sit beside P (seats 8 or 2) or beside S (seats 5 or 7); of the seats still open, Y also cannot sit beside R (seat 4), so Y must take seat 3.

  7. The last two open seats, 4 and 8, remain for Q and W. Since Q cannot sit beside V (seat 8 is beside V's seat 7), Q takes seat 4 and W takes seat 8.

Cross-check: Every clue holds against the seating 1-P, 2-T, 3-Y, 4-Q, 5-R, 6-S, 7-V, 8-W: S is exactly third to P's right, T is exactly third to R's right, Y sits beside neither P nor S, R does not sit beside Y, exactly one person sits between P and V, and Q does not sit beside V.

Result: T occupies seat 2 and Q occupies seat 4; the shorter arc between them (seat 2 to seat 3 to seat 4) passes through only one seat, seat 3. So exactly one person sits between T and Q.

optionFeedback.html: This corresponds to a seating in which exactly one person occupies the seat between T and Q, along the shorter path connecting their two seats.
This corresponds to a seating in which exactly two people occupy the seats between T and Q, along the shorter path connecting their two seats.
This corresponds to a seating in which exactly three people occupy the seats between T and Q, along the shorter path connecting their two seats.
This corresponds to a seating in which T and Q occupy adjacent seats, with no one between them.

title: Study the following information carefully to answer the given questions:
subject: Reasoning
subtopic: Square or Rectangular or Polygonal Arrangement
text: Study the following information carefully and answer the question. Eight persons—A, B, C, D, E, F, G, and H—sit around a square table. Four sit at the middle of the sides and face inward, while four sit at the corners and face outward. G sits second to the left of C. Three persons sit between D and B. H sits opposite A but does not sit at the middle of a side. D sits second to the left of A. F sits second to the right of C. E sits immediately to the right of B. Who sits immediately to the right of D?
solution:
Concept

In a mixed-facing seating arrangement, left and right are read from each seated person’s own viewpoint. At a square table, corner seats face outward and side-middle seats face inward, so their clockwise and counterclockwise directions are reversed. A valid answer therefore requires fixing all seats before reading an immediate-neighbor relation.

Application

  1. Number the seats 0 through 7 clockwise and place A at corner seat 0; choosing a starting seat only fixes the rotation and does not change any relationship.

  2. H is opposite A and is not at a side-middle, so H is at corner seat 4. Because A faces outward, A’s left runs counterclockwise; D, second to A’s left, is at corner seat 6.

  3. Three persons sit between D and B, so B is opposite D at corner seat 2. B also faces outward, making B’s immediate right the next clockwise seat; therefore E is at side-middle seat 3.

  4. The remaining side-middle seats are 1, 5, and 7 for C, F, and G. Since C faces inward, C’s second-left position is two seats clockwise and its second-right position is two seats counterclockwise.

  5. If C were at seat 1, G would need occupied seat 3. If C were at seat 5, F would need occupied seat 3. The only consistent case is C at seat 7, which places G at seat 1 and F at seat 5.

  6. The unique clockwise order is therefore A, G, B, E, H, F, D, C. D is at outward-facing corner seat 6, so D’s own right runs clockwise to seat 7, occupied by C.

Cross-check

The final order gives H opposite A, B opposite D with three persons on either arc, D second to A’s left, E immediately to B’s right, G second to C’s left, and F second to C’s right. Every clue holds with no collision, confirming that C sits immediately to D’s right.

optionFeedback.html: G is a person value governed by the second-left clue from the inward-facing reference person. For G, this relation fixes the leftward side reached after one intervening seat.
C is a person value serving as the inward-facing reference for two opposite second-position clues. Each relation places one intervening seat between C and the linked person.
F is a person value governed by the second-right clue from the inward-facing reference person. For F, this relation fixes the rightward side reached after one intervening seat.
A is a person value governed by an opposite relation and by D’s second-left relation. The second-position relation places one intervening seat between A and D.
“None of these” is a set-referential value representing the complement of the four named person values. It becomes applicable only when the derived neighbor lies outside that named set.

title: Eight friends, and are sitting around square table facing centre.
subject: Reasoning

text: Eight friends, P, Q, R, S, T, U, V and W are sitting around a square table facing centre. One each is sitting at the midpoints of the sides and one each at the corners of the table. Each person is wearing different colour T-shirt. One in Yellow color is occupying one of the corners. He has the Q in red T-shirt to his immediate left who is second to the right of 'V' in green T-shirt. W in white is opposite 'V' in Green and is between T and R. Concept: In a circular or square seating puzzle where everyone faces the centre, moving clockwise (as the layout is normally drawn) always lands on each person's immediate LEFT neighbour, and moving anticlockwise lands on their immediate RIGHT neighbour -- the reverse of the usual convention for people facing outward. In an 8-seat layout, a seat 4 positions away is 'opposite'; two corners 4 seats apart are 'diagonally opposite'; and when every person but one already has a distinct attribute stated for them directly, the one attribute left over must belong to the one person left over.

Application -- building the seating step by step:

  2. Q is T's immediate left; since facing-centre left means the next seat clockwise, Q takes seat 2.

Correct. Using the consistent seating order L, S, Q, K, M, J, P, R (listed clockwise), count four seats to K's right (counterclockwise): M (1), J (2), P (3), R (4). So R is fourth to the right of K.

Incorrect. In the consistent arrangement L S Q K M J P R, S is immediately left of L and sits two places left of Q; S is not fourth to the right of K. Counting K's right (counterclockwise) yields M, J, P, R (so S is not the fourth).
Incorrect. In the valid seating L S Q K M J P R, J is two places to the right of K (counting counterclockwise): M (1), J (2) — so J is not fourth to K's right. Counting further shows R is fourth.

title: Eight colleagues and are sitting surrounding an octagon table facing
subject: Reasoning
subtopic: Square or Rectangular or Polygonal Arrangement
text: Eight colleagues H, I, J, K, L, M, N, and O are sitting surrounding an octagon table facing each other at different corners of the table. H is the second left to K. I is the neighbor of M and N. O is second left of N. L is between J and H. J is immediate to M.Who is the third person left to J?
solution:
Concept: When all persons in a circular or polygonal seating arrangement face the centre of the table, moving in the "left" direction from any person corresponds to the clockwise direction as viewed from above. Every clue of the form "X is nth left/right of Y" or "X is the neighbour of Y" is really a positional equation on seat numbers taken modulo the total number of seats. The puzzle is solved by fixing one person's seat as a reference, translating every clue into such an equation, and finding the single arrangement of all persons that satisfies every equation at once.

  1. Fix J's seat as position 0 (the reference point). Number the 8 seats 0-7 running clockwise, and since everyone faces the centre, "left" means increasing position number (clockwise).

  2. "L is between J and H" makes L adjacent to both J and H, so J and H sit on the two sides of L. Checking the two possible placements of L relative to J shows only L at position 7 (with H at position 6) is consistent with the rest of the clues; the other placement later forces H's own clue onto J's seat, which is a contradiction.

  3. "J is immediate to M" places M next to J. With position 7 already taken by L, the only free seat next to J is position 1, so M sits at position 1.

  4. "I is the neighbour of M and N" means M and N are I's two neighbours. With M at position 1, checking both neighbour orders shows I must sit at position 2 (the other order collides with J's seat), which places N at position 3.

  5. The two remaining seats, 4 and 5, go to K and O. "H is second left of K" gives position(K) = position(H) - 2 = 6 - 2 = 4, so K takes position 4.

  6. "O is second left of N" gives position(O) = position(N) + 2 = 3 + 2 = 5, so O takes the last free seat, position 5.

  7. The complete clockwise seating is now fixed. The third person to the left of J is three seats clockwise from J's seat: 0 + 3 = 3, which is N's seat.

Final arrangement (clockwise from J):

Seat position

Person

0

J

1

M

2

I

3

N

4

K

5

O

6

H

7

L

Cross-check against every clue:

  • H is second left of K: K is at seat 4; two seats left (clockwise) of seat 4 is seat 6, which is H. Holds.

  • I is the neighbour of M and N: I (seat 2) sits between M (seat 1) and N (seat 3). Holds.

  • O is second left of N: N is at seat 3; two seats left of seat 3 is seat 5, which is O. Holds.

  • L is between J and H: L (seat 7) sits between H (seat 6) and J (seat 0). Holds.

  • J is immediate to M: J (seat 0) and M (seat 1) are adjacent seats. Holds.

So the third person to the left of J is N.

optionFeedback.html: Starting from J's seat and moving three seats in the left (clockwise) direction, since everyone faces the centre, lands exactly on this person's seat, matching the actual arrangement once it is fully worked out.

This is the person seated second to the left of N (from the clue "O is second left of N"). That count starts from N's seat, not from J's seat as the question asks, so it answers a different relationship than the one asked here.
This person sits immediately between M and N (being the neighbour of both), which is only one seat away from either of them, not three seats away from J in the left direction.
This person sits two seats to the left of K and is also adjacent to L; that position is fixed relative to K and L, not relative to being three seats to the left of J.

title: ISRO 2023 Aptitude Q86
subject: Reasoning

text:
छह लोग P, Q, R, S, T और U जमीन पर षटकोणीय आकार में बैठे हैं।

1. इस प्रकार बने षट्भुज की सभी भुजाएँ समान लंबाई की हैं।

कौन S से उतनी ही दूरी पर है जितनी T, S से दूरी पर है?
solution: शर्तों से चक्रीय क्रम S–U–R–Q–T–P मिलता है। परिमाप के साथ सबसे छोटा रास्ता लेने पर R और T, दोनों S से दो बराबर भुजाओं की दूरी पर हैं; इस अर्थ में अपेक्षित उत्तर R है। यदि दूरी का अर्थ सीधी दूरी है, तो प्रश्न अनिर्धारित है: केवल सभी भुजाएँ बराबर होने से षट्भुज नियमित नहीं हो जाता।

किसी बिंदु से उसी बिंदु की दूरी शून्य होती है।
दो भुजाओं से जुड़े शीर्षों के बीच की सीधी दूरी उन भुजाओं की लंबाइयों और उनके बीच के कोण पर निर्भर करती है।
निकटस्थ शीर्षों के बीच की सीधी दूरी उन्हें जोड़ने वाली भुजा की लंबाई होती है।

title: And live on six different floors of the same building.
subject: Reasoning
subtopic: Floor or Level Based Arrangement (Vertical Seating)
text: R, E, M, I, N and S live on six different floors of the same building. The lowermost floor in the building is numbered 1, the floor above it, number 2 and so on, till the topmost floor is numbered 6. Only four people live above I. Only S lives above M. N lives immediately above R. What is the sum of the floor numbers of E and N?
solution:
Concept

In a floor-arrangement puzzle, place the absolute clues before the relative ones. In a building of n floors, a clue of the form "exactly k people live above X" pins X to floor n - k, and a clue naming exactly who lives above someone pins both of them at once.

Only after every absolute position is fixed do you fit the relative blocks: a clue of the form "P lives immediately above Q" needs a pair of consecutive floors that are both still free.

Applying it to this building

  1. The six floors are numbered 1 at the bottom up to 6 at the top, and R, E, M, I, N and S occupy one floor each.

  2. Four people live above I, so four floors lie above I. That pins I to floor 6 - 4 = 2.

  3. Only S lives above M, so exactly one floor lies above M and S occupies it. That pins M to floor 5 and S to floor 6.

  4. Floors 1, 3 and 4 are still free, and they must be taken by R, N and E.

  5. N lives immediately above R, which needs two consecutive free floors. Among the free floors 1, 3 and 4 the consecutive pair is 3 and 4, so R is on floor 3 and N is on floor 4. The pair 1 and 2 is unusable because floor 2 already holds I.

  6. E takes the single floor left over, floor 1.

  7. The sum of the floor numbers of E and N is therefore 1 + 4 = 5.

  • Above I on floor 2 live R, N, M and S, which is exactly four people.

  • Above M on floor 5 lives S and nobody else.

  • N on floor 4 sits immediately above R on floor 3.

  • Every clue is satisfied and no other seating survives all three clues, so the sum 1 + 4 = 5 is forced.

A total of 7 comes from E and N standing on two different floors of this six-floor building whose numbers add to 7, which is the pair 1 and 6, the pair 2 and 5 or the pair 3 and 4.
A total of 4 comes from E and N standing on two different floors of this six-floor building whose numbers add to 4, which is the pair 1 and 3.
A total of 9 comes from E and N standing on two different floors of this six-floor building whose numbers add to 9, which is the pair 3 and 6 or the pair 4 and 5.

title: And live on six different floors of the same building.
subject: Reasoning
subtopic: Floor or Level Based Arrangement (Vertical Seating)
text: S, O, R, B, E and T live on six different floors of the same building. The lowermost floor in the building is numbered 1, the floor above it, number 2 and so on, till the topmost floor is numbered 6. Only two people live above B. Only E lives between S and O. R lives immediately above T. S lives on one of the floors below R. Who lives on floor number 5?
solution:
Concept. A floor-arrangement puzzle is solved by working outward from the most restrictive clue, not by guessing an arrangement. Three clue shapes do almost all the work: "only n people live above P" pins P exactly, because with F floors in all P must stand on floor F - n; "only X lives between P and Q" forces P, X and Q onto three consecutive floors with X in the middle, so they behave as one rigid block; and "R lives immediately above T" forces a rigid pair of adjacent floors. Place the pinned person first, fit the rigid block into whatever consecutive floors remain, then drop the rigid pair into what is left, and use any remaining above/below clue purely as a consistency check.

Application to this question.

  1. The building has six floors, numbered 1 at the bottom up to 6 at the top, and six residents: S, O, R, B, E and T.

  2. Only two people live above B, so exactly two floors lie above B. Therefore B stands on floor 6 - 2 = 4.

  3. Only E lives between S and O, so exactly one resident separates them and that resident is E. S, E and O must therefore occupy three consecutive floors with E in the middle.

  4. Floor 4 is already taken by B, so the runs 2-3-4, 3-4-5 and 4-5-6 are all blocked. The only free run of three consecutive floors is 1-2-3. Hence E stands on floor 2, and S and O take floors 1 and 3 in some order.

  5. Floors 5 and 6 are the only floors still empty, so R and T must fill them. R lives immediately above T, which forces T onto floor 5 and R onto floor 6.

  6. The last clue, S lives on one of the floors below R, is satisfied automatically: S is on floor 1 or 3, and R is on floor 6.

  7. Floor number 5 is therefore occupied by T.

  • Above B on floor 4 there are floors 5 and 6, that is exactly two residents, as required.

  • S and O stand on floors 1 and 3, and the single floor between them is floor 2, held by E, as required.

  • R on floor 6 is immediately above T on floor 5, as required.

  • S on floor 1 or 3 is below R on floor 6, as required.

  • S and O may swap floors 1 and 3, so the full arrangement is not unique, but floor 5 holds T in both arrangements. The answer to this question is therefore uniquely determined: T.

title: And live on six different floors of the same building.
subject: Reasoning
subtopic: Floor or Level Based Arrangement (Vertical Seating)
text: F, E, R, P, Q and L live on six different floors of the same building. The lowermost floor in the building is numbered 1, the floor above it, number 2 and so on, till the topmost floor is numbered 6. Only R lives above L. Only E lives below P. How many people live between P and L?
solution:
Concept. In a floor puzzle the word "only" makes a clue an exact count, not a mere comparison. "Only X lives above Y" says the number of people above Y is exactly one, which pins Y absolutely: in a building of n floors numbered 1 at the bottom to n at the top, a person with exactly k people above them lives on floor n − k, and a person with exactly k people below them lives on floor k + 1.

Concept (cont.). Once two floors are pinned, the number of people living strictly between floor a and floor b (with a < b) is b − a − 1. That count depends only on the two pinned floors, never on how the still-unplaced people are distributed among the remaining floors.

Application to this arrangement.

  1. Six people occupy six floors, one person per floor, numbered 1 (lowest) up to 6 (topmost).

  2. "Only R lives above L" → exactly one person lives above L, so L is on floor 6 − 1 = 5, and the single person above, R, is on floor 6.

  3. "Only E lives below P" → exactly one person lives below P, so P is on floor 1 + 1 = 2, and the single person below, E, is on floor 1.

  4. Floors 1, 2, 5 and 6 are now occupied by E, P, L and R, so the two people left, F and Q, take the two floors left, 3 and 4, in some order.

  5. Apply the between-count: with P on floor 2 and L on floor 5, the number of people strictly between them is 5 − 2 − 1 = 2 — the residents of floors 3 and 4.

Final arrangement.

Cross-check and contrast.

  • The two clues fix E, P, L and R uniquely and leave F and Q interchangeable on floors 3 and 4. The arrangement is therefore only partly determined, yet the quantity asked for is fully determined: whichever way F and Q sit, floors 3 and 4 are still the only floors strictly between floor 2 and floor 5, so the count is 2 either way.

  • Common trap: reading "only R lives above L" as the weaker "R lives above L" would allow L on any floor below R and make the count indeterminate. The word "only" is what converts a comparison into an exact count and pins the floors.

  • Sanity check on the endpoints: no one lives above R (floor 6) and no one lives below E (floor 1), which is consistent with R being the single person above L and E the single person below P.

Taking this count at face value, 4 floors lie strictly between P’s floor and L’s floor, so their floor numbers would differ by 5.

title: Five books and are kept one above the other in
subject: Reasoning
subtopic: Floor or Level Based Arrangement (Vertical Seating)
text: Five books A, B, C, D and E are kept one above the other in such a way that 'E' is above 'A', 'C' is below 'D', 'A' is above 'D' and 'B' is below 'C'. Which book is kept at the lowermost position?
solution:
Translate each clue into an 'above/below' relation (top of the stack is higher).

E is above A -> E > A. A is above D -> A > D. C is below D -> D > C. B is below C -> C > B.

Linking these gives the single ordering from top to bottom: E, A, D, C, B.

Hence the book at the lowermost position is B.

optionFeedback.html: In the final stack (top to bottom: E, A, D, C, B), C sits second from the bottom, with B still below it, so it is not at the lowermost position.
From A > D > C, D lies in the middle of the stack with both C and B beneath it, so it cannot be the lowermost book.
Combining the clues gives the order E > A > D > C > B, so B has no book beneath it.
Since E is above A and A is above D, A stays near the top of the stack, not at the bottom.

title: DSSSB TGT English 24 Aug 2025 5-7 PM Q19
subject: Reasoning
subtopic: Floor or Level Based Arrangement (Vertical Seating)
text:
Seven boxes, A, B, C, D, K, L and M, are kept one over the other, but not

necessarily in the same order.

Only two boxes are kept below K. Only one box is kept above L. Only one box

is kept between L and D. B is kept immediately above M. C is kept at some

place below A.

How many boxes are kept between A and B?
solution:
Concept

In a linear floor/box-stacking arrangement, first place any element that has an absolute-position clue (a stated count of items below or above it fixes that element's slot from one end). Once such anchors are fixed, apply the relative-order clues (immediately above/below, a stated gap between two elements) to lock the remaining slots, and use any leftover inequality clue (one element below another) only to break ties among the slots that are still open.

Application

  1. Number the seven slots 1 (bottom-most) to 7 (top-most). The clue about K's position states that two boxes are kept below K, so K takes slot 3 (slots 1 and 2 lie below it).

  2. The clue about L's position states that one box is kept above L, so L takes slot 6 (only slot 7 lies above it).

  3. The clue about the gap next to L and D states that one box is kept between L and D. With L fixed at slot 6, the only open slot that leaves exactly one box between it and L is slot 4, so D takes slot 4 and slot 5 becomes the single box between them.

  4. B is kept immediately above M, so B's slot number is exactly one more than M's. The still-open slots are 1, 2, 5 and 7; the only pair among these that differs by exactly one is 1 and 2, so M takes slot 1 and B takes slot 2.

  5. Slots 5 and 7 remain for A and C. C is kept at some place below A, meaning C's slot number is smaller, so C takes slot 5 and A takes slot 7.

  6. The complete bottom-to-top order is M, B, K, D, C, L, A.

Cross-check

Checking every clue against this order: two boxes (M, B) lie below K (slot 3); one box (A) lies above L (slot 6); exactly one box (C) lies between L and D; B sits immediately above M; and C sits below A. All five clues hold. Counting the boxes strictly between B (slot 2) and A (slot 7) covers slots 3 to 6 — K, D, C and L — so four boxes are kept between A and B.

optionFeedback.html: A count of four follows from spanning, both endpoints included, from the box placed by the clue about K's position to the box placed by the clue about L's position; that span covers four boxes.

A count of three follows from spanning, both endpoints included, from the box placed by the clue about the gap next to L and D to the box placed by the clue about L's position; that span covers three boxes.
A count of one follows from spanning, both endpoints included, only the box placed by the clue about the gap next to L and D; that span covers one box.

A count of two follows from spanning, both endpoints included, from the box placed by the clue about K's position to the box placed by the clue about the gap next to L and D; that span covers two boxes.

title: Sukanya is Ayushman’s wife. Lekha is Sukanya’s sister. Nisha is
subject: Reasoning
text: Sukanya is Ayushman’s wife. Lekha is Sukanya’s sister. Nisha is Lekha’s mother. Mukesh is Nisha’s husband. Piyush is Nisha’s son. How is Ayushman related to Mukesh?
solution:
Concept: In blood-relation puzzles, a person who marries into a family takes an “in-law” relationship to their spouse’s parents: the husband of a couple’s daughter is their son-in-law. To find how any two people relate, first turn every sentence in the stem into a parent-child or marriage link, build one family tree from those links, then read the relationship straight off the tree.

Application:

  1. Sukanya is Ayushman's wife, so Ayushman and Sukanya are married.

  2. Lekha is Sukanya's sister, so Lekha and Sukanya share the same mother and father.

  3. Nisha is Lekha's mother, and since Sukanya is Lekha's sister, Nisha is Sukanya's mother too.

  4. Mukesh is Nisha's husband, which makes Mukesh Sukanya's father.

  5. Piyush is Nisha's son, so Piyush is Sukanya's brother — Mukesh and Nisha's three children are Piyush, Lekha, and Sukanya.

  6. Ayushman is married to Mukesh's daughter Sukanya, so Ayushman is Mukesh's son-in-law.

Cross-check: Viewed from Mukesh's side: his son Piyush's wife would be his daughter-in-law, while the husbands of his daughters Lekha and Sukanya are his sons-in-law. Ayushman, as Sukanya's husband, falls in that second group, confirming the relationship independently of the step-by-step trace.

Ayushman is Mukesh's son-in-law.

optionFeedback.html: Brother-in-law describes a marriage link within Mukesh's own generation — either Ayushman marrying Mukesh's sister, or Mukesh marrying Ayushman's sister. The stem never states that Sukanya is Mukesh's sister, so this relationship does not hold between Ayushman and Mukesh.

Being Nisha's son is Piyush's own position in the family, earned by birth. Ayushman has no birth tie to Mukesh at all — his connection is only through marrying Sukanya — so the direct blood label 'son' does not describe his relationship to Mukesh.

Brother requires sharing the same parents as Mukesh. Ayushman was never born into Mukesh's family — his entire connection is through marriage — so no sibling label describes his relationship to Mukesh.
Sukanya, Ayushman's wife, shares Lekha's mother Nisha, and Nisha's husband Mukesh is therefore Sukanya's father — so Ayushman, as the husband of Mukesh's daughter, is Mukesh's son-in-law.

subject: Reasoning

P is daughter of N → N is parent

title: Kiran is the father of Ravi. Ravi is the brother
subject: Reasoning
text: Kiran is the father of Ravi. Ravi is the brother of Kavya. Then, how is Kavya related to Kiran ?
solution:
CONCEPT: In a family-relation (blood-relations) puzzle, two people who share the same father or mother are siblings. The word 'brother' fixes only the speaker's own gender as male — it does not, by itself, state the other sibling's gender; that comes from the name or wording given, since a father's child is called his son or his daughter depending on that gender.

APPLICATION: Kiran is the father of Ravi, so Ravi is Kiran's child. Ravi is the brother of Kavya, so Ravi and Kavya are siblings who share the same father, Kiran. The name Kavya is a female name, so Kavya is Kiran's daughter, not his son.

CROSS-CHECK — the other options do not fit:

  • Mother-in-law would require a marriage relationship (e.g. being the mother of one's spouse); no marriage appears anywhere in this puzzle, only a father-child link.

  • Sister correctly describes Kavya's relation to Ravi, but the question asks for Kavya's relation to Kiran, a different person.

  • Grandmother belongs one generation above Kiran; Kavya, as Ravi's sibling, is in the same generation as Ravi — one generation below Kiran, not above.

So Kavya is Kiran's daughter.

optionFeedback.html: A mother-in-law relationship exists only through marriage — for instance, being the mother of one's spouse. The puzzle never mentions any marriage, so this relationship type cannot apply here.
Kavya being Ravi's sibling makes ‘sister’ an accurate description of her relation to Ravi — but the question asks how she is related to Kiran, not to Ravi, so this answers the wrong pairing.

A grandmother sits one generation above a person's parent. Kiran is already established as a parent (of Ravi), so someone in the generation above him would have to be one of Kiran's own parents — which Kavya, described only as Ravi's sibling, is not.
Ravi is Kiran's child, and Kavya is described as Ravi's sibling, so Kavya shares the same father as Ravi — Kiran. Since Kavya is a female name, that parent-child link makes her Kiran's daughter.

title: Is the brother of is the father of is the
subject: Reasoning
text: A is the brother of B, C is the father of D, E is the mother of B. A and D are brothers. How E relates to C ?
solution:
To determine how E relates to C, we need to map out the family relationships step-by-step.

Step-by-Step Relationship Analysis
Analyze the statements:

"A is the brother of B": A and B are siblings.

"E is the mother of B": Since A and B are siblings, E is also the mother of A.

"A and D are brothers": Since A and D are brothers, they share the same parents. Therefore, E is also the mother of D.

"C is the father of D": Since D is A's brother, C is also the father of A and B.

Determine the final relationship:

E is the mother of the children (A, B, and D).

C is the father of the same children (A, B, and D).

Therefore, E and C are husband and wife.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. E is the mother of the children, while C is the father of the same children. This places E in the same generation as C, not in a younger generation as a niece would be.
Incorrect. E is the mother of C's children, which defines their relationship as spouses (husband and wife), not as siblings.
Incorrect. Selecting "Aunty" would imply E is C's sister-in-law or aunt. However, since E is the mother of C's children, this relationship is fundamentally incorrect.
Correct. As E is the mother of the children (A, B, and D) and C is the father of those same children, they are married to each other, making E the wife of C.

title: And are brothers. and are sisters. A's son is D's
subject: Reasoning
text: A and B are brothers. C and D are sisters. A's son is D's brother. How is B related to C?
solution:
To determine how B is related to C, let's map out the family connections step-by-step.

Step-by-Step Analysis
A and B are brothers: This means they share the same parents.

A's son is D's brother: If A has a son, and that son is the brother of D, then D must also be A's child.

title: Direction: Read the following information carefully and answer the questions
subject: Reasoning
text:
Direction: Read the following information carefully and answer the questions based on given information.
In a family of eight members, there are two married couples and no child has single parent. K is the brother-in-law of T. Y is the aunt of S. O is the grandson of N. Q is the daughter-in-law of K. P is not the daughter of N. S is not the brother of O. T is the uncle of Y.

How is Q related to N?
solution:
Concept:

In a family-relations puzzle, first fix each person's generation (using clues like grandson, aunt, uncle, brother-in-law) and gender, then read the asked relation off the constructed family tree. An “-in-law” relation always attaches through a marriage link — it is one step removed from the direct blood relation of the same base word (for example, a daughter-in-law is a son's wife, not one's own daughter).

Application:

  1. Q is the daughter-in-law of K, so K has a son and that son's wife is Q. K and the son's mother form the first married couple; the son and Q form the second married couple. The puzzle fixes the whole family at exactly TWO married couples, and “no child has a single parent” means every child in this tree belongs to one of those two couples — so any child of the son and Q could become a parent in turn only by forming a THIRD couple, which the family does not have. This tree is therefore capped at exactly three generations: K's generation, the son's generation, and any children of the son and Q.

  2. K is the brother-in-law of T, so T is the sibling of K's spouse — placing T in K's own generation.

  3. T is the uncle of Y, so T's sibling (K's spouse) is a parent of Y. That makes Y a child of K and K's spouse, and a sibling of K's son.

  4. Y is the aunt of S, so Y's sibling (K's son, married to Q) is a parent of S. S is therefore a child of K's son and Q, in the youngest generation.

  5. O is the grandson of N. A grandson is always two generations below his grandparent, and step 1 fixed this tree at exactly three generations — so only a member of the OLDEST generation (K or K's spouse) can have a grandson; K's own son, being one generation below K, cannot have a grandson within this three-generation limit. All eight names denote eight distinct people, and K already carries his own separate label, so N cannot be K himself. N can therefore only be K's spouse.

  6. With K, N, T, Y and Q now placed, the only unassigned name left is P, and the only role in the tree still without a name is K and N's son (Q's husband, parent of S) — so P must fill that role. “P is not the daughter of N” independently confirms P is male, consistent with being this son rather than a second daughter alongside Y.

  7. N's only grandchildren, through her son P and Q, are S (already fixed in step 4) and O — so O is S's sibling. “S is not the brother of O” then confirms S is female, which fits the tree without contradiction.

Cross-check:

  • Member count: K, N, T, Y, P, Q, S, O — exactly eight people, matching the given family size.

  • Married-couple count: (K, N) and (P, Q) — exactly two couples, matching “two married couples.”

  • “No child has a single parent” holds: Y and P (children of K and N) and S and O (children of P and Q) each have both parents present in the family.

Result:

Q is married to N's son (P), so by definition Q is N's daughter-in-law.

A “sister” label needs Q and N to share the same parents. Nothing in the family tree gives Q and N a common parent.
A “mother” label needs Q to be N's own parent. Nothing in the family tree makes Q a parent of N.
A “mother-in-law” label needs Q to be the parent of N's spouse. Nothing in the family tree makes Q a parent of N's spouse.
Q is the wife of N's son, established step by step through the family tree built from the clues; a son's wife is, by definition, his mother's daughter-in-law.

title: Girl introduced boy as the son of the daughter of the father of her uncle
subject: Reasoning
text: A girl introduced a boy as the son of the daughter of the father of her uncle. The boy is the girl's ______.
solution:
Concept

Relation-chain puzzles often leave the SIDE of a relative (paternal or maternal) unspecified — e.g. 'uncle' could be either parent's brother. Resolve that kind of ambiguity with two rules together: (1) since this is a single-answer puzzle, the reading that matches an actually offered choice is the intended one — a reading that can only ever land on a relation not in the option list is discarded; (2) among the readings that survive rule 1, the standard convention is to assume no additional unstated relatives — each remaining phrase names the person already required to connect the chain back to the querent, not a hypothetical extra sibling. Apply the general definitions — 'father of X' is X's parent, 'daughter of Y' is Y's female child, 'son of Z' is Z's male child — and sketch a small family tree as you trace the chain.

Step-by-step application

  1. Let U = the girl's uncle; in principle U could be her father's brother or her mother's brother.

  2. If U is the girl's PATERNAL uncle, “the father of U” is her paternal grandfather, and “his daughter” can only be U's sister — the girl's father's sister, i.e. an aunt (never the girl's mother, since the mother married into that family and isn't the paternal grandfather's own daughter). That aunt's son would be a cousin, a relation that isn't among the offered options — so by rule 1 this reading is discarded.

  3. So U must be the girl's MATERNAL uncle. “The father of U” = the girl's maternal grandfather, F.

  4. “The daughter of F” is a sister of U — either the girl's own mother, or a different sister of U (a maternal aunt). By rule 2 (no extra unstated relative), this daughter is the one already required to connect the chain back to the girl: her own mother, M.

  5. “The son of the daughter of F” = M's son, i.e. the girl's mother's son.

  6. A mother's son, being a person distinct from the girl, is the girl's brother.

Cross-check

Checking in reverse: the boy is F's grandson through his mother M; M is F's daughter and a sibling of the maternal uncle U — exactly the family tree the given diagram shows. Both decision points are load-bearing: taking U as the paternal uncle, or taking F's daughter as a different maternal aunt, would each land on a 'cousin' relation that has no matching option — only the fully maternal, direct-lineage reading lands on an offered choice, which is why the standard, published resolution of this well-known puzzle gives 'brother'.

Visual family tree

optionFeedback.html: Tracing the phrase step by step — the father of the girl's maternal uncle, that person's daughter (her own mother, by the puzzle's direct-lineage reading), and finally that daughter's son — lands on a person of the same generation as the girl herself, connected through the sibling link the phrase describes, which is exactly what 'brother' names.
This comes from treating the last relation word in the phrase as if it attaches straight back to the girl, making the boy her own son — but the phrase describes someone else's son, not the girl's.
This comes from reading only the middle part of the phrase — 'the father of her uncle' — and stopping there, without carrying the description through its final two steps (a daughter, then a son).

This confuses a relation created by marriage (son-in-law) with the phrase's relations, which are all built from direct parent-child links (father, daughter, son) — no marriage step ever enters the chain.

Which of the following mean(s) that F is the father of T?

(I) R % F & S % N & T

(II) R % F & S % N # T

(III) R # F & S % N # T

(IV) R % F + S # N # T
solution:
Concept — In a coded-relationship chain every symbol relates only the two letters standing immediately on either side of it, and the chain is read from left to right. Calling one person the father of another needs two independent facts to hold at the same time: that person has to be male, and the other has to be his child. Maleness comes from a male-specific link such as husband or son. Parenthood can be reached directly through a parent link, or indirectly through marriage, because the husband of a woman who is the mother of a child is that child's father; and since siblings share the same parents, a parent of one sibling is a parent of the other.

So two things have to be located inside a chain before F can be called the father of T:

  • a link that marks F as male, which here can only be the husband link or the son link;

  • a route from F to T that ends in parenthood, either because F is given directly as a parent of T, or because F is the husband of a woman who is the mother of T or of a sister of T.

Applying it — Each statement is decoded link by link, and the last column records what the decoded chain makes F to T.

Statement

Links, read from left to right

What the chain makes F to T

I. R % F & S % N & T

R is the mother of F; F is the husband of S; S is the mother of N; N is the husband of T

F is the husband of N's mother, so F is the father of N; T is the wife of N, which makes F the father-in-law of T

II. R % F & S % N # T

R is the mother of F; F is the husband of S; S is the mother of N; N is the sister of T

N is a sister of T, so N and T are siblings and S is the mother of T as well; F is the husband of S and is therefore the father of T

III. R # F & S % N # T

R is the sister of F; F is the husband of S; S is the mother of N; N is the sister of T

the same core chain: S is the mother of T, so F, being her husband, is the father of T; the link joining R to F adds nothing

IV. R % F + S # N # T

R is the mother of F; F is the son of S; S is the sister of N; N is the sister of T

F is marked as a son and sits one generation below S, N and T; S is a sister of N and N is a sister of T, so T is a sibling of F’s mother, that is F’s maternal aunt or uncle, and in no case his child

Cross-check — Statements II and III carry the same operative sub-chain, F & S % N # T: F is the husband of S, S is the mother of N, and N is the sister of T. That sub-chain is precisely the indirect route to fatherhood set out above, and the point where those two statements differ, R as the mother of F against R as the sister of F, lies outside it and changes nothing. The remaining two break at an identifiable link instead: in I the final link is a husband link, so T arrives as a spouse rather than as a child, and in IV the second link marks F himself as a son.

The statements that mean F is the father of T are therefore II and III.

solution:
Concept: in a symbol-coded blood-relation chain every operator fixes two things at once — the relationship it names and the gender of the person written on its left. '&' makes that person a husband (male), '%' makes that person a mother (female), '#' makes that person a sister (female), and '+' makes that person a son (male).

A chain is read link by link from left to right; each link binds only the pair it stands between, and the links together assemble one family tree. By definition X is the father-in-law of Y when X is male and Y is married to a child of X, so a chain qualifies only when it makes F male, gives F a child, and marries that child to M.

Applying the definition to each chain:

  • Chain I — F & T % S # U & M

    1. F & T: F is the husband of T, so F is male and T is his wife.

    2. T % S: T is the mother of S, so S is a child of T and of her husband F.

    3. S # U: S is the sister of U, so U is a sibling of S and therefore another child of F and T.

    4. U & M: U is the husband of M, so M is the wife of U.

    M is married to U, who is a child of F, and F is male — every part of the definition is met.

  • Chain II — F # T % S # U & M

    1. F # T: F is the sister of T, so F is female.

    2. T % S: T is the mother of S.

    3. S # U: S is the sister of U, so U is another child of T.

    4. U & M: U is the husband of M.

    F is the sister of the mother of M's husband, so F is an aunt of M's husband, and a female relative cannot be a father-in-law.

  • Chain III — F & T % S # U % M

    1. F & T: F is the husband of T.

    2. T % S: T is the mother of S, so S is a child of F and T.

    3. S # U: S is the sister of U, so U is another child of F and T.

    4. U % M: U is the mother of M, so M is the child of U.

    M is the child of a child of F, so F stands as M's maternal grandfather rather than as the father of M's spouse.

  • Chain IV — F & T # S # U % M

    1. F & T: F is the husband of T.

    2. T # S: T is the sister of S, so S is T's sibling and no parent-child link is created here.

    3. S # U: S is the sister of U, so U is a sibling of T as well.

    4. U % M: U is the mother of M.

    F is the husband of the sister of M's mother, so F stands as M's uncle by marriage.

solution:
In coded blood-relation puzzles, decode each symbol into its stated relation first, then chain the relations together — tracking gender and generation at each link — to work out how the two named people are connected.

  1. R - V means R is the wife of V, so R is female and married to V.

  2. V x T means V is the brother of T, so V and T are siblings and V is male.

  3. T ÷ W means T is the daughter of W, so W is a parent of T.

  4. Since V is T's sibling and T is W's child, V is also W's child — and because V is male, V is the son of W.

  5. R is the wife of V, and V is the son of W, so R is the wife of W's son.

That makes R the daughter-in-law of W. Cross-check: W's children are T (daughter) and V (son); R, married to the son V, fits exactly the daughter-in-law relationship — confirming the answer.

A son-in-law is, by definition, the husband of one's daughter — a male role. 'R - V' establishes R as V's wife, i.e. female, so R cannot fill a role that requires being male.

A mother-in-law is, by definition, a parent of one's spouse — someone from the generation above the reference person. R is connected to W only by marrying W's own child, which places R alongside that child's generation, not in a parental role above W.

For R to be W's mother, R would need to be a parent of W. But the chain only ever connects R to W's family through marriage — R is the wife of W's son — which places R in the son's generation, not as a parent of W.

Applying it to M ÷ L − N + P × Q

  3. N + P means N is the sister of P, so P is a sibling of N — and N is M's mother.

  4. P × Q means P is the brother of Q, which confirms that P is male.

P is male and is the brother of N, who is M's mother. The brother of one's mother is the maternal uncle. Hence P is the maternal uncle of M.

P's own link to V (step 1) already places her as V's daughter in the same generation as N.

title: DSSSB TGT Special Education Teacher 24 Jun 2025 Shift 3 Q25
subject: Reasoning
text:
In a certain code language,

‘A ÷ B’ means ‘A is the sister of B’,

‘A # B’ means ‘A is the brother of B’,

‘A + B’ means ‘A is the wife of B’ and

‘A % B’ means ‘A is the father of B’.

How is A related to K if ‘A + B % G ÷ H # K’?
solution:
Concept:

In coded blood-relation puzzles, each symbol stands for one direct family relation (parent-of, sibling-of, spouse-of). To find how one person relates to another placed several links away, decode every symbol in the chain one link at a time, then combine the direct relations using standard family rules: siblings share the same parents, and a person's spouse holds the same parental relation to that person's children.

Application:

  1. Decode each symbol used in ‘A + B % G ÷ H # K’: ‘+’ = wife of, ‘%’ = father of, ‘÷’ = sister of, ‘#’ = brother of.

  2. A + B → A is the wife of B.

  3. B % G → B is the father of G.

  4. G ÷ H → G is the sister of H, so G and H share the same parents.

  5. Since B is the father of G, and H shares G's parents, B is also the father of H.

  6. H # K → H is the brother of K, so H and K share the same parents.

  7. Since B is the father of H, and K shares H's parents, B is also the father of K.

  8. A is the wife of B, and B is the father of K, so A is the mother of K.

Cross-check:

Retracing the chain independently: A's own generation is fixed only by the '+' (wife-of) link to B, so A and B belong to one generation. Every later step (the '%' link to G, then the shared-sibling steps to H and K) stays inside B's child generation. So G, H, and K are all one generation below A and B, and A's relation to any of them, including K, is that of mother.

optionFeedback.html: 'Mother' denotes a female relation one generation senior to the referent, standing in a parent's position to the referent by descent.
'Sister' denotes a female relation in the same generation as the referent, standing in a sibling's position to the referent by descent.
'Daughter' denotes a female relation one generation junior to the referent, standing in a child's position to the referent by descent.
'Wife' denotes a female relation in the same generation as the referent, standing in a spouse's position to the referent by marriage.

title: Clock is so placed that at noon its minute hand
subject: Reasoning
text: A clock is so placed that at 12 noon its minute hand points towards North-east. In which direction does its hour hand point at 1:30 p.m.?
solution:
To determine the direction of the hour hand at 1:30 p.m., we must first calculate the rotation applied to the clock face.

Step-by-Step Analysis
Determine the Clock's Rotation:

Normally, at 12:00 noon, the minute hand points North.

In this scenario, the minute hand points North-East.

North-East is a 45-degree clockwise rotation from North. Therefore, the entire clock has been rotated 45 degrees clockwise.

Determine the Hour Hand's Position at 1:30 p.m.:

On a standard clock, the hour hand at 1:30 is halfway between the 1 and 2 marks.

Each hour mark represents 30 degrees (360 degrees / 12 hours).

At 1:00, the hour hand is at 30 degrees from the vertical (North). At 1:30, it has moved halfway to the 2 o'clock mark (an additional 15 degrees).

Standard position = 30 degrees + 15 degrees = 45 degrees East of North.

Apply the Clock's Rotation:

Since the clock is rotated 45 degrees clockwise, we add this rotation to the standard position.

Total direction = 45 degrees (standard position) + 45 degrees (clock rotation) = 90 degrees from North.

90 degrees from North is East.

title: Mahesh is going towards East. If he has to go
subject: Reasoning
text: Mahesh is going towards East. If he has to go towards North, which of the following options should he NOT choose?
solution:
Treat each 'right' as a 90 degrees clockwise turn and each 'left' as a 90 degrees turn the other way. Starting while facing East, the net turning of a full sequence decides the final direction.

From East, ending up facing North needs a net turn equal to one left turn (which is the same as three right turns).

Sequence right, right, left, right, right: the turns add up to a net of three rights, taking him from East to South to West to North - he faces North.

Sequence right, right, left, left, left: the rights and lefts combine to one net left, taking him from East to North - he faces North.

Sequence right, right, right: from East, three rights go South, West, North - he faces North.

Sequence right, left, right, left: every right is cancelled by the left that follows it, so the net turn is zero and he still faces East - this one never reaches North.

So the sequence he should NOT choose is right, left, right, left.

title: Man is facing North-West. He turns in the clockwise direction,
subject: Reasoning
text: A man is facing North-West. He turns 90° in the clockwise direction, then 180° in the anticlockwise direction and then another 90° in the same direction. Which direction is he facing now?
solution:
Concept

Direction problems are solved on the 8-point compass, read clockwise as N → NE → E → SE → S → SW → W → NW and back to N, where each adjacent point is 45° apart. A clockwise turn moves you along that order; an anticlockwise turn moves you against it (N → NW → W → SW → S …). Apply each turn to the direction you are CURRENTLY facing, one turn at a time, and “the same direction” always refers to the sense of the turn that came immediately before it.

Step-by-step

  1. Start facing North-West.

  2. Turn 90° clockwise: moving clockwise two 45° steps from North-West passes through North and lands on North-East. Now facing North-East.

  3. Turn 180° anticlockwise: a half-turn always points you to the exact opposite direction, so North-East becomes South-West. Now facing South-West.

  4. Turn 90° in the same direction: “same direction” means anticlockwise again. Moving anticlockwise two 45° steps from South-West passes through South and lands on South-East. Now facing South-East.

Cross-check

Track the net rotation in signed degrees (clockwise positive), with North-West at 315°: 315° + 90° − 180° − 90° = 135°. A bearing of 135° is South-East, confirming the result.

optionFeedback.html: South follows if the start is read as due North rather than North-West (dropping the diagonal); the three turns are then applied exactly as stated: 90° clockwise from North reaches East, the 180° turn reaches West, and the final 90° in the same anticlockwise sense reaches South. Starting from the actual North-West bearing does not produce this path.

South-West is reached if the starting orientation is misread as North-East instead of North-West — an easy mix-up between the two diagonals. Working through the same 90° clockwise, 180°, and 90° anticlockwise sequence from that wrong start does not correspond to the man's actual orientation given in the question.

West follows from misreading the initial bearing as due East rather than North-West. That substitution changes every subsequent turn's starting point, so tracking the stated 90° clockwise, 180°, and 90° anticlockwise sequence from this wrong start does not correspond to the man's actual orientation given in the question.

South-East follows directly from tracing the three turns from North-West: a clockwise quarter-turn reaches North-East, the 180° half-turn flips that to South-West, and a final anticlockwise quarter-turn lands on South-East. The signed-degree check 315° + 90° − 180° − 90° = 135° gives the same bearing of South-East.

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q84
subject: Reasoning
text: From a point Satish started walking towards north and walked 2 km. He then turned on his right and walked 3 km and again turned to his right and walked 4 km. Finally he turned to his left. In which direction he is now walking?
solution:
In direction-sense problems, every turn is measured relative to the direction currently faced. On a standard compass, the four cardinal directions in clockwise order are North, East, South, and West. A right turn always rotates the direction of motion 90° clockwise, and a left turn always rotates it 90° counter-clockwise.

  1. Satish starts at a point facing North and walks 2 km.

  2. He turns right: rotating 90° clockwise from North gives East. He walks 3 km facing East.

  3. He turns right again: rotating 90° clockwise from East gives South. He walks 4 km facing South.

  4. He turns left: rotating 90° counter-clockwise from South gives East. He is now walking towards East.

This can be verified using compass bearings, where North = 0°, East = 90°, South = 180°, and West = 270°. Each right turn adds 90° and each left turn subtracts 90°: 0° + 90° (right) = 90° (East); 90° + 90° (right) = 180° (South); 180° − 90° (left) = 90° (East). Both methods agree that Satish is finally walking towards East.

Hence, Satish is now walking towards East.

optionFeedback.html: East is the compass direction reached by rotating 90° clockwise from North.
West is the compass direction reached by rotating 90° counter-clockwise from North (equivalently 270° clockwise).
North is the compass direction taken as the 0° reference on a standard compass rose, directly opposite South.
South is the compass direction reached by rotating a full 180° from North, directly opposite it.

title: Tara starts from Point and walks towards the south. She
subject: Reasoning
text: Tara starts from Point C and walks 23 m towards the south. She takes a left turn, walks 10 m and then takes a left turn, walks 17 m, reaches Point D and stops. Bruce starts from Point P, which is 15 m from the east of Point D. He walks 6 m towards the north, takes a left turn, walks 16 m and stops at Point Q. What is the shortest distance between Point Q and Point C? (All turns are 90-degree turns only)
solution:
Concept: A direction-sense path is solved by fixing one origin and two perpendicular axes, then writing every leg as a change in exactly one coordinate — take east as the positive x-direction and north as the positive y-direction.

A left turn rotates the walker 90 degrees anticlockwise, so the facing cycles from north to west to south to east and back to north. Once both endpoints are written as coordinates, the shortest distance between them is the straight line joining them.

Application: track each leg of the two walks as a change in one coordinate.

  1. Place Point C at the origin (0, 0), with east as +x and north as +y.

  2. Tara walks 23 m south from C, reaching (0, -23), and is now facing south.

  3. Facing south, her left turn points her east; walking 10 m east takes her to (10, -23).

  4. Facing east, her next left turn points her north; walking 17 m north takes her to (10, -23 + 17) = (10, -6), which is Point D.

  5. Point P lies 15 m east of D, so P is at (10 + 15, -6) = (25, -6).

  6. Bruce walks 6 m north from P, reaching (25, -6 + 6) = (25, 0), and is now facing north.

  7. Facing north, his left turn points him west; walking 16 m west takes him to (25 - 16, 0) = (9, 0), which is Point Q.

  8. C is at (0, 0) and Q is at (9, 0), so the east-west change is 9 and the north-south change is 0. The straight-line distance is the square root of the sum of the squares of these two changes.

    √(92 + 02) = √81 = 9

Cross-check: Tara ends 10 m east and 6 m south of C, while Bruce ends 16 m west and 6 m north of P. Bruce’s 6 m northward leg exactly cancels Tara’s 6 m southward net displacement, so Q sits on the same east-west line as C and no north-south gap survives.

The whole east-west account is therefore 10 m east from Tara, plus 15 m east from D to P, minus 16 m west from Bruce, giving 9 m east. With the north-south gap zero, the straight-line distance equals that east-west gap.

The shortest distance between Point Q and Point C is 9 m.

text: Shyam walked 20 metres towards south. Then he turned to his left and walked 15 meters. He again turned to his left and walked 20 metres. He then turned to his right and walked 10 metres. How far and in which direction is Shyam from the starting point?
solution:
Concept: In direction-sense problems, track the walker's facing direction using compass bearings — North = 0°, East = 90°, South = 180°, West = 270°, increasing clockwise. A left turn subtracts 90° from the current bearing and a right turn adds 90° to it. Convert every leg of the walk into an East-West and North-South displacement, then find the net distance from the start using the distance formula.

  1. Start at the origin, facing South (bearing 180°). Walking 20 m south moves the position from (0, 0) to (0, −20).

  2. Turning left changes the bearing to 180° − 90° = 90° (East). Walking 15 m east moves the position to (15, −20).

  3. Turning left again changes the bearing to 90° − 90° = 0° (North). Walking 20 m north moves the position to (15, 0).

  4. Turning right changes the bearing to 0° + 90° = 90° (East). Walking 10 m east moves the position to (25, 0).

The straight-line distance √(25² + 0²) = 25 m confirms a purely eastward displacement with no residual north-south offset.
