title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2014 Q13
subject: Reasoning
text: A person travels 12 km due North, then 15 km due East, after that 15 km due West and then 18 km due South. How far is he from the starting point?
solution:
When a person walks through a sequence of directional legs, the straight-line distance back to the starting point (the resultant displacement) is found by resolving every leg onto two perpendicular axes — North-South and East-West — and combining the legs on each axis. Movements in opposite directions on the same axis cancel each other out (they subtract); if the net displacement on one axis works out to zero, the resultant distance equals just the magnitude of the net displacement on the other axis.

  1. Group the four legs onto the two axes: North (12 km) and South (18 km) lie on the North-South axis; East (15 km) and West (15 km) lie on the East-West axis.

  2. Net East-West displacement = 15 km East − 15 km West = 0 km, so the East and West legs cancel out exactly.

  3. Net North-South displacement = 12 km North − 18 km South = 6 km net towards the South.

  4. Since the East-West component is 0 km, the straight-line distance from the starting point equals the magnitude of the North-South component alone, i.e. 6 km.

As a check, using the general resultant-distance formula, distance = √((net East-West)² + (net North-South)²) = √(0² + 6²) = √36 = 6 km, which matches the direct reading above.

So the person ends up 6 km from the starting point.

title: Question: Directions: Each of the questions below consists of question

Directions: Read the information and answer the given questions.

  • A * B (18m) means A is 8m north of B

  • A% B (24m) means A is 14m south of B

  • A & B (28m) means A is 18m east of B

Now, consider the following information:

M * N (16m), O @ P (32m), N & O (36m), Q & P (42m), S @ R (58m), S% T (27m), U% Q (20m), R * U (22m), X * R (30m)

In which direction is M with respect to P?
solution:
In a coded direction-and-distance puzzle, each linking symbol fixes two things at once: a compass direction and a rule for converting the bracketed figure into the actual displacement it represents. Once every symbol's direction and conversion rule is read off the four defining statements, the whole network of relations can be redrawn on a standard grid (north = up, east = right), and any person's position relative to any other follows by adding displacement vectors along a connecting chain of statements.

  1. Read the four defining lines to fix each symbol's direction: '*' = north, '%' = south, '&' = east, '@' = west.

  2. Check the conversion rule from the same four lines: 18m to 8m, 24m to 14m, 28m to 18m, 35m to 25m - every bracketed figure is exactly 10m more than the real displacement, so actual distance = bracketed figure minus 10m.

  3. Apply this rule to the three statements that connect M to P: O @ P (32m) gives O is 22m west of P; N & O (36m) gives N is 26m east of O; M * N (16m) gives M is 6m north of N.

  4. Fix P at the origin (0, 0). Since O is 22m west of P, place O at (-22, 0).

  5. Since N is 26m east of O, N is at (-22 + 26, 0) = (4, 0) - so N is 4m east of P.

  6. Since M is 6m north of N, M is at (4, 0 + 6) = (4, 6) - so M is 4m east and 6m north of P.

  7. A point that is both to the east and to the north of the origin, with neither component zero, lies in the compass direction lying between due east and due north of that origin.

Re-checking just the east-west chain independently confirms this: the 22m westward leg (O to P) and the 26m eastward leg (N to O) combine to a net eastward shift from P to N, and the purely north-south leg (N to M) only ever adds a vertical shift on top of that - it cannot cancel or reverse the horizontal shift. So M can never end up purely north, or west, or south of P; the displacement must carry both an eastward and a northward part.

M lies to the Northeast of P.

Skipping the standard bracket-to-actual conversion on the O-to-P relation specifically (using its raw bracketed figure as if it were already the real distance) while converting every other relation as usual is the specific arithmetic slip that produces this reading for M's position relative to P.

Reading the M * N relation with subject and reference swapped (as if it described N's position relative to M, rather than M's position relative to N) while converting and applying every other relation as usual is the specific misreading that produces this reading for M's position relative to P.

title: Which of the following has the same relationship as 'Correspondent

title: 'Wise' is related to 'Clever' in the same way as
subject: Reasoning
text: 'Wise' is related to 'Clever' in the same way as 'Lethargic / Lifeless ' is related to '_______'.
solution:
This is a synonym-based word analogy: the first pair — 'Wise' and 'Clever' — are two words carrying nearly the same meaning (both describe an intelligent, mentally sharp person). To complete such an analogy, the missing word must share the same core meaning as the second stem term, not merely its general theme.

'Lethargic' and 'Lifeless' both describe someone drained of energy and unwilling to exert effort — a state of dullness or inactivity. Among the given options, 'Lazy' carries exactly this meaning: an unwillingness to work or move, i.e., low energy and inactivity. This mirrors the Wise-Clever relationship precisely — the same core meaning expressed in different words.

The remaining options sit in a different dimension altogether — intelligence, not energy or vitality:

  • Foolish — describes a lack of sense or intelligence; the opposite quality of 'wise', not a match for the low-energy sense of 'lethargic/lifeless'.

  • Cunning — describes being clever in a sly, deceptive way; still an intelligence-related trait, unrelated to energy or vitality.

  • Idiot — denotes a very unintelligent person; the same intelligence dimension as 'Foolish', not energy-related.

Hence, 'Lazy' is the word that completes the synonym analogy, matching 'Lethargic / Lifeless' the same way 'Clever' matches 'Wise'.

optionFeedback.html: 'Foolish' means lacking good sense or sound judgment — essentially the OPPOSITE of 'wise', not a word sharing 'wise's meaning. That opposite-type relationship doesn't match the same-meaning pattern the 'Wise-Clever' pair sets up.

'Cunning' means clever in a sly, deceptive way — it stays close to restating 'clever' itself rather than pairing with the analogy's actual second stem term, so it doesn't complete the pattern correctly.

'Lazy' means unwilling to exert effort or move, i.e., lacking energy — exactly the meaning shared by 'lethargic' and 'lifeless'. Just as 'Clever' shares 'wise's meaning, 'Lazy' shares the meaning of the second stem term.
'Idiot' means a very unintelligent person — the same OPPOSITE-of-'wise' trap as 'Foolish', not a word sharing 'wise's meaning, so it breaks the same-meaning pattern too.

title: The following questions consists of two words each of them
subject: Reasoning
text:
The following questions consists of two words each of them have certain relationship to each other, followed by four lettered pairs of words. Select the lettered pair that has the same relationship as of the original pair of words.

Carnivore: Herbivore
solution:
Concept

A word-pair analogy asks you to identify the underlying relationship that connects the two given words, then find the lettered pair that is joined by the very same relationship in the same direction. The relationship itself — not the topic of the words — is what must match.

Application

Define the link in the original pair Carnivore : Herbivore. Both words name an animal by the kind of food it eats: a carnivore is an animal whose food is flesh, and a herbivore is an animal whose food is plants. So the hidden bridge is “defined by the food it eats,” and the ordered foods are flesh first, plants second.

Now look for the pair that places those two foods in the same order: the food of a carnivore followed by the food of a herbivore. The pair Flesh : Plant does exactly this — flesh is what the carnivore eats and plant is what the herbivore eats, in matching order — so it carries the identical relationship as the original pair.

Cross-check

Test each alternative against the rule “food of a flesh-eater : food of a plant-eater”:

  • Animal : Bird — this is a category and one of its members (a bird is a kind of animal), which is a class-to-subclass link, not a diet link.

  • Camel : Giraffe — both are plant-eating animals, so there is no flesh-eater versus plant-eater contrast at all.

  • Horse : Lion — these are the animals themselves rather than their foods, and they run plant-eater then flesh-eater, the reverse of the required order.

Only Flesh : Plant restates the carnivore-then-herbivore diet relationship in the correct order, so it is the matching pair.

optionFeedback.html: Animal and bird sit in a category-and-member relation: a bird is one kind of animal. That is a class-to-subclass pairing, a different kind of link from the original word pair.
Camel and giraffe share the same diet as each other — both feed on plants — so the two words sit in a same-category relation rather than the kind of paired relation the original word pair shows.
Flesh is the food a carnivore feeds on and plant is the food a herbivore feeds on, taken in that order — so these two words sit in a meat-eater's-food to plant-eater's-food relation.
Horse and lion name two animals — a plant-eater and a meat-eater — so the words sit at the level of the creatures, while the order here runs plant-eater first and meat-eater second.

title: In each of the following question group of three interrelated
subject: Reasoning
text:

solution:
The three given words form a group based on where their edible parts grow.

Potato (a tuber), carrot (a root) and radish (a root) are all crops whose edible part grows underground.

Among the alternatives, the groundnut (peanut) is the only one that also grows underground: after its flowers are pollinated above the ground, the developing pods bury themselves in the soil and mature below the surface.

Tomato (a fruit on a vine), spinach (a leafy green) and sesame (seed pods on a tall stalk) all grow above the ground, so they do not belong to the group.

Hence the word that belongs to the same group is Groundnut.

optionFeedback.html: A tomato grows above the ground as a fruit on a vine, so it does not share the defining feature of the given group, whose members all grow underground.
Like potato, carrot and radish, a groundnut (peanut) develops and matures underground. It therefore belongs to the same group: edible parts that grow below the soil.
Spinach is a leafy green vegetable whose edible part grows above the ground, so it does not fit the group of crops that grow underground.
Sesame seeds form in pods that develop above the ground on tall stalks, so sesame does not share the underground-growth feature of the given words.

title: What is related to 'Sympathy' in the same way as
subject: Reasoning
text: What is related to 'Sympathy' in the same way as 'Virtue' is related to 'Vice'?
solution:
Concept: In a word-pair analogy, first identify the LOGICAL RELATION inside the given pair, then reproduce that exact relation on the new word. Here the relation in Virtue : Vice is ANTONYMY — a virtue is a morally good quality and a vice is its moral opposite. So the task reduces to: find the word that is the OPPOSITE of Sympathy.

Application: Sympathy is the feeling of pity, compassion or fellow-feeling for another's suffering. Its direct opposite is the disposition to be indifferent to — or to enjoy — another's suffering, which is exactly Cruelty. Therefore Cruelty completes the analogy: Virtue : Vice :: Sympathy : Cruelty (good↔bad opposites in both pairs).

Contrast: Compare the other choices against the required ANTONYM test:

  • Kindness — a near-synonym of Sympathy, not its opposite, so it breaks the good↔bad pattern.

  • Emotion — a broader category that Sympathy belongs to (a part–whole link), not an antonym.

  • Charity — an associated benevolent act, again on the same positive side rather than the opposite side.

Cross-check: Only the opposite-meaning word mirrors Virtue → Vice; substituting any positive or category word fails the antonym relation. Hence Cruelty is the answer.

optionFeedback.html: Emotion is the broad category that sympathy itself falls under, a part-to-whole link rather than the opposite-meaning relation that Virtue : Vice demands.
Cruelty means indifference to, or even pleasure in, another's suffering; in meaning it stands directly opposite to sympathetic fellow-feeling.
Kindness sits on the same compassionate side as sympathy — it is a near-synonym, not an antonym, so it cannot mirror an opposites relation.
Charity is a benevolent act associated with sympathy and stays on its positive side; the model pair requires the contrary quality, not a related virtue.

solution:

This word names the confident expectation that conditions will improve; that is the direct opposite of despair, so it completes the antonym pattern exactly as victory does for defeat.

title: What is related to 'Courage' in the same way as
subject: Reasoning
text: What is related to 'Courage' in the same way as 'Kindness' is related to 'Cruelty'?
solution:
This is an antonym-pair analogy: the second word in the given pair is the opposite of the first, so the missing word must be the opposite of the target word.

'Kindness' and 'Cruelty' are opposite personality traits: a kind disposition versus a cruel one. Applying the same antonym relationship to 'Courage', the missing word must name the disposition of someone who lacks courage.

  • Bravery: means the same as courage (a synonym), so it cannot supply the required opposite.

  • Valour: also means the same as courage (a synonym), so it fails the relationship for the same reason.

  • Fear: names a passing emotion that even courageous people can feel in danger, not the stable character trait of lacking courage.

'Cowardice' is the disposition-word that stands in direct opposition to courage, completing the analogy the same way 'Cruelty' opposes 'Kindness'.

optionFeedback.html: Bravery is a synonym of courage — it means fearlessness in the face of danger, the same quality as courage itself. Since the given pair links two opposite traits, a word with the same meaning as courage cannot complete the analogy.
Cowardice names the character trait of avoiding danger or difficulty out of a lack of courage — a direct opposite disposition to courage, exactly parallel to how cruelty opposes kindness.
Fear is the feeling a person has when facing danger, and both courageous and cowardly people can feel it — calling it the opposite of courage confuses a shared feeling with a personality label.
Valour, like courage, describes boldness and heroism in danger — it is a synonym, not an opposite, so pairing it with courage would repeat the same quality rather than reverse it.

solution:
This item follows the pattern Instrument : Physical quantity it measures : Standard unit of that quantity. For the pattern to hold, all three elements of a pair must correctly correspond to one another - the instrument must actually measure the stated quantity, and the stated unit must actually be the standard unit for that quantity.

In the given set, a thermometer measures temperature, and temperature is expressed in degrees - the instrument, the quantity, and the unit all match. Checking the options against the same triad: a scale measures length, and length is expressed in meters, so every element of this pair corresponds correctly, exactly mirroring the given relationship.

  • Barometer : Pressure : Watt - a barometer does measure pressure, but pressure is expressed in units such as the pascal, not the watt, which is the unit of power, so the quantity and unit named here do not correspond.

Scale : Length : Meter is the only pair where the instrument, the quantity it measures, and the unit all correctly correspond, so it shares the same relationship as the given set.

A voltmeter measures potential difference (voltage), not current. The SI unit of current is the ampere.

Analogies of the pattern Noun : Adjective test word-formation: the adjective describes 'of, relating to, or occurring during' the time period named by the noun. English forms many such time-of-day adjectives (e.g. Night -> Nocturnal, from the same root sense of 'occurring at night').

  • Evening is itself a time-period noun, parallel to Night or Morning, not the derived adjective, so it breaks the noun-to-adjective pattern.

Matutinal completes the analogy, following the same noun-to-adjective, time-of-day relationship as Night : Nocturnal.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q13
subject: Reasoning
text:
‘After’ and ‘before’ are converse relational terms: if event X is after event Y, event Y is before event X. Choose the pair that has the same relationship.

After : Before
solution:
Concept

Converse relational terms describe the same relation from opposite viewpoints. If one term expresses a relation from X to Y, its converse expresses that relation from Y to X.

Application

  1. In “After : Before,” if event X is after event Y, event Y is before event X.

  2. Likewise, if person X is person Y’s successor, person Y is person X’s predecessor.

  3. Thus, “Successor : Predecessor” preserves the same converse relation in the same order.

Contrast and cross-check

  • “First : Second” lists ordinal positions in forward order; the two words are not converse descriptions of one relation.

  • “Present : Past” names time periods relative to now; the words do not reverse one relation between two entities.

  • “Contemporary : Historic” gives descriptive time categories rather than converse relational terms.

  • “Successor : Predecessor” passes the converse check: if X is Y’s successor, Y is X’s predecessor.

Therefore, the matching pair is “Successor : Predecessor.”

This pair contains the terms “Present : Past.”

This pair contains the terms “Successor : Predecessor.”

Two numbers share the same digital root exactly when their difference is a multiple of 9. Each option here is a number pair; three pairs share a digital root and one does not.

  1. 46 - 10: digit sum of 46 is 4 + 6 = 10, which reduces further to 1 + 0 = 1 (digital root 1); digit sum of 10 is 1 + 0 = 1 (digital root 1). Same digital root, so this pair is consistent.

  2. 42 - 33: digit sum of 42 is 4 + 2 = 6 (digital root 6); digit sum of 33 is 3 + 3 = 6 (digital root 6). Same digital root, so this pair is consistent.

  3. 25 - 43: digit sum of 25 is 2 + 5 = 7 (digital root 7); digit sum of 43 is 4 + 3 = 7 (digital root 7). Same digital root, so this pair is consistent.

  4. 12 - 91: digit sum of 12 is 1 + 2 = 3 (digital root 3); digit sum of 91 is 9 + 1 = 10, which reduces further to 1 + 0 = 1 (digital root 1). The digital roots 3 and 1 do not match, so this pair breaks the pattern.

Cross-check with differences: a matched digital-root pair always differs by a multiple of 9 - 46 minus 10 = 36 = 9 times 4, 42 minus 33 = 9 = 9 times 1, and 25 minus 43 = -18, a multiple of 9. But 12 minus 91 = -79, and 79 is not a multiple of 9, confirming the mismatch found above.

12 - 91 is the only pair whose numbers do not share a digital root (equivalently, the only pair whose difference is not a multiple of 9), so it is the odd number pair.

42 - 33: The digit sum of 42 is 4 + 2 = 6, and the digit sum of 33 is 3 + 3 = 6 - the same digital root, so this pair follows the pattern.
25 - 43: The digit sum of 25 is 2 + 5 = 7, and the digit sum of 43 is 4 + 3 = 7 - the same digital root, so this pair follows the pattern.

12 - 91: The digit sum of 12 is 1 + 2 = 3, while the digit sum of 91 reduces to 1 (9 + 1 = 10, then 1 + 0 = 1). Since 3 and 1 are different digital roots, this pair does not fit the shared pattern of the other three, making it the odd number pair.

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q80
subject: Reasoning
text: The number of squares in the following figure is
solution:
Concept

To count every square in a square grid of side n (made of n × n unit cells), count squares of each size k = 1, 2, ..., n separately. A square of side k can have its top-left corner placed in (n − k + 1) row positions and (n − k + 1) column positions, so there are (n − k + 1)2 squares of that size. The total number of squares is the sum of these counts over every size from 1 to n.

Application

Here the figure is a 4 × 4 grid of unit cells (n = 4), so squares of four different sizes must be counted:

  1. Size 1×1: (4 − 1 + 1)2 = 42 = 16 squares — every unit cell.

  2. Size 2×2: (4 − 2 + 1)2 = 32 = 9 squares.

  3. Size 3×3: (4 − 3 + 1)2 = 22 = 4 squares.

  4. Size 4×4: (4 − 4 + 1)2 = 12 = 1 square — the outer boundary.

Adding these gives 16 + 9 + 4 + 1 = 30 squares in total. The two diagonal lines drawn corner-to-corner only cross the grid at points that already lie on existing grid lines, so they split a few unit cells into triangles but do not close off any new right-angled region — they add no extra square.

Cross-check

The same total can be verified with the sum-of-squares formula n(n + 1)(2n + 1) / 6. For n = 4 this gives 4 × 5 × 9 / 6 = 180 / 6 = 30, which matches the direct count.

Result

So the figure contains 30 squares.

title: How many triangles are there in the following figure?
subject: Reasoning
text: How many triangles are there in the following figure?
solution:
Concept: When several straight lines meet at one point (an apex) and land on n distinct points of a straight base line, every pair of those base points, taken together with the apex, is automatically a triangle, because the two connecting lines and the base segment between them are already drawn. That gives C(n, 2) triangles from the fan alone. On top of the fan, separately look for (a) smaller triangles carved out by any extra diagonal cutting across a fan-triangle, and (b) larger triangles that appear only because two segments are actually one continuous straight line through a shared vertex, letting a side run further than it first looks. A reliable count always checks all three layers, and never stops at the smallest visible pieces.

Applying it here:

  1. Five straight lines run from the apex down to five points on the base line (the two outer corners and three points in between). Any 2 of these 5 points, taken with the apex, form a triangle whose sides are already drawn, giving C(5, 2) = 10 triangles from this fan alone.

  2. Above each of those 4 base segments, one diagonal rises from its left end and meets the cevian standing over its right end at a point partway up that cevian, not at the base itself. That touch-point is a new, distinct vertex, so the diagonal splits the one-segment fan-triangle above each base segment into two different smaller triangles: a lower one (diagonal + the short stretch of the cevian below the touch-point + the base segment) and an upper one (diagonal + the apex + the remaining stretch of the same cevian above the touch-point, ending at the touch-point rather than at the far base point). Because each of these 8 triangles uses a touch-point instead of a base point, none of them repeats any triangle already counted in Step 1. Four segments times 2 gives 8 further triangles.

  3. Below the base line, the middle base point drops a straight line to a point beneath the figure, and the two outer base corners also run straight down to that same point, forming an inverted triangle that is itself split into two halves by that middle vertical line: 3 triangles in this region (the two halves plus the whole).

  4. The line from the apex to the middle base point does not stop at the base; it continues, unbroken, all the way down to the point below. Because it is genuinely one straight line, each outer edge of the upper figure combines with it and with the matching lower edge to trace one full-height triangle running from the apex to the bottom point: 2 more triangles that are easy to miss if the upper and lower halves are counted separately.

  5. Total: 10 + 8 + 3 + 2 = 23.

title: Read the following information carefully and answer the questions below
subject: Reasoning
text:
Read the following information carefully and answer the question below it.

Rashmi is very fond of collecting greeting cards. Her collection of 211 cards has a good mix of Birthday cards, New Year cards, Deepawali cards, Christmas cards, and even a Marriage Anniversary card. The number of Birthday cards is equal to the sum of the other cards except the Marriage Anniversary card. The number of New Year cards is double the number of Deepawali cards, which in turn is double the number of Christmas cards.

Ques: The number of Birthday cards in the collection is
solution:
Concept: When several quantities in a word problem are linked by a chain of 'double of' ratios and one quantity is defined as the sum of specific other quantities, express every linked quantity as a multiple of one common base unit, write a single equation from the stated grand total, solve for that base unit, and substitute back for the quantity the question asks about.

  1. Let the number of Christmas cards be c.

  2. Deepawali cards are double the Christmas cards, so Deepawali cards = 2c.

  3. New Year cards are double the Deepawali cards, so New Year cards = 2 × 2c = 4c.

  4. The passage mentions only one Marriage Anniversary card, so that category contributes exactly 1 card to the total.

  5. Birthday cards equal the sum of every other category except the Marriage Anniversary card: Birthday cards = New Year cards + Deepawali cards + Christmas cards = 4c + 2c + c = 7c.

  6. The full collection is the sum of all five categories: Total = Birthday cards + New Year cards + Deepawali cards + Christmas cards + Marriage Anniversary card = 7c + 4c + 2c + c + 1 = 14c + 1.

  7. Equate this to the stated collection size: 14c + 1 = 211, so 14c = 210 and c = 15.

  8. Substitute back: Birthday cards = 7c = 7 × 15 = 105.

Cross-check: Because Birthday cards are defined as the sum of the other three non-Marriage-Anniversary categories, the 210 remaining cards (211 minus the single Marriage Anniversary card) must split into two equal halves — the Birthday-card half and the combined New Year, Deepawali and Christmas half — so 210 ÷ 2 = 105 confirms the count directly, independent of the individual doubling values. Individually, Christmas = 15, Deepawali = 30, New Year = 60 and Marriage Anniversary = 1, and 105 + 60 + 30 + 15 + 1 = 211, matching the stated collection size exactly.

So Rashmi's collection has 105 Birthday cards.

105 is exactly the New Year, Deepawali and Christmas cards added together — the passage's only exclusion from that sum is the single Marriage Anniversary card — making it the one figure consistent with the passage's stated 211-card total.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q9
subject: Reasoning
text: Which of the following words cannot be formed using the letters of ‘PROFESSIONAL’?
solution:
Concept

A word can be formed from another word only when every required letter occurs no more times than it occurs in the source word.

A reliable method is to build a letter-frequency inventory for the source and compare each candidate’s required frequency with that inventory.

Application

  1. The source word PROFESSIONAL contains P1, R1, O2, F1, E1, S2, I1, N1, A1, and L1; it contains M0.

  2. PASSION requires P1, A1, S2, I1, O1, and N1, all within the source inventory.

  3. LESSON requires L1, E1, S2, O1, and N1, all within the source inventory.

  4. NORMAL requires N1, O1, R1, M1, A1, and L1. Its requirement M1 exceeds the source inventory M0.

  5. FINAL requires F1, I1, N1, A1, and L1, all within the source inventory.

Cross-check

Deleting the letters used by PASSION, LESSON, or FINAL from separate copies of PROFESSIONAL leaves no negative count. Trying the same with NORMAL fails immediately at M because the source contains no M.

Therefore, NORMAL cannot be formed from the letters of PROFESSIONAL.

optionFeedback.html: For PASSION, the required/source counts are P 1/1, A 1/1, S 2/2, I 1/1, O 1/2, and N 1/1.
For LESSON, the required/source counts are L 1/1, E 1/1, S 2/2, O 1/2, and N 1/1.
For NORMAL, the required/source counts are N 1/1, O 1/2, R 1/1, M 1/0, A 1/1, and L 1/1.
For FINAL, the required/source counts are F 1/1, I 1/1, N 1/1, A 1/1, and L 1/1.

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q91
subject: Reasoning
text:
Read the following information and answer the question:

Dinesh, Ritesh, Rajesh and Ramesh are classmates. Dinesh and Ritesh study Physics and Biology. Rajesh and Dinesh study Physics and Mathematics. Ritesh and Ramesh study Chemistry and Physics. Rajesh and Ramesh study Chemistry and Mathematics.

Who among these students studies Mathematics, Biology and Physics?
solution:
Concept

In a linked-attribute puzzle, each statement pairs two people with two shared subjects. A person's full subject profile is not fixed by a single sentence — it is the union of every subject pair attributed to them across all the statements that name them. Two statements about the same person must be merged before comparing that person against the question's target combination.

Application

Read every statement as a person-to-subject-pair link:

  1. Statement 1 links Dinesh and Ritesh to Physics and Biology.

  2. Statement 2 links Rajesh and Dinesh to Physics and Mathematics.

  3. Statement 3 links Ritesh and Ramesh to Chemistry and Physics.

  4. Statement 4 links Rajesh and Ramesh to Chemistry and Mathematics.

Each person is named in exactly two statements; merge those two subject pairs to get their combined profile:

Person

Combined Subject Profile (from the two statements naming them)

Dinesh

Physics, Biology, Mathematics

Ritesh

Physics, Biology, Chemistry

Rajesh

Physics, Mathematics, Chemistry

Physics, Chemistry, Mathematics

The question's target combination is Mathematics, Biology, and Physics. Comparing each merged profile against this target identifies exactly one exact match.

  • Rajesh's and Ramesh's profiles both carry Mathematics but neither carries Biology, since Biology appears only in statement 1, which names Dinesh and Ritesh — so neither profile can equal the target.

  • That leaves only the profile built from statements 1 and 2 — Physics, Biology, and Mathematics — as the exact match for the target combination, confirming Dinesh.

title: Suppose you are married and you and your partner attend
subject: Reasoning
text: Suppose you are married and you and your partner attend a party with three other married couples. Several handshakes took place. No one shook hands with himself (or herself) or with their partner, and no one shook hands with the same person more than once. After all hand shaking was completed, suppose you asked each person, including your partner, how many hands they had shaken. Each person gave a different answer. How many hands did your spouse shake?
solution:
Answer: 3 — your spouse shook 3 hands.

Explanation:

There are 4 couples (you plus three other couples), so 8 people total. Each person could have shaken between 0 and 6 hands (they cannot shake their own hand or their partner's). You asked the other seven people and heard seven different answers, so those answers must be the numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.

  • If someone shook 6 hands, they shook hands with every person except their partner. That partner therefore shook 0 hands.

  • More generally, if a person shook k hands, their partner must have shaken 6 − k hands. So answers pair up to sum to 6 (0 with 6, 1 with 5, 2 with 4).

  • Those three complementary pairs account for six of the seven people you asked. The only remaining answer among the seven is 3, so the person left (your spouse) must have shaken 3 hands.

Therefore your spouse shook 3 hands.

Those pairings leave 3 as the only remaining count for your spouse, so 1 is not correct.

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q86
subject: Reasoning
text: Some playing cards are divided among A, B, C, D and E in such a way that A gets one card less than B, C gets 2 cards more than D, and E gets 3 cards more than B. D and B get an equal number of cards. Who will get the least number of cards?
solution:
Concept

When a puzzle states only relative differences between quantities (more/less/equal), assign one variable to the quantity most statements refer to, rewrite every other quantity as that variable plus or minus a constant, and compare the constants -- the smallest constant offset identifies the smallest quantity, without needing to know the variable's actual value.

Application

Let the number of cards B receives be x. Translate each condition into an equation in terms of x:

  1. "A gets one card less than B" gives A = x - 1.

  2. "D and B get an equal number of cards" gives D = x.

  3. "C gets 2 cards more than D" gives C = D + 2 = x + 2.

  4. "E gets 3 cards more than B" gives E = x + 3.

Expressed in terms of x: A = x - 1, B = x, D = x, C = x + 2, E = x + 3. Comparing the constant offsets (-1, 0, 0, +2, +3), A carries the smallest offset, so A holds the fewest cards.

Cross-check

Substitute any value satisfying the conditions, say x = 10: A = 9, B = 10, D = 10, C = 12, E = 13. Ordering these -- 9, 10, 10, 12, 13 -- confirms A holds the least number of cards, matching the algebraic comparison.

Hence, A gets the least number of cards.

optionFeedback.html: D's count comes from the condition that D gets two cards fewer than C.
C's count comes from the condition that C gets two cards more than D.
B's count comes from the condition that B and D receive equal numbers of cards.
A's count comes from the condition that A gets one card fewer than B.

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q83
subject: Reasoning
text: I meet with my friend on each Sunday. On first Sunday I met with him at 12.30 PM, on second Sunday at 1.20 PM, on third Sunday at 2.30 PM, on fourth Sunday at 4 PM. When did I meet my friend on fifth Sunday?
solution:
When the successive differences of a sequence themselves form an arithmetic progression (that is, the second differences are constant), the sequence follows this constant-second-difference pattern. The next term is found by extending the pattern of differences, not by adding a fixed interval.

  1. Convert every recorded meeting time to minutes measured from 12:00 noon: Sunday 1 = 12:30 PM = 30 minutes; Sunday 2 = 1:20 PM = 80 minutes; Sunday 3 = 2:30 PM = 150 minutes; Sunday 4 = 4:00 PM = 240 minutes.

  2. Find the first differences between consecutive Sundays: 80 minus 30 = 50 minutes; 150 minus 80 = 70 minutes; 240 minus 150 = 90 minutes.

  3. Find the second differences, that is, the differences between the first differences: 70 minus 50 = 20 minutes; 90 minus 70 = 20 minutes — a constant value.

  4. Since the second difference is constant at 20 minutes, extend the pattern: the next first difference is 90 plus 20 = 110 minutes.

  5. Add this to Sunday 4's value: 240 plus 110 = 350 minutes measured from 12:00 noon.

  6. Convert 350 minutes back into a clock time: 350 minutes equals 5 hours and 50 minutes, so the fifth meeting is at 5:50 PM.

As an independent check, fit the values with the standard formula for a sequence with constant second difference d and first term-to-term gap a: T(n) = T(1) + (n - 1) x a + [(n - 1)(n - 2) / 2] x d, using a = 50 and d = 20. For the fifth Sunday (n = 5): T(5) = 30 + 4 x 50 + 6 x 20 = 30 + 200 + 120 = 350 minutes, the same value obtained by extending the difference pattern, confirming 5:50 PM.

optionFeedback.html: This option's time falls within the 4 PM hour block.
This option's time falls within the 5 PM hour block.
This option's time falls within the 6 PM hour block.
This option's time falls within the 7 PM hour block.

title: How many minimum number of colors will be required to
subject: Reasoning
text: How many minimum number of colours will be required to paint all the faces of a cube such that no two adjacent faces have the same colour?
solution:
Concept — Colouring a solid so that no two faces sharing an edge receive the same colour is a graph-colouring problem. The number of colours can never be fewer than the largest group of faces that are pairwise adjacent (each one touching every other); that count is only confirmed as the answer once you also exhibit a valid colouring that achieves it. Faces that never touch may reuse a colour.

Applying it to the cube — A cube has 6 faces that form 3 pairs of opposite faces. Opposite faces sit across from each other and never share an edge, so each pair can be given a single colour. Faces taken from two different pairs always meet along an edge, so they must differ.

Opposite pair

Colour

Top and Bottom

Colour 1

Front and Back

Colour 2

Left and Right

Colour 3

This scheme uses 3 colours, and every pair of faces that actually touch carries different colours.

Check — Fewer is impossible: at every corner of the cube three faces meet, and those three are mutually adjacent, so they alone already force at least 3 distinct colours. More is unnecessary: the opposite-pair scheme above already satisfies the rule with 3. Hence the minimum is 3.

optionFeedback.html: Three colours are enough because the cube's six faces split into three pairs that sit directly opposite one another; opposite faces never share an edge, so each pair can carry one shared colour while every pair of faces that do touch still ends up different.

This is what you get if you picture the cube as a vertical band of four side faces that each take a colour in turn, then colour the top and bottom by repeating two of those. That mental model locks in the side faces' colours before checking the actual edge contacts between them.

This value treats the cube as if a colour could be repeated only once — almost every face coloured uniquely, with a single repeat permitted. That one-repeat limit is a self-imposed restriction the question never states; the only real constraint is that faces sharing an edge must differ.

This is the total number of faces on a cube, so it assigns every single face its own colour. That treats the cube as though every face were in contact with every other face, which is the assumption worth examining here.

subject: Reasoning
text: Three positions of a cube are shown below. Which number will be opposite to the face containing 3?
solution:
In a puzzle showing multiple views of a cube, two faces shown together in the same view always share an edge, so they are adjacent and can never be opposite each other. Consequently, if two different views both display the same pair of faces, the one face left over in each of those views is that face's true opposite — this is the Two-Common-Faces Rule.

  1. The first view shows faces 1, 2, and 5, while the third view shows faces 5, 2, and 3 — both views share the same pair, 2 and 5.

  2. By the rule above, the face left over in the first view (1) must be opposite the face left over in the third view (3).

  3. Independently, the first view places 1 next to 2 and 5, and the second view places 1 next to 6 and 4 — so 1 is adjacent to all four of the other faces (2, 4, 5, 6). A face with four adjacent neighbours has only one face left to be its opposite, which confirms 1 is opposite 3.

So the face opposite the one marked 3 is 1.

optionFeedback.html: The two views that repeat the pair 2 and 5 are the first and third — leaving 1 and 3 as the two faces excluded from that shared pair, so 1 sits directly across from 3. This also matches the adjacency check: 1 touches 2, 4, 5, and 6 across the views that show it, accounting for all four of its neighbours and leaving only 3 unaccounted for — its opposite.
4's opposite comes from comparing the views, and it works out to 5, not 3 — 4 is never paired with 3 by the two-common-faces rule in any pair of views here.
5 appears in the same view as 3 (the third view shows 5, 2, and 3 together), and faces shown together in one view are adjacent, not opposite — so 5 cannot be the face across from 3.
6's opposite works out to 2, not 3 — comparing the views that contain 6 against the others leaves 2, not 3, as the excluded face paired with it.

title: Two different positions of the same dice are shown, the
subject: Reasoning
text: Two different positions of the same dice are shown, the six faces of which are marked from A to F. Select the letter that will be on the face opposite to the face showing the letter ‘C’.
solution:
When two positions of the same die are shown, the three faces visible in any single view (its Top, its Front-facing face, and its Right-facing face) are always mutually adjacent, so none of them can be opposite one another. A letter common to both views lets us align the two views along that shared face; the remaining difference between the views then becomes a pure spin about that shared face's axis, and tracking that spin (Front → Right → Back → Left → Front) tells us exactly which hidden face pairs with which visible one.

  1. In the first position: Top = F, Front = E, Right = C, so F, E and C are mutually adjacent — none of them is opposite another among the three.

  2. In the second position: Top = D, Front = B, Right = F, so D, B and F are mutually adjacent likewise.

  3. F is the letter common to both positions. Tipping the second die so its Right face (F) becomes the new Top (matching the first die's Top) moves its old Top (D) to the new Left, while its Front (B) is unaffected by this tip; the second position now reads Top = F, Left = D, Front = B.

  4. Both dice now show F on Top, so the only remaining difference between them is a spin about the vertical (Top) axis. Comparing the first die's Front → Right pair (E → C) with the re-oriented second die's Front → Left pair (B → D) shows the spin must run clockwise (viewed from above) through Front → Right → Back → Left → Front — a counter-clockwise spin would force the Front face to read C instead of B, which contradicts the given data.

  5. Applying that clockwise spin to the first die's own hidden faces: its Front (E) moves into the Right slot, its Right (C) moves into the Back slot, its hidden Left moves into the Front slot, and its hidden Back moves into the Left slot. Matching this against the re-oriented second position (Front = B, Left = D) gives: the first die's hidden Left = B and its hidden Back = D.

  6. Left is always opposite Right on a die, so the first die's hidden Left (B) is opposite its Right face (C).

Checking the remaining pairs confirms consistency: Front (E) pairs with the newly-found Back (D), and Top (F) pairs with the one letter that never appears in either view, A — so the three opposite pairs are F–A, E–D and C–B, using all six letters A–F exactly once.

So the face opposite C is B.

optionFeedback.html: F is the letter common to both given positions — it appears as the Top face in the first position and lands in the very slot (the right-facing position) that C occupied there in the second position. That positional overlap between two separately drawn views tempts the idea that F and C must be opposite faces, but a face's true opposite is fixed by the die's own geometry, not by which drawing slot a letter happens to occupy across two different views.

Aligning the second position so its shared face (F) sits on Top the same way it does in the first position turns the remaining difference between the two drawings into a single 90° spin about the vertical axis. Tracking that spin shows the first position's hidden Left face — which is always opposite its Right face, C — lands on B. So B and C are the opposite pair.

A is the one letter that never appears in either given position. That absence tempts the assumption that whichever letter stays completely hidden throughout must automatically be the answer to any 'opposite face' question — but with six faces and only three shown per view, more than one letter can stay unseen, so simply never being shown does not by itself identify the face opposite the one asked about here.

D is the Top face in the second position and never appears together with C in either drawing. It's tempting to assume that any two letters which never appear together in the same view must be opposite faces, but several letters share that same 'never seen together' relationship with C here, so non-co-occurrence alone does not establish an opposite pair; the actual rotation does not place D opposite C.

title: Cube whose faces are marked with letters is shown below
subject: Reasoning
text: A cube whose faces are marked with letters is shown below in different positions as viewed from different directions. Find the missing letter indicated by the question mark (?).
solution:
On a cube, the six faces form exactly three opposite pairs, and any two faces that appear together in a single view — its top, front and right, say — are, by definition, adjacent, never opposite.

So across several rotated views of the same cube, every pair of letters ever seen together on one view is ruled out as an opposite pair; comparing enough views, together with tracking how faces move under a rotation, pins down every letter's one valid opposite partner.

Apply this to the four given views of the cube:

Front

Right

Cube 1

D

M

S

Cube 2

S

M

W

Cube 3

Y

U

D

Cube 4

W

U

?

Work through the deduction:

  1. Cube 1 shows D, M and S together, so no two of D, M and S can be opposite each other.

  2. Cube 2 shows S, M and W together, so no two of S, M and W can be opposite each other.

  3. Cube 3 shows Y, U and D together, so no two of Y, U and D can be opposite each other.

  4. D is therefore ruled out as the opposite of M and S (from Cube 1) and of U and Y (from Cube 3) — the only letter left for D is W, so D is opposite W.

  5. This adjacency check alone still leaves two possibilities for the remaining letters M, S, Y, U — either (M opposite Y, S opposite U) or (M opposite U, S opposite Y) — since only M-S and Y-U are directly ruled out. Cube 3 and Cube 4 share the same front face, U, so Cube 4 is simply Cube 3 turned about that front-back axis; tracking this turn (not adjacency alone) settles which pairing is correct.

  6. In Cube 3, the hidden left face is opposite the visible right face (D), which is W. So, around the U-axis, Cube 3's faces run Top = Y, Right = D, Left = W, in that rotational order.

  7. Turning Cube 3 about this same axis until its Left face (W) comes to the Top — exactly Cube 4's view — carries Cube 3's old Top face (Y) around into the new Right position. So Cube 4's right face is Y, which fixes M as Y's opposite (not U).

As a further check: Cube 1 and Cube 2 also share one face, M (front); turning Cube 1 about that axis carries its right face (S) onto Cube 2's top face (S) exactly as required, and the same turn carries Cube 1's hidden bottom face onto Cube 2's right face (W) — so Cube 1's bottom face is W. Since top and bottom are always opposite, this independently confirms D is opposite W, matching the elimination above.

Hence the missing letter marked by the question mark is Y.

D lies opposite W on this cube. In Cube 4 the top face is W, so D is the hidden bottom face here and cannot be the visible right face.
Re-derive the three opposite-face pairs from the four views, then apply them to Cube 4's top (W) and front (U) faces and re-check your reasoning for the right face.

title: Cube is cut in two equal parts along plane parallel
subject: Reasoning
subtopic: Painted & Cut Cube Problems, Rotation & Comparison of Dice
text: A cube is cut in two equal parts along a plane parallel to one of its faces. One piece is then coloured red on the two larger faces and green on the remaining, while the other is coloured green on two smaller adjacent faces and red on the remaining. Each is then cut into 32 cubes of same size and mixed up. What is the number of cubes with at least one green face each?
solution:
Concept

When a block built from unit cubes is painted on some outer faces and then diced back into those unit cubes, a small cube carries a given colour on a face exactly when its row/column position falls inside the region that painted face covers; if the colour runs along an entire side wall of the block, every layer stacked beneath that wall carries the colour equally.

Application to this question

The original cube has edge 4, so cutting it once (parallel to a face) gives two equal 4 x 4 x 2 slabs; dicing each slab into unit cubes gives 32 cubes per piece, matching the question.

First piece -- red on the two 4 x 4 faces, green on the four 4 x 2 side walls:

  1. The two big 4 x 4 faces (top and bottom of the slab) are red, so green appears only on the four side walls.

  2. A unit cube touches a green side wall exactly when it sits on the outer ring of the 4 x 4 footprint, because the green wraps the full height of the 2-layer slab.

  3. A 4 x 4 grid has 16 cells; removing the 2 x 2 interior block that never touches a side wall leaves 12 outer-ring cells per layer.

  4. With 2 identical layers, the first piece contributes 12 x 2 = 24 unit cubes with a green face.

Second piece -- green on two adjacent smaller 4 x 2 faces, red on the rest:

  1. Only two of the four side walls are green here, and they are adjacent (they meet along one vertical edge of the slab), so green touches one full row and one full column of the 4 x 4 footprint, not the whole ring.

  2. The row contributes 4 cells and the column contributes 4 cells, but the corner cell where they meet is shared, so it is counted once: 4 + 4 - 1 = 7 cells per layer.

  3. Across the 2 layers of this slab, the second piece contributes 7 x 2 = 14 unit cubes with a green face.

Adding the two pieces together, the number of unit cubes with at least one green face is 24 + 14 = 38.

Cross-check

Count the cubes with no green face instead: the first piece leaves its 2 x 2 interior column untouched by green in both layers (2 x 2 x 2 = 8 cubes), and the second piece leaves the 3 x 3 block away from the green row/column untouched in both layers (3 x 3 x 2 = 18 cubes); 8 + 18 = 26 all-red cubes. The two slabs together hold 64 unit cubes, so 64 - 26 = 38 must carry at least one green face -- the same figure, confirming the count.

optionFeedback.html: This total undercounts the second piece's green-faced cubes: it treats the shared cell at the meeting edge of the two adjacent green walls as excluded from that piece's footprint count rather than included, leaving out cubes that do carry a green face.

This total equals the number of unit cubes in a single piece overall (32), not the narrower count of cubes that actually carry a green face -- it reads as though the whole piece's cube total was taken as the answer without isolating which of those cubes touch a green wall.

This total is obtained by adding the unit cubes touching the four green side walls of the first piece to the unit cubes touching the two adjacent green side walls of the second piece, giving 38 cubes with at least one green face; a complementary check on the all-red cubes in both pieces confirms this figure.

This total matches treating the second piece the same way as the first, as if its green colour wrapped all four side walls instead of just two adjacent ones, over-counting how many of its cubes end up with a green face.

title: Cube with each edge of cm is painted on all
subject: Reasoning
subtopic: Painted & Cut Cube Problems, Rotation & Comparison of Dice
text: A cube with each edge of 4 cm is painted on all faces. How many of 1 cm cubes, cut out of the larger cube, will not have paint on any of its sides?
solution:
Concept: When a large painted cube is cut into smaller unit cubes, only the cubes lying strictly inside (not touching any outer face) stay unpainted. These inner cubes form a smaller cube called the core.

Formula: Number of unpainted cubes = (n - 2)^3, where n is the number of unit cubes along one edge (Edge of large cube / Edge of small cube).

Given: Edge of the large cube = 4 cm, edge of each small cube = 1 cm.

Step 1 - Find n: n = 4 cm / 1 cm = 4.

Step 2 - Apply the formula: Unpainted cubes = (4 - 2)^3 = 2^3 = 2 x 2 x 2 = 8.

Therefore, exactly 8 of the smaller cubes have no paint on any face. The answer is 8.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The unpainted cubes form a (4 - 2) = 2 unit cube on every side, so their count is a perfect cube (2^3). The value 3 is not a perfect cube of (n - 2) and does not match the inner-core count here.

Incorrect. 4 is the value of n (the number of unit cubes along one edge) or the count along a single line, not the three-dimensional inner core. The unpainted cubes require cubing (n - 2), not n itself.
Incorrect. 6 is the number of faces of a cube, not a count of interior cubes. The unpainted cubes come from cubing (n - 2), which does not give 6 for n = 4.
Correct. With n = 4, the unpainted inner core is a (4 - 2) = 2 unit cube, giving 2^3 = 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 cubes with no paint on any face.

title: Cube is colored orange on one face, pink on the
subject: Reasoning
subtopic: Painted & Cut Cube Problems, Rotation & Comparison of Dice
text: A cube is colored orange on one face, pink on the opposite face, green on one face and silver on the remaining faces. This cube is now cut into 125 smaller cubes of equal size. How many smaller cubes have at most two faces colored?
solution:
To determine the number of smaller cubes with "at most two faces colored," we first analyze the structure of the 5 × 5 × 5 cube.

Step-by-Step Analysis
Understand the total: The large cube is cut into 125 smaller cubes (5 × 5 × 5 = 125).

Identify cubes with more than two faces colored:

In a standard cube cut, only the corner cubes have three faces exposed on the outside.

A cube has 8 corners, meaning 8 smaller cubes have three faces colored.

Apply the "at most two" condition:

"At most two" means cubes with 0, 1, or 2 faces colored.

This is equivalent to taking the total number of cubes and subtracting those that have more than two faces colored.

Total cubes (125) - Cubes with 3 faces colored (8) = 117.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. This assumes that all 125 small cubes have at most two faces colored. However, this ignores the 8 corner pieces which always have three faces colored in a standard cube.

Incorrect based on standard geometric logic. This answer would imply that only 4 corners have three faces colored. This might be the intended answer only if the original cube had specific faces uncolored, but based on the text provided, 117 is the geometrically standard result.
Correct. By subtracting the 8 corner cubes (which have 3 faces colored) from the total of 125, we are left with the 117 cubes that have 0, 1, or 2 faces colored.
Incorrect. This result suggests a miscalculation in the subtraction process. You must subtract all 8 corner pieces from the total to isolate the cubes with three faces colored.

title: Cube is made up of one cm. square cubes placed
subject: Reasoning
subtopic: Painted & Cut Cube Problems, Rotation & Comparison of Dice
text: A cube is made up of 125 one-cm unit cubes placed on a table. How many of these small cubes are visible on exactly three sides?
solution:
Concept

In a large cube cut into unit cubes, a small cube is exposed on exactly three sides only at a CORNER, because three mutually perpendicular outer faces meet there. A free-standing cube has 8 corners, but the moment the cube is PLACED ON A TABLE, the whole bottom face rests on the table and is no longer visible. So only the corners of the TOP layer can still show three exposed faces.

Setup

125 unit cubes form a 5 × 5 × 5 stack, since 5 × 5 × 5 = 125. Visible faces are the top face and the four vertical side faces; the bottom face is hidden against the table.

Counting the three-side cubes

  1. Look at the four corners of the TOP layer. Each touches the top face plus two vertical side faces, so each shows exactly three faces. That gives 4 such cubes.

  2. Now check the four corners of the BOTTOM layer. Each rests on the table (bottom face hidden) and is capped by the cube above (top face hidden), leaving only its two vertical sides visible, i.e. just two faces, not three.

  3. Edge cubes (between corners) show two faces, face-centre cubes show one face, and interior cubes show none, so none of these are three-side cubes.

Hence exactly 4 cubes are visible on three sides.

Cross-check

Contrast with the same cube floating in space, where all six outer faces are visible: then every one of the 8 geometric corners shows three faces, giving 8. Placing it on the table hides the bottom face and removes the four bottom corners from the three-side count, halving 8 to 4 -- which is consistent with our direct count.

optionFeedback.html: Each corner of the top layer meets the top face plus two vertical side faces, so a top corner is exactly the kind of unit cube that shows three faces once the slab rests on the table.

This counts every geometric corner of the block as if it were floating in mid-air with all six faces open. It overlooks that the block is resting on a table, so the bottom layer's corners have their lowest face pressed against the surface and never show three faces.

This is the count of edges on a cube, which a solver may recall and pick by reflex. The number of edges of the big block has nothing to do with how many small cubes expose three faces, so reaching for 12 confuses an edge tally with a cube tally.

This is the kind of figure you reach by treating whole rows or layers of border cubes as if each one qualified, for instance multiplying a side length by the number of layers. Three-face exposure is far rarer than such a row- or layer-based count assumes, so the product is much too large.

text: Three positions of a cube are shown below. Which number will be opposite to the face containing 4?
solution:
Concept

On a cube every face has exactly one opposite face and exactly four adjacent faces, and opposite faces can never be visible together in a single view. So any two faces that appear together in one position are ADJACENT, not opposite. Two tools follow from this: (i) the opposite of a target face must be a number that never shares a view with it; and (ii) once a face is seen next to four different faces, the single remaining face must be its opposite.

Application

Read the three positions as Top / Front / Right faces:

Position

Top

Front

Right

First

3

4

5

Second

1

3

5

Third

2

4

3

Collect the faces seen sharing a view with 4:

  • First position: 4 appears with 3 and 5.

  • Third position: 4 appears with 2 and 3.

So 4 is adjacent to 2, 3 and 5. Removing 4 and these three neighbours from {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} leaves two faces that never share a view with 4 — namely 1 and 6 — so the opposite of 4 is one of these two; the views of 4 alone cannot yet decide which.

Resolve the tie using 3. Across the positions 3 is seen with 4 and 5 (first), with 1 and 5 (second) and with 2 (third), so 3 is adjacent to four distinct faces {1, 2, 4, 5}. A face has only four neighbours, so the one face never beside 3 — which is 6 — must be opposite 3. With 6 now fixed as the opposite of 3, it is no longer available to sit opposite 4, leaving 1 as the only possibility.

So the face opposite 4 is 1.

Cross-check

Complete all three pairs: 3 is opposite 6 (just shown) and 4 is opposite 1, which leaves 2 and 5 to pair with each other, so 5 is opposite 2. The three opposite pairs 4–1, 3–6 and 5–2 use each of 1–6 exactly once and contradict none of the given views, a fully consistent assignment that confirms 1 sits opposite 4.

optionFeedback.html: The value 2 is seen together with 4 in the third position (top 2, front 4), so 2 and 4 share a view and must be adjacent faces, not opposite ones. A face adjacent to 4 can never be the one opposite it.

Neither 1 nor 6 ever shares a view with 4, so both start as candidates for its opposite. But 3 is seen beside four different faces, which fixes 6 as the face opposite 3; that uses up 6 and leaves 1 as the face opposite 4. The full pairing 4 with 1, 3 with 6 and 5 with 2 is consistent with every position shown.
The value 5 is shown alongside 4 in the first position (front 4, right 5), so 5 and 4 lie in the same view and are therefore adjacent. Adjacent faces cannot be opposite, so 5 is ruled out.

It is tempting to call 6 the opposite of 4 because 6 never appears in any position. But 3 is seen next to four different faces across the positions, and a face has only four neighbours, so the single face never beside 3 — which is 6 — must be opposite 3. With 6 already paired to 3, it cannot also be opposite 4.

title: Three position of cube are shown below. Which number will
subject: Reasoning
subtopic: Painted & Cut Cube Problems, Rotation & Comparison of Dice
text: Three position of a cube are shown below. Which number will be opposite to the face containing 5?
solution:
Concept

A cube has 6 faces forming 3 pairs of opposite faces. Two faces seen together in any single view are always ADJACENT, never opposite. So the rule is: collect every face that shares a corner/edge with a given face across the views; whichever remaining face never appears beside it is the one OPPOSITE to it.

Application

Read the three views (Top / Left-front / Right):

  1. View 1 — Top 6, Front 4, Right 2: so 6 is adjacent to 4 and 2.

  2. View 2 — Top 3, Front 1, Right 2: so 3 is adjacent to 1 and 2.

  3. View 3 — Top 5, Front 6, Right 1: so 5 is adjacent to 6 and 1.

Now fix the pairs by elimination:

  1. 6 sits next to 4, 2 (view 1) and next to 5, 1 (view 3). The only face never seen beside 6 is 3, so 6 is opposite 3.

  2. 2 sits next to 6, 4 (view 1) and next to 3, 1 (view 2) — i.e. beside 1, 3, 4, 6. The only face never beside 2 is 5, so 2 is opposite 5.

  3. The two faces left over, 1 and 4, must form the last pair, so 1 is opposite 4.

The face opposite 5 is 2.

Cross-check

The three deduced pairs are 5–2, 6–3, 1–4. Test every view: no view shows both members of any pair together — View 1 (6,4,2), View 2 (3,1,2), View 3 (5,6,1) each contain three faces from three different pairs. The pairing is consistent, confirming 5 lies opposite 2.

optionFeedback.html: 4 cannot be opposite 5: view 3 already shows 5 sharing the cube with 6 and 1, and 4 turns out to pair with 1 (the leftover pair). Picking 4 usually comes from pairing the two largest 'front' numbers (4 and 5) without tracking which faces actually meet in the views.

3 is the face opposite 6, not 5 — 6 is the one number never seen beside 3 across the views. Choosing 3 tends to come from mixing up the top faces (6 and 3 both appear on top) and assigning 3 to the wrong partner.
6 is directly beside 5 in view 3 (5 on top, 6 in front), so they share an edge and therefore cannot be opposite. Selecting 6 ignores that adjacency and treats two touching faces as a pair.

2 holds because, across the views, 2 is seen next to 1, 3, 4 and 6, leaving 5 as the only face it never touches — and two faces that are never adjacent across consistent views are opposite. Hence 2 is the face directly opposite 5.

title: Solid cube of each side cms has been painted red,
subject: Reasoning
subtopic: Painted & Cut Cube Problems, Rotation & Comparison of Dice
text: A solid cube of each side 8 cms has been painted red, blue and black on pairs of opposite faces. It is then cut into cubical blocks of each side 2 cm. How many cubes will have one face painted?
solution:
When a cube is painted on all six outer faces and then cut into equal smaller cubes, every small cube's position inside the big cube decides how many painted faces it shows: a corner cube touches three outer faces, an edge cube (not a corner) touches two, a face-centre cube touches only one, and an interior cube touches none.

If each edge of the big cube is divided into n equal parts, these counts always follow fixed formulas: corners = 8, edge cubes = 12(n − 2), face-centre cubes = 6(n − 2)2, interior cubes = (n − 2)3 — no matter how many different colours were used on the outer faces, since colour only labels which face was painted, not how many faces a given small cube touches.

Applying this here:

  1. Big cube side = 8 cm, small cube side = 2 cm, so the edge is divided into n = 8 ÷ 2 = 4 equal parts.

  2. Total small cubes = n3 = 43 = 64.

  3. Small cubes with exactly one painted face = 6(n − 2)2 = 6 × (4 − 2)2 = 6 × 22 = 6 × 4 = 24.

Cross-check against the total: corner cubes = 8, edge cubes = 12(4 − 2) = 24, face-centre cubes = 24 (from the step above), interior cubes = (4 − 2)3 = 8. Sum = 8 + 24 + 24 + 8 = 64, which matches the total number of small cubes, confirming the one-face count.

So 24 small cubes have exactly one face painted.

optionFeedback.html: This count matches the corner small cubes of the big cube — each corner cube sits at a vertex and touches three of the big cube's outer faces, so it actually carries three painted faces, not one; picking the corner-cube count here confuses the three-face group with the one-face group.

16 is simply 4 × 4 — the total number of small cubes visible on one full face of the big cube. But not every cube on that face carries just a single painted face: many of those 16 also touch a second or third outer face because they lie on that face's border, so the one-face count is smaller than the whole face total.

Exactly 24 small cubes carry one painted face: these are the small cubes filling the centre block of each of the big cube's six faces, sitting away from every edge and corner of the big cube — a set of 4 such cubes per face across all 6 faces.

This overshoots the one-face group by folding in a handful of cubes that actually sit along a seam between two painted faces; a cube touching two outer faces at once already carries two painted faces, so it cannot belong among the one-face cubes.

title: In KG team Chirag is taller than yash but not
subject: Reasoning
text: In a KG team Chirag is taller than yash but not as tall as akriti, Prashant is shorter than chirag but taller than Rupashi. Who among them is shortest?
solution:
Answer: The shortest person cannot be determined from the given information.

  • From the first statements: Akriti is taller than Chirag, and Chirag is taller than Yash. So: Akriti > Chirag > Yash.

  • From the second statement: Prashant is shorter than Chirag but taller than Rupashi. So: Chirag > Prashant > Rupashi.

  • Combining the known relations gives: Akriti > Chirag > Prashant > Rupashi, and Chirag > Yash. However, the relative order of Yash and Rupashi is not given.

  • Because there is no relation between Yash and Rupashi, either could be the shortest. Therefore the shortest person cannot be determined uniquely from the given information.

optionFeedback.html: Chirag cannot be the shortest because he is taller than Yash and also taller than Prashant (Prashant is described as shorter than Chirag). Therefore Chirag is not the shortest.
Akriti is taller than Chirag, so Akriti cannot be the shortest.
Yash is shorter than Chirag, but there is no information comparing Yash to Rupashi or to Prashant. Yash could be the shortest, but this is not certain from the given information.
The data is insufficient to identify a unique shortest person because there is no relation given between Yash and Rupashi; either could be the shortest.

title: Ravi is shorter than Kartik but taller than Gagan and
subject: Reasoning
text: Ravi is shorter than Kartik but taller than Gagan and Tarun, who are taller than Saksham. Sunil is taller than Aarav but shorter than Saksham. Who is the tallest of all?
solution:
Convert each statement into a height comparison (taller > shorter) and merge them into a single chain.

Statement 1: "Ravi is shorter than Kartik but taller than Gagan and Tarun" → Kartik > Ravi > Gagan, Tarun.

Statement 1 (continued): "…Gagan and Tarun, who are taller than Saksham" → Gagan, Tarun > Saksham.

Statement 2: "Sunil is taller than Aarav but shorter than Saksham" → Saksham > Sunil > Aarav.

Combined chain (tallest → shortest): Kartik > Ravi > Gagan/Tarun > Saksham > Sunil > Aarav.

Kartik sits at the top of the chain, so Kartik is the tallest of all.

optionFeedback.html: ❌ Incorrect. Aarav is taller than nobody in the group, which makes him the shortest, not the tallest.
❌ Incorrect. Tarun is shorter than Ravi (and therefore shorter than Kartik too), so he cannot be the tallest.
✅ Correct. Kartik is taller than Ravi, and Ravi is taller than everyone else mentioned, so Kartik sits at the very top of the chain.
❌ Incorrect. Gagan is shorter than Ravi (and therefore shorter than Kartik too), so he cannot be the tallest.

title: In row of boys, Vivek stands thirteenth from the left
subject: Reasoning
text: In a row of boys, Vivek stands thirteenth from the left and Ravi is thirteenth from the right. If they interchange their places, Ravi would be eighteenth from the right. How many boys are there in the row?
solution:
For any single seat in a row of people, if that seat is P-th from the left end, it is automatically (Total − P + 1)-th from the right end. Rearranged, this gives the identity: Total = (position from left) + (position from right) − 1 — because that one seat gets counted once from each direction, so the two counts overlap by exactly one.

Applying this to the row of boys:

  1. Vivek's original seat is 13th from the left.

  2. When Vivek and Ravi swap seats, Ravi moves into Vivek's original seat.

  3. The problem states that after the swap, Ravi (now in that seat) is 18th from the right — so Vivek's original seat is 18th from the right.

  4. That single seat is therefore both 13th from the left and 18th from the right, so by the identity: Total = 13 + 18 − 1 = 30.

Cross-check with the total of 30: Ravi's original seat was 13th from the right, which by the same identity is 30 − 13 + 1 = 18th from the left. After the swap, Vivek moves into that seat and becomes 18th from the left — consistent with a row of 30 boys.

So there are 30 boys in the row.

Vivek's position from the left (13) and Ravi's shifted position from the right (18) both describe the same seat in the row, counted from opposite ends; combining them and removing that single double-counted seat gives 30 boys in total.
This adds Vivek's original position and Ravi's shifted position directly, treating them as counts in two different rows rather than positions within the same one.

The smallest offset belongs to M, so M is the youngest of the four.

title: In row of boys, Sandeep is eleventh from the right
subject: Reasoning
text: In a row of boys, Sandeep is eleventh from the right and Deepak is also eleventh from the left. When Sandeep and Deepak interchange their positions, Deepak become seventeenth from the left. How many boys are there in the row?
solution:
Concept

In any single row of a fixed number of items, for any one position the count from the left plus the count from the right always equals the total number of items plus one: (rank from left) + (rank from right) = Total + 1. A useful corollary: when two people swap seats, each one simply inherits the other's exact seat, so the new rank of the mover equals the rank of the seat it moved into.

Application

  1. Sandeep sits at the seat that is 11th from the right end of the row.

  2. When Sandeep and Deepak swap, Deepak moves into Sandeep's seat, so Deepak now occupies the seat that is 11th from the right.

  3. We are told that in this new seat Deepak is 17th from the left. So this one seat is at the same time 17th from the left and 11th from the right.

  4. Apply the identity to that single seat: Total + 1 = (rank from left) + (rank from right) = 17 + 11 = 28.

  5. Therefore Total = 28 - 1 = 27 boys.

Cross-check

Independent check via Deepak's shift: Deepak started 11th from the left and ended 17th from the left, a move of 6 seats to the right. Sandeep was 11th from the right, i.e. (27 - 11 + 1) = 17th from the left, which is exactly where Deepak landed - and 17 is indeed 6 more than 11. The two methods agree, confirming a row of 27.

The overlap between a left-rank and a right-rank that point to the same seat should be accounted for only one time; double-discounting it distorts the line length.

This figure comes from blending positions that belong to different moments - mixing a person's seat before the interchange with the seat description that only holds after it - or from inserting seats that the statement never mentions. Only the two ranks that describe one identical seat at one identical moment may be combined.

It is also consistent with tracing the mover's seat directly onto the place vacated by the other boy, so the whole statement stays internally coherent for it.

This figure arises from a faulty conversion of a right-side rank into a left-side rank: it uses the plain difference from the total instead of the inclusive count that keeps the boundary seat. A rank counted from one end always includes the seat sitting at that very end, and treating the conversion as a bare subtraction drops that endpoint seat from the tally.

In a comparison (ranking) problem, every statement of the form "X is taller than Y" gives one directed link X > Y. Combine all links into a single chain by transitivity: if X > Y and Y > Z then X > Z. The person who has nobody above them is 1st; the person who has exactly one person above them is 2nd, and so on. title: If Akshay is 13th in the queue from either end

text: If Akshay is 13th in the queue from either end then, how many people are there in the queue?
solution:
When a person's rank is known from both the front and the back of a line, the total number of people in the line equals the sum of the two ranks minus one. This is because that person occupies one shared spot that both counts include, so a plain sum of the two ranks would count that person twice.

  1. Let Akshay's position from the front = 13 and his position from the back = 13, since he is stated to be 13th from either end.

  2. Apply the identity: Total people = (position from front) + (position from back) minus 1.

  3. Substitute the values: Total = 13 + 13 minus 1.

  4. Compute the total: Total = 25.

Cross-check: in a queue of 25 people, if Akshay is 13th counted from the front, his position counted from the back is Total minus (position from front) plus 1, i.e. 25 minus 13 plus 1 = 13, which matches the given condition exactly, confirming the queue has 25 people.

So there are 25 people in the queue.

title: In an exam, Hiral scored more marks than Jaya. Kiara
subject: Reasoning
text: In an exam, Hiral scored more marks than Jaya. Kiara has less marks than Zubin. Latika has as much marks as Jaya. John has more marks than Hiral. What conclusion can definitely be drawn from the above statements?
solution:
In a 'which conclusion definitely follows' reasoning item, two people's marks can be compared with certainty only when a chain of stated greater-than or equal-to relations directly connects them. If two people are each linked only to different individuals, and those separate chains never meet, no relation between the two can be fixed -- concluding one would require an assumption the statements never make.

  1. From 'Hiral scored more marks than Jaya': Hiral is greater than Jaya.

  2. From 'John has more marks than Hiral': John is greater than Hiral, so combined with the previous step, John is greater than Hiral, and Hiral is greater than Jaya.

  3. From 'Latika has as much marks as Jaya': Latika equals Jaya. Substituting Latika for Jaya in the chain gives Hiral is greater than Latika directly.

  4. Separately, 'Kiara has less marks than Zubin' gives Zubin is greater than Kiara -- a second, standalone relation that touches none of Hiral, Jaya, Latika, or John.

Two disconnected groups now exist: Group 1 links John, Hiral, Jaya and Latika (John greater than Hiral, Hiral greater than Jaya, Jaya equal to Latika); Group 2 links Zubin and Kiara (Zubin greater than Kiara) only. Since the two groups share no common person, any comparison that crosses between them -- Zubin against John, Jaya against Kiara, or Kiara against Latika -- is left open by the statements and cannot be fixed either way.

The only relation that is forced by the statements, without crossing between the two groups, is that Hiral has more marks than Latika -- equivalently, Latika has lesser marks than Hiral.

This assumes Jaya and Kiara can be ranked against each other, but Kiara is only compared with Zubin in the statements, and that comparison is never linked to Jaya's -- so no certain relation between them can be drawn.

Latika's marks equal Jaya's, and Hiral's marks exceed Jaya's, so Hiral's marks must exceed Latika's as well -- this follows directly by chaining the two given statements, without needing any extra assumption.

title: In row of girls, Nayana is 15th from the left
subject: Reasoning
text: In a row of girls, Nayana is 15th from the left and Sumana is 23rd from the right. If they interchange their positions, then Nayana becomes 18th from the left then at what position will Sumana be from the right?
solution:
For a row of n people, a person's rank from the left (L) and rank from the right (R) at the same seat always satisfy L + R = n + 1.

When two people interchange seats, each one's new rank (from either end) equals the other person's old rank at that exact seat — the row itself does not change, only who occupies which seat.

  1. Nayana's original rank from the left was 15th. After interchanging seats with Sumana, Nayana's new rank from the left is given as 18th. Since Nayana now sits in Sumana's original seat, this new rank equals Sumana's original rank from the left. So Sumana's original rank from the left = 18th.

  2. Sumana's original rank from the right is given as 23rd. Applying L + R = n + 1 to Sumana's original seat: 18 + 23 = n + 1, so n = 40 girls are in the row.

  3. After interchanging, Sumana sits in Nayana's original seat, whose rank from the left was 15th. So Sumana's new rank from the left = 15th.

  4. Converting to a rank from the right using n = 40: R = n + 1 − L = 41 − 15 = 26th.

Check: with n = 40, Nayana's original seat (15th from the left) is also (41 − 15) = 26th from the right, and her new seat (18th from the left) is also (41 − 18) = 23rd from the right — Sumana's original rank, exactly as given. Both interchanged ranks line up, confirming Sumana's new position is 26th from the right.

This follows from adding Nayana's original rank from the left (15th) directly to Sumana's original rank from the right (23rd), as if the two numbers already described the same seat in the row — they belong to two different girls' two different original seats, and combining them this way gives the wrong headcount for the row.

After the interchange, Sumana occupies the exact seat Nayana held before the swap. Converting that seat's rank from the left into a rank from the right, using the row's actual total worked out from Sumana's own original left- and right-end ranks, places her here.

This follows from carrying the change in Nayana's rank from the left straight over to Sumana's rank from the right, as if a shift measured from one end of the row applies the same way when measured from the opposite end. title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2014 Q8

When a person's position is counted as r1 from one end of a line-up and r2 from the other end, the total number of people in that line-up equals r1 + r2 - 1 — the person occupying that single position is counted once from each direction, so one count must be removed to avoid double-counting them.
